Tissue factor's dark side appears when it shows up where it should not: inflamed monocytes can express it inside the bloodstream in sepsis, and many cancers express it, contributing respectively to the runaway clotting of disseminated intravascular coagulation and to the thrombosis risk of malignancy.

sections.heading: The Common Pathway: Thrombin, Fibrinogen and Fibrin
sections.body:
Both tributaries converge on factor X, and from there a single sequence, the common pathway, carries the process to a finished clot. Activated factor X, Xa, assembles on the phospholipid surface of activated platelets with calcium and its cofactor, activated factor V, forming the prothrombinase complex. The cofactor's contribution is staggering: prothrombinase converts prothrombin to thrombin some hundreds of thousands of times faster than factor Xa working alone, another illustration of the cascade's central design principle, that enzymes in this system work meaningfully only as membrane-anchored teams. Prothrombin, factor II, is the most abundant of the zymogens, and its conversion releases thrombin, factor IIa, the undisputed protagonist of coagulation.

Thrombin is a serine protease with an agenda rather than a single job. Its headline act is cutting fibrinogen. Fibrinogen is a large, soluble, elongated protein, present in plasma at a gram-and-a-half to four grams per liter, built of two symmetrical halves with sticky regions masked by short acidic peptide caps. Thrombin snips off these caps, the fibrinopeptides A and B, and the trimmed molecule, now called fibrin monomer, spontaneously self-assembles: monomers stack half-staggered into two-stranded protofibrils, protofibrils bundle laterally into fibers, and fibers branch into a three-dimensional gel. Within moments the wound is filled with a web of fibrin strands entangling platelets, red cells and plasma, the visible clot. The initial mesh, however, is held only by physical fits, and can be redissolved by mild chemical insult. Permanence is the work of factor XIII, itself activated by thrombin, which forges covalent bonds between adjacent fibrin strands, cross-linking the gel into a resilient elastic polymer. Factor XIII deficiency produces a telltale story: normal initial clotting with delayed re-bleeding hours or days later, and classically poor wound healing, because the clot forms but cannot hold.

Beyond fibrin, thrombin drives virtually every loop in the system. It is the most potent physiological platelet activator, working through the protease-activated receptors PAR-1 and PAR-4, so the enzyme born on platelet surfaces recruits more platelets. It activates the cofactors V and VIII and the protease XI, the feedback triad that converts the initial spark into the full thrombin burst, as the cell-based model details. It activates factor XIII to weld the mesh, and it activates TAFI, a fibrinolysis inhibitor that makes the finished clot harder to dissolve. And in one of physiology's best twists, thrombin that escapes the wound and touches healthy endothelium is captured by thrombomodulin and converted into an anticoagulant, activating protein C to shut the cascade down, a mechanism covered with the other brakes.

The common pathway is where the two classical laboratory tests overlap: deficiencies of factors X, V, prothrombin or fibrinogen prolong both the PT and the aPTT, which is the logic clinicians use when reading the test pair. It is also rich drug territory. Heparin works by supercharging antithrombin's destruction of thrombin and Xa; the direct oral anticoagulants divide between Xa inhibitors, rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban, whose generic names embed the xa, and the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran. Finally, thrombin explains the old practice of applying topical thrombin powder to surgical bleeding, and fibrin explains fibrin glue, the surgical sealant that is simply the last step of the cascade packaged in a syringe: fibrinogen in one barrel, thrombin in the other, a clot on demand where the two meet.

sections.heading: The Cell-Based Model: How Clotting Really Happens in the Body
sections.body:
The waterfall diagram of two independent pathways, published in coherent form in 1964 by Macfarlane in one journal and Davie and Ratnoff in another, organized a generation of discoveries and still governs how laboratory tests are interpreted. But it never quite matched the clinic. If the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways were genuinely parallel routes to factor X, either alone should suffice, yet hemophiliacs, missing only the intrinsic factors VIII or IX, bleed catastrophically despite a perfect extrinsic pathway, while factor XII–deficient patients, whose intrinsic pathway cannot even start in a test tube, do not bleed at all. In the 1990s and early 2000s, work led by Maureane Hoffman and Dougald Monroe reframed coagulation as a process organized not by pathways in solution but by cell surfaces, unfolding in three overlapping phases: initiation, amplification and propagation. The cell-based model is now the standard picture of hemostasis in the body.

Initiation happens on the tissue factor–bearing cell, a fibroblast or smooth muscle cell exposed by injury. Factor VIIa binds tissue factor and generates small amounts of factors Xa and IXa; Xa with factor Va makes a first pinch of thrombin, only a few molecules' worth, far too little to clot fibrinogen at any useful scale. TFPI and antithrombin quench the reaction quickly, and any Xa that drifts off the cell is destroyed almost at once, though factor IXa, more resistant, can diffuse to nearby platelets. The output of initiation is best understood as a signal, not a product: a priming dose of thrombin released at the boundary of the wound.

Amplification is what that priming thrombin does when it reaches the platelets already adhering to the wound. In a burst of feedback, thrombin activates the platelets fully through their PAR receptors, activates factor XI on the platelet surface, activates factor V released from platelet granules, and cleaves factor VIII free of its carrier, von Willebrand factor, activating it too. In seconds, the platelet plug is transformed from passive scrum into a primed factory floor: activated platelets displaying phosphatidylserine, studded with the activated cofactors Va and VIIIa, with XIa stationed to make more IXa on site.

Propagation then delivers the payload. On the platelet surface, factor IXa, arriving from initiation and freshly minted by XIa, joins VIIIa to form intrinsic tenase, which manufactures Xa in quantity exactly where prothrombinase can capture it; Xa pairs with Va and generates the thrombin burst, a concentration of thrombin hundreds of times greater than initiation produced, sufficient to flash-convert fibrinogen to fibrin throughout the plug, activate XIII, trigger TAFI and consolidate a durable clot. The model dissolves the old paradoxes cleanly. Hemophilia is catastrophic because without VIII or IX there is no platelet-surface tenase and therefore no burst: initiation still fires, a wispy initial clot forms, but it cannot be consolidated, which matches the hemophiliac pattern of delayed, deep re-bleeding rather than prolonged surface oozing. Factor XII is dispensable because the body's XI activation is thrombin's job, not contact activation's. And the model explains why clotting stays put: the machinery runs only on activated platelet membranes, which exist only at the wound, while intact neighboring endothelium actively dismantles any escaping enzymes. Coagulation, in the modern picture, is not plumbing but geography: the right reactions confined to the right surfaces.

sections.heading: Keeping Clotting in Check: Antithrombin, Protein C and Protein S
sections.body:
A system built to amplify a molecular whisper into an avalanche needs brakes at least as powerful as its engine, and the anticoagulant machinery is exactly that: a set of always-on damping systems that confine the avalanche to the wound and stop it when the job is done. Quantitatively, the most important brake is antithrombin, a plasma protein of the serpin family that works as a suicide trap: it dangles a bait loop that proteases attack, and the act of biting springs the trap, locking enzyme and inhibitor into an inert complex that the liver clears. Antithrombin neutralizes thrombin and factor Xa above all, with side business against IXa, XIa and XIIa. On its own it works slowly, which is by design; the accelerant is heparan sulfate, the whisker-like molecules coating healthy endothelium, which bind antithrombin and contort it into a spring-loaded configuration roughly a thousand times faster. The drug heparin is simply this accelerant in injectable form, purified from animal tissue: unfractionated heparin promotes destruction of both thrombin and Xa, while the low-molecular-weight heparins, enoxaparin and its relatives, are trimmed chains too short to bridge antithrombin to thrombin and therefore act mainly on Xa. This mechanism explains a practical point: heparin cannot work without adequate antithrombin, so patients with antithrombin deficiency can be mysteriously resistant to it. Inherited antithrombin deficiency, first described by Egeberg in 1965, is rare but carries the highest thrombosis risk of the classic inherited thrombophilias.

The second great brake is the protein C system, and it runs on a beautiful inversion: it uses thrombin itself as the off switch. Healthy endothelium displays thrombomodulin, a receptor that captures free thrombin drifting beyond the wound. Bound to thrombomodulin, thrombin's personality changes completely: it can no longer cut fibrinogen or activate platelets, and instead becomes an efficient activator of protein C, a vitamin K–dependent plasma zymogen, a reaction further concentrated by the endothelial protein C receptor. Activated protein C, working with its cofactor protein S, then destroys the cascade's two accelerator pedals, the activated cofactors Va and VIIIa, by cutting them at specific sites. The geography is the genius: in the middle of a wound, where endothelium is absent, thrombin clots; at the healthy margins, where thrombomodulin abounds, the same molecule dismantles the machine that made it. Clotting is thereby self-limiting in space, fading out precisely where the vessel lining resumes.

The third brake, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, TFPI, was described with the ignition system: it caps the tissue factor spark moments after firing, ensuring that sustained clotting requires the platelet-surface propagation machinery rather than a continuously burning trigger.

The clinical mirror image of each brake confirms its importance. Deficiencies of protein C or protein S cause familial thrombosis; the most common inherited thrombophilia of all, factor V Leiden, discussed later, is a mutation that makes factor Va resist activated protein C's scissors. Homozygous protein C deficiency produces neonatal purpura fulminans, a lethal storm of microvascular clotting in newborns. And warfarin therapy carries a famous trap: because protein C is vitamin K dependent and has a short half-life of around eight hours, starting warfarin can depress the brake before the engine, transiently tipping the balance toward clotting, the mechanism behind warfarin-induced skin necrosis and the reason warfarin is overlapped with heparin at initiation. In sepsis, inflammation strips thrombomodulin and heparan sulfate from endothelium, disabling two brakes at once, which is part of why severe infection so often derails coagulation.

sections.heading: Fibrinolysis: How the Body Dissolves a Clot
sections.body:
A clot is scaffolding, not architecture; once the vessel wall has repaired itself beneath it, the fibrin must go, and vessels plugged in error must be reopened. Fibrinolysis is the demolition system, and it mirrors coagulation's design: an inert plasma zymogen, plasminogen, converted at the right place and time into a powerful protease, plasmin, which digests fibrin into fragments, with activators, inhibitors and clever surface chemistry confining the destruction to its target. Plasminogen, made in the liver and abundant in plasma, has a crucial habit: it binds to lysine residues in fibrin as the clot forms, so every clot is built with its own demolition charges embedded. The principal detonator is tissue plasminogen activator, tPA, released steadily and upon stimulation by endothelial cells. Free tPA in plasma is a feeble enzyme, but on a fibrin surface, tPA and plasminogen dock side by side and the reaction accelerates enormously; fibrin is thus the cofactor for its own destruction, a design that aims plasmin almost exclusively at clots rather than at circulating fibrinogen. A second activator, urokinase, works in tissues and ducts. Plasmin chews the cross-linked mesh into soluble fibrin degradation products, among them a fragment called D-dimer, two cross-linked D domains that can only exist if a cross-linked clot was formed and then dissolved. That biochemical fingerprint is the basis of one of the most used tests in emergency medicine: a negative D-dimer makes recent significant clotting, as in deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, very unlikely, while a positive result is nonspecific, since surgery, pregnancy, infection and age all raise it.

The brakes on fibrinolysis are as layered as the brakes on clotting. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, PAI-1, neutralizes tPA in plasma; alpha-2 antiplasmin instantly quenches any plasmin that escapes the clot surface, and is itself stitched into the clot by factor XIII so the mesh resists digestion from within; and TAFI, activated by the thrombin–thrombomodulin complex, prunes the exposed lysines off fibrin, stripping the docking sites plasminogen and tPA need. The finished clot's lifespan is thus a negotiated settlement between welders and cutters, tuned so that hemostatic plugs persist for the days a vessel needs to heal while stray fibrin is cleared promptly.

Medicine has learned to push this system in both directions. Pushing forward, thrombolytic therapy administers recombinant tPA, alteplase and successors such as tenecteplase, to dissolve clots that are actively killing tissue: within the treatment window in ischemic stroke, in massive pulmonary embolism, and historically in heart attack before catheter-based artery opening became standard. The bleeding risk is the mechanism's shadow: enough plasmin activity to clear a cerebral artery can also dissolve the useful clot sealing a stomach ulcer. Streptokinase, a bacterial plasminogen activator from streptococci, was the first thrombolytic and is a reminder that bacteria evolved clot-dissolving tools to spread through tissue. Pushing the other way, antifibrinolytic drugs, above all tranexamic acid, a synthetic lysine lookalike that blinds plasminogen by occupying its lysine-binding sites, stabilize clots when bleeding is the enemy. The landmark CRASH-2 trial, published in 2010 with over twenty thousand trauma patients, showed that early tranexamic acid reduces death from bleeding, and the drug is now carried in ambulances, used in postpartum hemorrhage and major surgery, and taken in tablet form for heavy menstrual bleeding.

sections.heading: When Clotting Fails: Hemophilia, von Willebrand Disease and Low Platelets
sections.body:
Bleeding disorders sort themselves by which arm of hemostasis is broken, and the sorting shows in the pattern of bleeding. Failures of primary hemostasis, platelets or von Willebrand factor, produce surface bleeding: easy bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, and pinpoint skin hemorrhages called petechiae. Failures of secondary hemostasis, the clotting factors, produce deep bleeding: into joints and muscles, delayed re-bleeding after injury or surgery, and dangerous internal hemorrhage, because the platelet plug forms normally but cannot be consolidated with cross-linked fibrin.

Hemophilia is the archetype of factor failure. Hemophilia A is deficiency of factor VIII and affects roughly one in five thousand male births; hemophilia B, deficiency of factor IX, sometimes called Christmas disease after Stephen Christmas, the boy in whom it was characterized in 1952, is about one-fifth as common. Both are X-linked recessive, carried by mothers and expressed almost exclusively in sons, and both are graded by residual factor activity: severe disease, under one percent activity, brings spontaneous bleeding into knees, ankles and elbows, which untreated destroys the joints over years. History's most famous carrier was Queen Victoria, whose son Leopold died of hemorrhage and whose granddaughters carried factor IX deficiency into the Spanish, German and Russian royal houses, most fatefully to Alexei, heir to the Russian throne. Treatment has traveled an extraordinary arc: from plasma, to cryoprecipitate in the 1960s, to freeze-dried factor concentrates that made home treatment possible, through the catastrophe of the late 1970s and 1980s when pooled-plasma concentrates transmitted HIV and hepatitis C to a large fraction of the world's hemophiliacs, to recombinant factors in the 1990s, and now to weekly or monthly prophylaxis, the bispecific antibody emicizumab that substitutes for factor VIII's bridging job, and approved gene therapies that have freed some adults from infusions entirely.

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder of all, with laboratory abnormalities detectable in something like one percent of the population, though far fewer are symptomatic. Because von Willebrand factor both glues platelets to wounds and carries factor VIII in plasma, its deficiency straddles both arms of hemostasis, but the usual picture is mucosal: nosebleeds, bruising and heavy periods, often unrecognized for years. Most cases are mild quantitative deficiency, type 1, managed when needed with desmopressin, a hormone analog that squeezes stored von Willebrand factor out of endothelial cells, or with factor concentrates for the rarer severe types.

Platelet disorders complete the picture. Thrombocytopenia, a low platelet count, becomes clinically risky as counts fall below fifty thousand per microliter for surgery and below ten to twenty thousand for spontaneous bleeding. Its causes divide into underproduction, marrow suppression by chemotherapy, leukemia or B12 deficiency; sequestration in an enlarged spleen; and destruction, as in immune thrombocytopenia, where antibodies clear platelets, or the drug reaction heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which paradoxically causes clotting. Qualitative platelet defects exist too, from the rare inherited absences of the key receptors, Glanzmann thrombasthenia lacking IIb/IIIa and Bernard–Soulier syndrome lacking Ib, to the everyday acquired defect of aspirin. Finally, liver failure and vitamin K deficiency reproduce factor deficiency without any genetics, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, the runaway activation of clotting in sepsis or obstetric catastrophe, bleeds precisely because it clots: the system consumes its own factors and platelets faster than they can be replaced.

sections.heading: When Clotting Goes Too Far: Thrombosis, DVT and Pulmonary Embolism
sections.body:
Thrombosis is clotting in the wrong place: a thrombus is a clot formed inside an intact vessel, and it kills more people worldwide than any other single mechanism, since heart attacks and most strokes are, at the final step, arterial thromboses. The intellectual frame for why clots form dates to the German pathologist Rudolf Virchow, whose name attaches to the triad of predisposing conditions: changes in the vessel wall, changes in blood flow, and changes in the blood's composition. The triad still organizes clinical thinking. Arterial thrombosis is mostly a wall problem: an atherosclerotic plaque ruptures, exposing its lipid core and tissue factor, and platelets pile onto it exactly as they would onto a wound, occluding the artery; this is why arterial disease is treated with antiplatelet drugs like aspirin. Venous thrombosis is mostly a flow-and-blood problem: in the deep veins of the legs, especially in the pockets behind venous valves, sluggish flow lets activated factors accumulate, and fibrin-rich red clots grow without any plaque at all; this is why venous disease is treated with anticoagulants.

Deep vein thrombosis, DVT, classically presents as a swollen, warm, aching calf or thigh, though it can be silent. Its notorious danger is embolization: a fragment breaks free, rides the venous return through the right heart, and lodges in the pulmonary arteries as a pulmonary embolism, PE, blocking blood flow through the lungs. A large PE causes sudden breathlessness, chest pain, collapse and, in the worst cases, death within minutes; small ones may cause only unexplained breathlessness or a fast heart rate. Together DVT and PE, called venous thromboembolism, affect on the order of one to two people per thousand each year, and PE remains one of the leading preventable causes of hospital death, which is why modern hospitals assess essentially every inpatient for clot-prevention measures, from early mobilization and compression stockings to prophylactic heparin doses.

The risk factors read directly off Virchow's triad. Stasis: surgery, especially hip and knee replacement, plaster casts, paralysis, long-haul immobility, hospitalization itself. Blood composition: cancer, which secretes tissue factor and procoagulants; pregnancy and the weeks after delivery; estrogen-containing contraceptives and hormone therapy; dehydration; and the inherited thrombophilias. Chief among the inherited causes is factor V Leiden, a single-letter mutation described in 1994 in Leiden, the Netherlands, which alters the site where activated protein C cuts factor Va, making the accelerator pedal resistant to the brake; roughly five percent of people of European ancestry carry one copy, which raises venous clot risk several-fold, while two copies raise it dramatically. The prothrombin G20210A variant, and the rarer deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S, complete the usual panel. Wall injury: trauma, indwelling catheters and previous DVT, which scars valves and begets stasis.

Diagnosis leans on probability scoring, the D-dimer test to rule out, and imaging to rule in: compression ultrasound for leg veins and CT pulmonary angiography for the lungs. Treatment is anticoagulation, typically for three months or longer depending on whether the clot was provoked by a passing cause, and the drugs themselves, from heparin bridges to warfarin to the direct oral agents, are the subject of the final section. The public health message hiding in the biology is unglamorous but real: hydration, movement on long journeys, prompt attention to a swollen leg, and taking prescribed prophylaxis seriously after surgery prevent a substantial share of these deaths.

sections.heading: Testing and Treating: PT, INR, aPTT and Blood-Thinning Drugs
sections.body:
The laboratory sees coagulation through a handful of tests, each a window on part of the machine. The platelet count, part of every complete blood count, checks the raw material of primary hemostasis. The prothrombin time, PT, fires the extrinsic trigger, tissue factor, into citrated plasma and times the clot, normally roughly eleven to thirteen and a half seconds; it is sensitive to factors VII, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen, and because reagents differ between laboratories, results for patients on warfarin are reported as the international normalized ratio, INR, standardized so that 1.0 is normal everywhere and the usual therapeutic window is 2.0 to 3.0. The activated partial thromboplastin time, aPTT, fires the contact trigger instead, is normally in the vicinity of twenty-five to thirty-five seconds, screens the intrinsic and common factors, XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen, and monitors unfractionated heparin. Reading the pair is a diagnostic algorithm in itself: isolated long PT points at factor VII, early warfarin or early liver disease; isolated long aPTT points at hemophilia, von Willebrand disease with low factor VIII, heparin, or the clinically silent factor XII deficiency; both prolonged points at the common pathway, high-dose anticoagulation, severe liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation. Fibrinogen can be measured directly, D-dimer tracks clot turnover, specific factor assays quantify individual deficiencies, and a mixing study, blending patient plasma with normal plasma, distinguishes a missing factor, which corrects, from an inhibitor such as an antibody, which does not. Viscoelastic tests such as thromboelastography watch a whole clot form and dissolve in real time and guide transfusion in trauma and cardiac surgery.

The drug cabinet maps onto the biology just as neatly. Antiplatelet drugs serve arterial disease: aspirin permanently disables platelet cyclooxygenase and thus thromboxane production; the P2Y12 inhibitors, clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor, block the ADP amplification loop and are paired with aspirin after coronary stents. Anticoagulants serve venous disease, atrial fibrillation and mechanical valves. Unfractionated heparin, discovered in 1916 by the medical student Jay McLean, works instantly by supercharging antithrombin, is given intravenously, monitored by aPTT, and can be reversed with protamine; its trimmed derivatives, the low-molecular-weight heparins such as enoxaparin, target factor Xa preferentially, inject subcutaneously with predictable dosing, and made outpatient DVT treatment routine. Warfarin, developed from the moldy sweet clover that caused cattle to bleed in the 1920s and introduced to medicine in the 1950s, blocks vitamin K recycling and so starves the liver of working factors II, VII, IX and X; it is cheap and effective but slow, food- and drug-interacting, and INR-monitored for life, and it remains essential for mechanical heart valves. The direct oral anticoagulants, introduced from 2010, inhibit a single enzyme apiece: dabigatran binds thrombin, while rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban bind factor Xa. They need no routine monitoring and, in the trials that established them, matched or beat warfarin for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation with less brain hemorrhage; specific antidotes now exist, idarucizumab for dabigatran and andexanet alfa for the Xa inhibitors, alongside vitamin K and factor concentrates for warfarin. Every one of these drugs is a controlled injury to a system this guide has described, and the universal price is bleeding risk, which is why dosing, monitoring and never adjusting these medicines without a prescriber are not fine print but the core of their safe use.

guides.safetyNote: This guide explains the biology of blood clotting for education; it is not medical advice and cannot replace a clinician. Uncontrolled or heavy bleeding, bleeding that will not stop with firm direct pressure, signs of a deep vein clot such as a swollen painful leg, or sudden chest pain and breathlessness that could mean a clot in the lungs are emergencies: apply direct pressure to external bleeding and call emergency services. Never start, stop or change a dose of any blood-thinning medicine such as warfarin, heparin or the newer anticoagulants except on a prescriber's instruction, because both bleeding and clotting can be fatal.

guides.title: How Blood Circulates Through the Body
guides.summary: A complete account of the human circulatory system: how the heart pumps, how the pulmonary and systemic circuits are wired, what happens in arteries, capillaries and veins, and how pressure, flow and blood distribution are controlled second by second. It closes with the ways circulation fails and what those failures look like.

sections.heading: Why the Body Needs a Circulation at All
sections.body: Every cell in a human body burns fuel and produces waste, and every cell must exchange those materials with its surroundings. In a single-celled organism this is trivial: oxygen and glucose simply wander in by diffusion and carbon dioxide wanders out. Diffusion is fast over microscopic distances and catastrophically slow over large ones, because the time it takes scales roughly with the square of the distance. Oxygen crosses one hundredth of a millimetre in about a twentieth of a second. To cross a single centimetre by diffusion alone would take on the order of several hours, and to cross the width of a thigh would take days. A human being is roughly a hundred thousand times thicker than the distance diffusion can service in useful time, so an animal of any size that relied on diffusion alone would suffocate in its own core. The circulatory system is the engineering answer to that constraint. Rather than waiting for molecules to wander, the body moves the fluid they are dissolved in, using bulk flow driven by a pump. Blood is pushed out to within roughly a tenth of a millimetre of nearly every living cell, which brings the diffusion distance back down to the scale at which diffusion is quick again. Circulation therefore does not replace diffusion; it shortens the distance over which diffusion has to work. Every exchange that actually matters, at the lung and at the tissue, still happens by passive diffusion across a thin membrane. The pump and the plumbing exist only to keep delivering fresh fluid to those membranes. What travels in that fluid is far more than oxygen. Blood carries glucose, fatty acids and amino acids from the gut and liver; carbon dioxide, urea, creatinine and lactate away to lung, kidney and liver; hormones from ductless glands to distant targets; white cells and antibodies to sites of infection; platelets and clotting proteins to sites of injury; and heat from the deep organs out to the skin, which is how a working muscle avoids cooking itself. A resting adult moves roughly five litres of blood every minute, which is close to the entire blood volume, so the average red cell completes a full lap of the body about once a minute at rest and three or four times a minute during hard exercise. Over a seventy-year lifetime the heart beats something like two and a half billion times and moves on the order of two hundred million litres. The system is best understood as a closed loop of tubes containing a pump, a set of distribution pipes, an enormous mesh of exchange vessels, and a set of collection pipes returning to the pump. Understanding circulation means understanding what each of those four parts contributes, and what happens to pressure and flow as blood passes through them.

sections.heading: The Heart as a Pump: Chambers, Valves and Great Vessels
sections.body: The human heart is a fist-sized muscular organ weighing roughly 250 to 350 grams, sitting in the middle of the chest behind the sternum and tilted so that its tip, the apex, points down and to the left. It is not one pump but two, laid side by side and beating together. The right heart receives blood returning from the body and sends it to the lungs. The left heart receives blood returning from the lungs and sends it to the body. A muscular wall called the septum separates them, and in a normal adult heart there is no communication between the two sides. Each side has two chambers. The atrium is a thin-walled receiving chamber; the ventricle beneath it is the thick-walled ejecting chamber. Blood enters the right atrium from the superior vena cava draining the head and arms, the inferior vena cava draining the trunk and legs, and the coronary sinus draining the heart's own muscle. It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then out through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery, which divides to the two lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through four pulmonary veins into the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta. The valves are passive. None of them is muscular and none is opened or closed by a nerve; each simply flaps shut when pressure behind it exceeds pressure in front. The two atrioventricular valves, tricuspid on the right and mitral on the left, have thin leaflets tethered by fine tendinous cords to papillary muscles projecting from the ventricular wall. Those cords do not pull the valve shut; they stop it from everting backwards into the atrium when ventricular pressure rises, in the same way that the stays of an umbrella stop it blowing inside out. The two semilunar valves, pulmonary and aortic, are three-cupped pockets that fill and balloon shut the moment forward flow stops. The two ventricles are strikingly unequal in build. The left ventricular wall is typically 8 to 12 millimetres thick, the right only 3 to 5, because the left must generate roughly 120 millimetres of mercury of pressure to drive blood around the whole body while the right needs only about 25 to push blood through the low-resistance lungs. Yet both eject the same volume with each beat, roughly 70 millilitres at rest, because they sit in series in a closed loop; any sustained mismatch would empty one circuit and flood the other within a minute. This obligatory equality of output between the two sides, despite a fivefold difference in pressure and workload, is one of the defining facts of cardiac physiology and explains why a failing left ventricle eventually backs blood up into the lungs.

sections.heading: Two Circuits in Series: Pulmonary and Systemic
sections.body: The circulation is a single closed loop folded into two circuits arranged one after the other. The pulmonary circuit runs right ventricle to lungs to left atrium. The systemic circuit runs left ventricle to body to right atrium. Because they are in series, every millilitre of blood must pass through both in turn, and it is impossible for the body to be perfused with blood that has not just been through the lungs. Tracing a single red cell makes the geography concrete. Suppose it starts in the right atrium, having arrived from a toe. It crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle and is ejected into the pulmonary artery, which branches down to pulmonary capillaries lying in the wall of the air sacs. There it picks up oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide across a barrier only about half a micrometre thick. It returns to the left atrium, drops into the left ventricle, and is thrown into the aorta. From the aorta it may take any one of thousands of branching paths: up the carotid to the brain, down the coeliac trunk to the stomach, off the renal artery to a kidney, or all the way down the aorta into the leg. Whichever it takes, it will pass through one capillary bed, then be collected into venules and veins and returned to the right atrium to begin again. The important exception to the one-capillary-bed rule is the portal circulations, where blood passes through two capillary beds in series before returning to the heart. The hepatic portal system is the largest: blood draining the intestines, stomach, pancreas and spleen does not go straight back to the heart but is collected into the portal vein and delivered to the liver, so everything absorbed from food is inspected and processed before it reaches the rest of the body. A smaller hypophyseal portal system carries releasing hormones from the hypothalamus directly to the pituitary. A third, in the kidney, carries blood from the glomerular capillaries into a second network around the tubules. The two circuits also differ profoundly in their pressures and their purpose. The systemic circuit is a high-pressure distribution system, averaging around 93 to 100 millimetres of mercury in the aorta, because it must push blood uphill to the brain, through many parallel organs, and against considerable resistance. The pulmonary circuit is a low-pressure system, averaging about 15 millimetres of mercury, because the lungs sit right next to the heart, offer very low resistance, and because high pressure would force fluid out of the capillaries into the air sacs and drown the patient. That deliberate low pressure is why the right ventricle is thin, and why any disease that raises pulmonary pressure strains the right heart specifically.

sections.heading: The Cardiac Cycle: One Beat, Step by Step
sections.body: A heartbeat is a repeating cycle of contraction, called systole, and relaxation, called diastole. At a resting rate of 75 beats per minute the whole cycle lasts 0.8 seconds, of which roughly 0.3 seconds is ventricular systole and 0.5 seconds is diastole. That ratio matters enormously: the heart muscle is fed only during diastole, so anything that shortens diastole, above all a fast heart rate, squeezes the heart's own blood supply. The cycle is easiest to follow as a sequence of pressure crossings. During late diastole both atria and ventricles are relaxed, the atrioventricular valves hang open, and blood coasts passively from the great veins straight through the atria into the ventricles. Roughly 70 to 80 per cent of ventricular filling happens this way, without any atrial contraction at all. The atria then contract, topping the ventricles up with the remaining 20 to 30 per cent, the so-called atrial kick. This is why a person can lose organised atrial contraction entirely, as in atrial fibrillation, and still survive, though they lose that final increment of filling and may feel it badly during exertion. The ventricles then depolarise and contract. Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut, and the first heart sound is produced. For a brief interval, roughly 50 milliseconds, all four valves are closed and the ventricle contracts without shortening, squeezing an incompressible volume of blood: this is isovolumetric contraction, and pressure climbs steeply. When left ventricular pressure passes aortic pressure, about 80 millimetres of mercury in a resting adult, the aortic valve opens and ejection begins. Pressure peaks around 120 millimetres of mercury, the ventricle empties most of its stroke volume in the first third of ejection, and flow then tails off. As the muscle begins to relax, ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, blood momentarily tries to flow backwards, and the aortic and pulmonary valves shut, producing the second heart sound. A small notch appears on the aortic pressure trace at that instant, the dicrotic notch. Another brief all-valves-closed period follows, isovolumetric relaxation, during which pressure plummets without any change in volume. When ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure the atrioventricular valves reopen and filling begins again. The numbers attached to this cycle are worth memorising because clinicians reason with them constantly. End-diastolic volume, the fullest the ventricle gets, is about 120 millilitres. End-systolic volume, what is left after ejection, is about 50 millilitres. The difference, the stroke volume, is about 70 millilitres. The fraction ejected, 70 divided by 120, is the ejection fraction, normally 55 to 70 per cent. Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, so 70 millilitres times 75 beats gives about 5.25 litres per minute at rest, rising to 20 or even 35 litres per minute in a trained athlete at maximum effort.

sections.heading: The Electrical System That Sets the Rhythm
sections.body: Cardiac muscle does not wait for a nerve to tell it to beat. The heart contains its own pacemaker tissue and will beat steadily in a dish, or in a transplanted chest with every nerve to it cut. The nervous system modulates the rate but does not create it. This property, automaticity, arises because certain cells have leaky membranes that drift slowly upward in voltage until they reach a threshold and fire, then repolarise and begin drifting again. The fastest of these sits in the wall of the right atrium near the entry of the superior vena cava: the sinoatrial node, discovered by Arthur Keith and Martin Flack in 1907. It drifts to threshold about 60 to 100 times a minute and therefore sets the pace for the whole organ, a principle called overdrive suppression, in which the fastest pacemaker captures all the slower ones. If the sinoatrial node fails, the atrioventricular junction takes over at 40 to 60 beats per minute, and if that fails the ventricular conducting tissue produces an unreliable 20 to 40. Those escape rhythms are the reason a person with complete heart block is often conscious but exhausted rather than instantly dead. From the sinoatrial node the impulse spreads across both atria through the muscle itself, making them contract, and converges on the atrioventricular node in the floor of the right atrium. This node is the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles; a ring of fibrous tissue insulates them everywhere else. The atrioventricular node conducts deliberately slowly, imposing a delay of roughly 0.1 second. That delay is functional, not a flaw: it gives the atria time to finish emptying before the ventricles squeeze, and it protects the ventricles from following the atria if the atria start firing at 400 times a minute. Below the node the signal enters the bundle of His, splits into right and left bundle branches, and fans out into the Purkinje fibres that run just beneath the inner lining of the ventricles. These fibres conduct at about 2 to 4 metres per second, several times faster than ordinary heart muscle, so the entire ventricular mass is activated within about 60 to 100 milliseconds and contracts almost as one. Activation starts at the apex and sweeps upward, which wrings blood toward the outflow valves rather than sloshing it about. The electrocardiogram records the summed voltage of all this from the skin. The P wave is atrial depolarisation; the PR interval, normally 120 to 200 milliseconds, is dominated by the atrioventricular delay; the QRS complex, normally under 120 milliseconds, is ventricular depolarisation; the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is buried inside the QRS and is not normally visible. Reading those deflections against the mechanical cycle is how a clinician infers, from a strip of paper, whether the electrical origin and the conduction path are intact.

sections.heading: What Blood Is Made Of
sections.body: Blood is a suspension, not a solution. Spun in a centrifuge, a tube of blood separates into a straw-coloured fluid and a packed red column. The fluid, plasma, makes up roughly 55 per cent of the volume; the cells make up the other 45 per cent, a proportion called the haematocrit, typically 40 to 50 per cent in men and 36 to 46 per cent in women. Total blood volume in an average adult is about five litres, or roughly 70 millilitres per kilogram of body weight, a number that matters acutely when estimating how much someone can afford to lose. Plasma is about 92 per cent water by weight. Dissolved in it are electrolytes, chiefly sodium at around 140 millimoles per litre and chloride at around 100, which set the osmotic tone of the whole body; glucose, normally 4 to 6 millimoles per litre; and about 7 grams per decilitre of protein. Albumin is the most abundant protein and is the main generator of colloid osmotic pressure, the inward pull that keeps water inside capillaries. Globulins include the antibodies. Fibrinogen is the soluble precursor that clotting converts into the insoluble fibrin mesh of a clot; serum is simply plasma with the fibrinogen used up. Red cells, or erythrocytes, number about 5 million per microlitre. Each is a biconcave disc roughly 7 to 8 micrometres across and 2 micrometres thick, with no nucleus and no mitochondria, which frees almost its entire interior for haemoglobin and means it cannot consume the oxygen it carries. That shape gives a large surface for its volume and lets the cell fold to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself. Each cell holds around 270 million haemoglobin molecules, and each haemoglobin carries up to four oxygen molecules on four iron-containing haem groups. A litre of fully saturated blood carries about 200 millilitres of oxygen, roughly seventy times what plain plasma could dissolve. Red cells live about 120 days, are made in the marrow under the control of the kidney hormone erythropoietin, and are dismantled mainly in the spleen and liver. White cells number only 4,000 to 11,000 per microlitre but do the immune work: neutrophils that swallow bacteria, lymphocytes that run adaptive immunity, monocytes that become tissue macrophages, and eosinophils and basophils involved in parasites and allergy. Platelets, at 150,000 to 400,000 per microlitre, are cell fragments shed from marrow megakaryocytes; they plug small breaches and trigger the clotting cascade. Blood is also non-Newtonian. Its viscosity is roughly four times that of water, rises steeply as haematocrit rises, and falls when it flows fast in narrow tubes because the red cells migrate to the axis. This is why polycythaemia, an excess of red cells, is a genuine thrombotic hazard, and why severe anaemia paradoxically increases cardiac output.

sections.heading: Arteries: Pressure Reservoirs and the Pulse
sections.body: Arteries are not passive pipes. The aorta and the great arteries leaving it have walls rich in elastin, a rubbery protein that lets them stretch by ten to fifteen per cent with each beat and spring back afterwards. This turns a violently intermittent pump into a nearly continuous flow. The heart ejects for only about a third of the cycle, yet blood keeps moving through the tissues during the other two thirds because the stretched aorta recoils and squeezes the stored blood onward. The German physiologist Otto Frank formalised this in 1899 as the Windkessel model, borrowing the name of the air chamber that eighteenth-century fire engines used to smooth the pulsation of a hand pump. The consequence is the arterial pressure waveform everyone has had measured. Pressure peaks at systole, typically 110 to 130 millimetres of mercury in a healthy adult, and falls during diastole to a trough of 70 to 85 before the next beat arrives. The difference between the two, the pulse pressure, is roughly 40 and reflects how much volume was ejected against how stiff the arteries are. Mean arterial pressure is not the arithmetic average, because the heart spends longer in diastole than systole; the standard approximation is diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure, so 80 plus one third of 40 gives about 93 millimetres of mercury. Mean arterial pressure is the number that actually determines organ perfusion, and clinicians generally want it above 60 to 65 to keep kidneys and brain supplied. As arteries age their elastin frays and is replaced by stiffer collagen, and calcium is deposited in the wall. A stiff aorta cannot absorb the stroke volume, so systolic pressure rises while diastolic pressure may actually fall, widening the pulse pressure. Isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly, with readings such as 170 over 70, is the signature of a stiff vascular tree rather than of an over-vigorous heart, and it is an independent predictor of stroke. Muscular arteries further out, such as the brachial or femoral, have proportionally more smooth muscle and less elastin, and act as adjustable distribution channels. Beyond them lie the arterioles, vessels of roughly 10 to 100 micrometres in diameter with thick muscular walls relative to their bore. These are the resistance vessels, and they are where most of the pressure in the system is dissipated: pressure falls only slightly from the aorta to a small artery, then collapses from about 90 millimetres of mercury to around 35 across the arterioles alone. The pulse felt at the wrist is not the blood arriving. It is a pressure wave travelling through the arterial wall at roughly 4 to 10 metres per second, far faster than the blood itself, which moves at about 0.3 to 0.4 metres per second in the aorta and slows steadily thereafter. Pulse wave velocity is now measured clinically as a direct index of arterial stiffness and cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: Capillaries and the Exchange of Everything
sections.body: Capillaries are where the entire circulatory system finally does its job. Everything upstream is delivery and everything downstream is collection; the exchange itself happens across a tube whose wall is a single layer of endothelial cells with a basement membrane, roughly 0.5 micrometres thick in total. A typical capillary is 5 to 10 micrometres in internal diameter, just wide enough for a red cell to pass in single file, often deforming to do so, and about 0.5 to 1 millimetre long. The scale of the network is difficult to grasp. Estimates put the number of capillaries in an adult at something on the order of ten billion, with a combined surface area of several hundred to perhaps a thousand square metres. Although each capillary is tiny, they are arranged in parallel, so their total cross-sectional area is enormous, perhaps 2,000 to 5,000 square centimetres compared with the aorta's 3 to 5. Because flow equals area multiplied by velocity, and total flow is constant around the loop, blood slows to roughly 0.3 to 1 millimetre per second in capillaries. A red cell spends about one to two seconds crossing one, which is precisely the time needed for full gas exchange. The circulation is designed to be slow exactly where slowness pays. Exchange happens by several routes. Small lipid-soluble molecules, including oxygen and carbon dioxide, diffuse straight through the endothelial cell membranes across the whole surface, which is why gas exchange is limited by blood flow rather than by permeability. Water and small water-soluble solutes such as glucose and ions pass through junctions and pores between cells. Large proteins cross poorly, by vesicles or through the fenestrations present in specialised capillaries. Capillaries come in three grades of leakiness. Continuous capillaries, found in muscle, skin, lung and, in their tightest form, the brain, have unbroken endothelium and narrow junctions; in the brain those junctions are sealed into the blood-brain barrier, which excludes most drugs and toxins. Fenestrated capillaries, in kidney glomeruli, intestinal villi and endocrine glands, are punched with 60 to 80 nanometre windows for rapid fluid and small-solute movement. Sinusoidal capillaries in liver, spleen and bone marrow have wide gaps that let whole proteins and even cells pass. Not every capillary is open at once. In resting skeletal muscle perhaps a quarter to a third of capillaries carry flow, controlled by precapillary sphincters and arteriolar tone; during exercise recruitment opens the rest, shortening the diffusion distance to each fibre and multiplying exchange surface without any increase in pressure. This recruitment, rather than raw flow, is one of the main ways working tissue increases its oxygen supply. Capillary density mirrors metabolic appetite. Heart muscle and the grey matter of the brain carry roughly 2,500 to 4,000 capillaries per square millimetre of cross-section, resting skeletal muscle several hundred, and tissues such as tendon, cartilage and the cornea have none at all and must live on diffusion from neighbouring beds or from the fluid bathing them. That is why cartilage heals so poorly and why the cornea can be transplanted without matching a donor.

sections.heading: Starling Forces: Why Fluid Leaves and Returns
sections.body: Blood is not merely a courier passing molecules across a membrane; a genuine current of water leaks out of capillaries and must be recovered, and the balance sheet governing that leak explains swelling, dehydration and a large fraction of clinical medicine. Ernest Starling described the principle in 1896, and the framework still carries his name. Four pressures act on the capillary wall. Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; it is about 32 to 35 millimetres of mercury at the arterial end of a systemic capillary and falls to about 15 at the venous end. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure pushes back in, and in most tissues is near zero or slightly negative, around minus 3. Plasma colloid osmotic pressure, generated almost entirely by albumin at roughly 25 to 28 millimetres of mercury, pulls fluid in. Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, from the small amount of protein that escapes, pulls fluid out, at around 5 to 8. Netting these gives outward filtration at the arterial end of perhaps 10 to 13 millimetres of mercury and inward reabsorption at the venous end of a few millimetres. The classical teaching was that roughly nine tenths of what filters out is reabsorbed further along, and that the remainder, some 2 to 4 litres a day across the whole body, returns via the lymphatic system. The modern revision, based on direct measurement and on recognition of the endothelial glycocalyx, is that in most tissues at steady state there is little or no venous-end reabsorption at all: filtration is low but continuous along the whole capillary, and essentially all of it goes home by lymph. Kidney and intestinal capillaries remain genuine exceptions where reabsorption does occur. Being honest about this revision matters, because the older model underpinned decades of intravenous fluid practice that is now being reconsidered. The lymphatic system is therefore not an optional extra but the return leg of the circulation. Blind lymphatic capillaries with overlapping flap-valve endothelium take up interstitial fluid and escaped protein, and progressively larger lymph vessels, propelled by their own smooth muscle and by surrounding movement and one-way valves, carry it through lymph nodes and finally into the great veins at the base of the neck by way of the thoracic duct. Swelling, or oedema, is what happens when this balance tips: raised capillary pressure in heart failure or in a leg with venous obstruction; low albumin in liver disease, malnutrition or nephrotic syndrome; increased permeability in inflammation, burns or sepsis; or blocked lymphatics after surgery, radiotherapy or filarial infection. Each mechanism produces a different pattern of swelling, and identifying which of the four Starling terms has gone wrong is usually the fastest route to the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Veins: The Body's Blood Reservoir and the Return Journey
sections.body: Veins are the forgotten half of the circulation, and they hold most of the blood. At any instant roughly 60 to 70 per cent of total blood volume sits in the systemic veins and venules, about 10 to 12 per cent in the pulmonary circuit, another 8 to 10 in the heart chambers, and only 13 to 15 per cent in all the systemic arteries put together. Veins are therefore capacitance vessels: their job is storage as much as transport, and constricting them is one of the fastest ways the body can raise effective circulating volume without adding a drop of fluid. Venous walls are thin, with far less elastin and smooth muscle than an artery of the same calibre, and their lumens are correspondingly wide. A vein at low pressure is not round but collapsed into an ellipse or a dumbbell, so a small rise in pressure produces a large rise in contained volume simply by making the vessel circular, before the wall has to stretch at all. This high compliance, roughly twenty times that of an artery, is why a modest venoconstriction driven by sympathetic nerves can shift half a litre of blood back toward the heart in seconds. Pressures in the venous system are correspondingly low: around 15 to 20 millimetres of mercury in venules, 8 to 10 in larger veins, and effectively zero to 5 in the great veins and right atrium. The central venous pressure at the right atrium is the reference point of the whole circulation, and it is functionally the pressure against which the systemic circuit drains. With so little pressure to work with, moving blood from the foot back to the chest, a vertical distance of over a metre against gravity in a standing adult, requires help. Three mechanisms provide it. First, one-way bicuspid valves are spaced along the veins of the limbs, dividing the column of blood into short segments so that no single valve has to bear the full hydrostatic load. Second, the skeletal muscle pump: contracting calf and thigh muscles squeeze the deep veins between them, and because the valves permit only headward flow, each contraction pushes a bolus toward the heart. A brisk walk can lower foot venous pressure from about 90 millimetres of mercury to under 30. Third, the respiratory pump: inspiration lowers pressure in the chest and raises it in the abdomen, so each breath draws blood upward. The failure modes follow directly. Standing still for a long period disables the muscle pump, blood pools, venous return falls and a person faints, which is why soldiers on parade are taught to flex their calves. Incompetent valves after thrombosis or repeated distension produce varicose veins, chronic venous hypertension, brown skin staining and eventually ulceration near the ankle. And stagnant flow in immobile deep veins, one of the three arms of Virchow's triad along with vessel injury and increased coagulability, is what makes long-haul flights and post-operative bed rest a thrombosis risk.

sections.heading: The Physics of Flow: Pressure, Resistance and Poiseuille's Law
sections.body: The whole circulation obeys a single simple relationship that mirrors Ohm's law in electricity: flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance. Applied to the entire body, cardiac output equals mean arterial pressure minus right atrial pressure, divided by total peripheral resistance. Rearranged, mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by resistance, which is the single most useful equation in cardiovascular medicine. Every drug that changes blood pressure does so by altering one of those two terms, and every form of shock is a collapse of one of them. Resistance in a tube was described by the French physician Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille, working in the 1840s on the flow of liquids through narrow pipes. His law states that resistance is proportional to the viscosity of the fluid and the length of the tube, and inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius. The fourth power is the point. Halving a vessel's radius multiplies its resistance by sixteen. A vessel that dilates by a mere 19 per cent doubles its flow. This is why arterioles, with their thick muscular coats and modest calibre, can act as precision taps for the whole body, and why a coronary artery narrowed to half its diameter by plaque loses far more capacity than intuition suggests. Two further rules govern how vessels combine. Vessels in series add their resistances directly, so the total resistance of a route from aorta to vena cava is the sum of artery, arteriole, capillary and vein. Vessels in parallel add their conductances instead, so adding more parallel channels always lowers total resistance. The capillary bed, despite each individual capillary having a very high resistance, contributes only modest total resistance because there are billions of them side by side. Likewise, the major organs hang off the aorta in parallel, which means each receives the same driving pressure and can regulate its own share independently. Flow is normally laminar, moving in concentric layers with the fastest stream in the centre, and laminar flow is silent. When velocity rises past a critical point, or when a vessel is narrowed or irregular, flow becomes turbulent, wasteful of energy and audible as a bruit or murmur. The transition is predicted by the dimensionless Reynolds number, which rises with velocity, diameter and density and falls with viscosity; values above roughly 2,000 in a smooth tube favour turbulence. Anaemia lowers viscosity and raises the Reynolds number, which is why severely anaemic patients often have a flow murmur with an entirely normal heart. The Law of Laplace supplies the last piece: wall tension is proportional to pressure multiplied by radius. A dilated ventricle or an aneurysmal aorta must therefore generate or withstand far more wall tension at the same pressure, which is why dilation is self-reinforcing and why aneurysms above about 5.5 centimetres are repaired.

sections.heading: Second-by-Second Control: Baroreflexes and the Nervous System
sections.body: Blood pressure must be held within a narrow band despite standing up, running, bleeding and eating, and the body does it with a feedback loop that responds within a single heartbeat. The sensors are baroreceptors, stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the wall of the carotid sinus, at the fork of each carotid artery in the neck, and in the arch of the aorta. They do not measure pressure directly; they measure how much the wall is stretched, and they fire faster as it stretches more. Their signals travel to the medulla of the brainstem, the carotid receptors by the glossopharyngeal nerve and the aortic receptors by the vagus, converging on the nucleus tractus solitarius. From there the brainstem adjusts two outflows. Increased baroreceptor firing, meaning pressure is high, triggers more parasympathetic vagal traffic to the sinoatrial node, slowing the heart, and less sympathetic traffic to heart and vessels, so contractility falls, arterioles dilate and veins relax. Decreased firing, meaning pressure has fallen, does the reverse: heart rate and contractility rise, arterioles constrict to raise resistance, and veins constrict to push stored blood back toward the heart. The everyday demonstration is standing up. On rising, gravity strands 500 to 800 millilitres of blood in the legs and abdomen within seconds. Venous return falls, stroke volume falls, and pressure at the carotid sinus drops. The baroreflex fires within one or two beats, heart rate climbs by 10 to 20 beats per minute, resistance rises, and pressure is restored, usually with no more than a moment of lightheadedness. When the reflex is slow or blunted, by age, dehydration, diabetes-related autonomic damage or blood-pressure medication, the result is orthostatic hypotension, formally a fall of 20 millimetres of mercury systolic or 10 diastolic within three minutes of standing, and a common cause of falls in older people. The baroreflex is fast but not durable. Over a day or two it resets to whatever pressure it has been seeing, which is why it cannot correct chronic hypertension and why long-term pressure control belongs to the kidney. Slower hormonal systems do that work. When renal perfusion falls, the kidney releases renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which the lungs convert to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that also triggers aldosterone release and hence sodium and water retention. Antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary conserves water and, at high concentrations, constricts vessels. Atrial natriuretic peptide, released when the atria are stretched by excess volume, does the opposite and promotes salt loss. Chemoreceptors add a parallel channel. Peripheral ones in the carotid and aortic bodies sense low oxygen, high carbon dioxide and acidity; central ones in the medulla sense carbon dioxide. Their main job is breathing, but in severe hypoxia or ischaemia they powerfully raise sympathetic drive, a last-ditch pressor response.

sections.heading: Local Control: How Tissues Order Their Own Blood Supply
sections.body: Central control sets the overall pressure, but it cannot know that one particular muscle has started working or that one patch of intestine has just received a meal. That decision is made locally, by the vessels themselves and by the tissue around them, and the mechanisms are remarkably effective. Because every organ hangs in parallel off a common arterial pressure, each can open or close its own tap without depriving the others, provided the total demand does not outrun the pump. Metabolic hyperaemia is the most important of these mechanisms. Active tissue produces carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, adenosine, potassium ions, lactate and inorganic phosphate, and consumes oxygen. Every one of those changes dilates local arterioles. The effect is a self-correcting loop: work raises metabolites, metabolites open vessels, flow rises, metabolites wash out, and flow settles at whatever level matches demand. In hard exercise, blood flow to a working skeletal muscle can rise twenty-fold or more, from around 3 to 4 millilitres per 100 grams per minute at rest to 60 to 80 or higher. Autoregulation is a second local mechanism, this time defending constancy rather than matching demand. Brain, kidney and heart hold their flow nearly steady across a wide range of perfusion pressures, in the brain typically from about 60 to 150 millimetres of mercury of mean arterial pressure. Part of this is the myogenic response described by William Bayliss in 1902: stretch a vascular smooth muscle cell by raising pressure inside the vessel and it contracts, narrowing the lumen and cancelling the flow increase. In the kidney a second mechanism, tubuloglomerular feedback, senses sodium chloride delivery at the macula densa and adjusts the afferent arteriole accordingly. The endothelium turned out to be an active endocrine organ rather than an inert lining, a discovery that earned Robert Furchgott, Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad the Nobel Prize in 1998. Furchgott showed in 1980 that acetylcholine dilates vessels only if the endothelium is intact, and the mediator was later identified as nitric oxide. Endothelial cells continuously release nitric oxide, which diffuses into the underlying smooth muscle, raises cyclic GMP and relaxes it. Production increases when flow rises and drags on the surface, a phenomenon called shear stress, so a vessel carrying more flow automatically widens. The same endothelium releases prostacyclin, which dilates and inhibits platelets, and endothelin-1, one of the most powerful constrictors known. Nitroglycerin for angina works by donating nitric oxide, and sildenafil works by blocking the enzyme that degrades cyclic GMP. There is one systematic exception worth remembering. In every systemic tissue, low oxygen dilates vessels. In the lung, low oxygen constricts them. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward well ventilated ones, improving the match between air and blood. It is beneficial locally and harmful globally: at altitude, or in chronic lung disease, the whole lung is hypoxic, every vessel constricts, pulmonary pressure rises and the right ventricle is strained.

sections.heading: Regional Circulations and How They Differ
sections.body: Organs do not share blood equally, and their vascular arrangements are tailored to what they do. Of a resting cardiac output of about 5 litres per minute, the liver and gut take roughly 25 per cent, the kidneys 20 to 25, skeletal muscle 15 to 20, the brain 13 to 15, the skin 5, and the heart muscle itself 4 to 5. Those shares change dramatically with circumstance: in maximal exercise muscle can claim over 80 per cent of a greatly enlarged output while gut and kidney flow is cut by more than half. The coronary circulation is the most paradoxical. The heart extracts 60 to 75 per cent of the oxygen from the blood reaching it even at rest, against a whole-body average nearer 25 per cent, so it cannot meet extra demand by extracting more and must increase flow instead, up to four or five times. Worse, the left ventricle compresses its own vessels when it contracts, so left coronary flow occurs almost entirely in diastole. A fast heart rate shortens diastole and squeezes coronary supply precisely when demand is highest, which is why angina classically appears on exertion and why rate-slowing drugs relieve it. The cerebral circulation is protected above all others. The brain has essentially no fuel store and suffers irreversible damage within minutes of arrest. It receives about 750 millilitres per minute, held nearly constant by autoregulation, and is fed by four arteries, two carotid and two vertebral, which join in the circle of Willis at the base of the brain so that one can partly cover for another. Cerebral vessels are exquisitely sensitive to carbon dioxide: hyperventilating lowers arterial carbon dioxide, constricts cerebral vessels and can cause dizziness, a fact once exploited to lower raised intracranial pressure. The brain also sits inside a rigid skull, so perfusion depends on mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure. The renal circulation is built for filtration, not for nutrition. The kidneys receive a fifth of cardiac output for organs weighing under 300 grams, and their glomerular capillaries sit between two arterioles rather than between an arteriole and a venule, allowing pressure to be held high enough, around 55 millimetres of mercury, to drive 180 litres of filtrate a day. The splanchnic circulation serves absorption and doubles as a reservoir, holding around a litre of blood that can be mobilised by sympathetic constriction during haemorrhage. Skin circulation is mainly thermal, with arteriovenous shunts in fingers, toes, nose and ears that open to dump heat and close to conserve it, so skin flow can swing from under 50 millilitres per minute in cold to several litres in heat. This is why heavy exercise in hot weather sets skin and muscle in direct competition for the same cardiac output, and why performance and heat tolerance collapse together once dehydration reduces the volume available to share between them.

sections.heading: Fetal Circulation and the Great Switch at Birth
sections.body: Before birth the lungs are collapsed and fluid-filled, and gas exchange happens at the placenta. The fetal circulation is therefore wired differently, with three shunts that route most blood past the lungs, and all three must close within hours to days of the first breath. Oxygenated blood arrives from the placenta in the single umbilical vein at around 80 per cent saturation, the most oxygenated blood in the fetus. Roughly half bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and joins the inferior vena cava. Reaching the right atrium, it is preferentially streamed by the crista dividens across the foramen ovale, a flap valve in the atrial septum, straight into the left atrium. From there it goes to the left ventricle, the aorta, and out first to the coronary and carotid arteries, so the heart and brain get the best-oxygenated blood available. Blood returning from the head in the superior vena cava is poorly oxygenated and is directed instead into the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery. Because the unexpanded lungs have very high resistance, about 90 per cent of it takes a short cut through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta, downstream of the vessels to head and arms. That blood supplies the lower body and returns to the placenta through the two umbilical arteries. The net result is a parallel rather than a series circulation, with both ventricles feeding the aorta, and the right ventricle actually doing the larger share of the work. Birth reverses the pressure gradients within minutes. The first breaths inflate the lungs, and lung expansion plus the rise in alveolar oxygen relieves hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so pulmonary vascular resistance falls sharply. At the same time clamping the cord removes the large low-resistance placental bed, so systemic resistance rises. Pulmonary blood flow increases severalfold and return to the left atrium rises, pushing left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure and pressing the flap of the foramen ovale shut. It fuses anatomically over the following months, though in around a quarter of adults a probe-patent foramen persists and is a recognised, if usually harmless, route for a clot to cross to the arterial side. The ductus arteriosus constricts as arterial oxygen rises and as placental prostaglandin E2 disappears, functionally closing within 24 to 72 hours and fibrosing into the ligamentum arteriosum. Prematurity often delays this, and a persistently patent ductus is treated with prostaglandin inhibitors such as indomethacin or ibuprofen, or surgically. Conversely, in babies with certain duct-dependent heart defects, prostaglandin E1 is infused deliberately to hold the duct open until surgery. The ductus venosus closes over days, becoming the ligamentum venosum. Pulmonary vascular resistance continues to fall over the following six to eight weeks as the thick muscular walls of the fetal pulmonary arterioles thin out. That slow remodelling is why some congenital heart defects that shunt blood from left to right, such as a large ventricular septal defect, produce no murmur or symptoms in the first days of life and only declare themselves once the lungs will accept the extra flow.

sections.heading: When Circulation Fails: Shock, Ischaemia and Warning Signs
sections.body: Circulatory failure means that tissue is not getting enough oxygenated blood, and it can arise from failure of the pump, loss of the fluid, loss of vessel tone, or a physical obstruction. Recognising which of those four is happening is the practical skill, because the four demand different responses and the wrong one can kill. Hypovolaemic shock is loss of volume, from bleeding, burns, vomiting, diarrhoea or diabetic ketoacidosis. Compensation is impressively good: an adult can lose up to about 15 per cent of blood volume, roughly 750 millilitres, with little more than mild anxiety and a normal blood pressure, because baroreflex vasoconstriction and venoconstriction cover the deficit. At 15 to 30 per cent the heart rate climbs above 100, the pulse pressure narrows because diastolic pressure rises while systolic does not, capillary refill at the fingertip slows past two seconds, and the skin turns cool and pale. Systolic pressure typically does not fall until 30 to 40 per cent has gone, which is why a normal blood pressure in a young trauma patient is dangerously reassuring. Narrowing pulse pressure and rising heart rate are the early signals; a falling systolic is a late one. The response is to stop the bleeding and replace volume. Cardiogenic shock is pump failure, usually after a large heart attack. Here the ventricle cannot eject, so pressures back up behind it: the lungs fill with fluid, the patient is breathless and crackly at the bases, and the neck veins are distended. Distributive shock, which includes sepsis and anaphylaxis, is loss of vascular tone; resistance collapses, so the patient is often warm and flushed with a bounding pulse early on despite a very low pressure. Obstructive shock is mechanical blockage: a massive pulmonary embolus, a tension pneumothorax squeezing the great veins, or cardiac tamponade in which fluid around the heart prevents filling. Chronic failures are commoner than acute ones. Atherosclerosis narrows arteries over decades, producing angina in the heart, claudication in the legs, and transient ischaemic attacks in the brain; plaque rupture with sudden clot formation is what converts stable narrowing into a heart attack or stroke. Heart failure is inadequate output at normal filling pressures, producing breathlessness on exertion, breathlessness lying flat, and swelling of the ankles. Deep vein thrombosis causes a hot, swollen, tender calf, and can throw a clot to the lungs. Certain patterns warrant immediate emergency help rather than observation. Central crushing chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, especially with sweating, nausea or pain into arm or jaw. Sudden one-sided face, arm or leg weakness or slurred speech. Sudden severe breathlessness with chest pain. A limb that is cold, white, painful and pulseless. Bleeding that soaks through dressings, or signs of concealed bleeding after injury. While waiting, direct firm pressure controls most external bleeding, lying flat with legs raised may help a faint, and nobody in shock should be given anything to drink.

guides.safetyNote: This guide explains normal physiology; it is not a substitute for medical assessment. Chest pain, sudden weakness or slurred speech, a cold pulseless limb, heavy bleeding or collapse are emergencies — call emergency services immediately rather than waiting to see whether they settle.

guides.title: Hematopoiesis: How Blood Cells Are Made
guides.summary: A full account of how the body manufactures red cells, white cells and platelets from a tiny population of stem cells in the bone marrow, and how that factory is regulated, measured and repaired when it fails.

sections.heading: Why Blood Manufacture Matters
sections.body:
Blood is the only organ in the body that is a liquid, and it is also the one that wears out fastest. A human adult carries roughly five litres of it, containing about twenty-five trillion red cells, somewhere between twenty and fifty billion white cells, and around a trillion platelets. None of these cells lasts long. A red cell survives about 120 days before its membrane stiffens and the spleen removes it. A circulating neutrophil, the commonest white cell, lasts somewhere between eight hours and a few days. A platelet lasts eight to ten days. Because the total number in circulation stays remarkably constant, the marrow must replace exactly what is lost, and the arithmetic of that replacement is startling: about two million red cells and roughly the same number of platelets are produced every second, alongside a hundred billion or so white cells per day. Over a lifetime a person manufactures several hundred kilograms of blood cells, far more than their own body weight, from a founding population of stem cells that may number only fifty to two hundred thousand truly active individuals.

This process is called hematopoiesis, from the Greek haima for blood and poiesis for making. It matters clinically for a simple reason: almost every serious disease of blood is a disease of production, destruction, or the balance between them. Anaemia can arise because the marrow cannot build red cells, because the raw materials are missing, or because the cells are being destroyed faster than they can be replaced, and the treatment differs completely in each case. Infection risk rises sharply when neutrophil output fails, which is why chemotherapy is dosed against the marrow's recovery time rather than the tumour's. Bleeding follows platelet failure. Leukaemia is hematopoiesis with the brakes cut, where a single mutated progenitor floods the marrow with cells that never mature.

Understanding the system also explains why the marrow is such a common casualty of unrelated illness. It is the body's most metabolically demanding tissue, running continuously at high rate, so it is the first to falter under radiation, cytotoxic drugs, nutrient deficiency, chronic inflammation, or invasion by cancer from elsewhere. It is also why bone marrow transplantation works at all: because the entire hierarchy descends from a stem cell that can be harvested, moved and re-established in another person, the whole organ can be replaced by an infusion into a vein, without a surgeon ever opening a bone. Few other organs can be transplanted through a drip. That single fact, established through work from the 1950s onward and recognised with the 1990 Nobel Prize awarded to E. Donnall Thomas, rests entirely on the architecture described in the pages that follow.

sections.heading: Where Blood Is Made Across a Lifetime
sections.body:
The site of blood manufacture moves several times before a person is born, and then moves again through childhood. In the first weeks after conception, blood cells appear in the yolk sac, in structures called blood islands, around days 16 to 19 of human development.
