This first wave is primitive rather than definitive: it produces large nucleated red cells carrying embryonic haemoglobins such as Gower-1 and Portland, which bind oxygen more tightly than adult haemoglobin does, an advantage when extracting oxygen across the placenta from the mother's circulation. These primitive cells are a stopgap. They cannot sustain a growing fetus and they do not give rise to a self-renewing stem cell pool.

The definitive system arises separately, from a region of the embryo called the aorta-gonad-mesonephros or AGM, at around days 27 to 40. Here, cells lining the floor of the dorsal aorta undergo an endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, budding directly off the vessel wall into the bloodstream as true hematopoietic stem cells. This origin, confirmed by live imaging in zebrafish and mouse embryos in the late 2000s, explains a persistent oddity: blood stem cells share many surface markers and transcription factors with the endothelium that lines blood vessels, because they are, developmentally, its offspring.

These founding stem cells colonise the fetal liver, which becomes the dominant blood-forming organ from about week six to week 24 of gestation, with the spleen contributing modestly. Only in the second half of pregnancy does the marrow take over, and by birth it is the principal site. In a newborn, essentially all marrow is red marrow, meaning actively hematopoietic. From childhood onwards, marrow in the peripheral skeleton is progressively replaced by fat, becoming yellow marrow, in a retreat that proceeds from fingers and toes inward. By roughly age 25 active hematopoiesis is largely confined to the axial skeleton: the vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull and the proximal ends of the femur and humerus. This is why a marrow biopsy is taken from the posterior iliac crest of the pelvis, and why a sternal aspiration was the classical alternative.

The retreat is not irreversible. Under severe chronic demand, yellow marrow can reconvert to red, and if that is insufficient the liver and spleen can resume production, a phenomenon called extramedullary hematopoiesis. It is seen in thalassaemia major, in myelofibrosis where scarring evicts the marrow, and in severe chronic haemolysis. The consequence is a large firm spleen, sometimes an enlarged liver, and in children with untreated thalassaemia, expansion of the marrow cavity that thins and deforms the skull and facial bones, producing the characteristic frontal bossing and the radiological hair-on-end appearance.

The sequence leaves a fingerprint in haemoglobin itself. Fetal haemoglobin, built from two alpha and two gamma chains, binds oxygen more avidly than the adult form because it interacts only weakly with 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. The switch from gamma to beta chains occurs over the first six months of life, which is why beta-thalassaemia and sickle cell disease are silent at birth and declare themselves between three and twelve months of age, and why drugs such as hydroxyurea that reawaken gamma-chain production remain valuable.

sections.heading: The Hematopoietic Stem Cell
sections.body:
At the apex of the system sits the hematopoietic stem cell, defined not by how it looks, which is unremarkable, but by what it can do. Two properties define it: multipotency, the ability to generate every blood lineage, and self-renewal, the ability to divide and produce at least one daughter that remains a stem cell. Neither property alone is sufficient. A cell that makes all lineages but exhausts itself is a multipotent progenitor; a cell that renews but makes only one lineage is a committed precursor.

The functional test that established these cells came from Ernest McCulloch and James Till in Toronto in 1961. They irradiated mice to destroy their marrow, injected marrow cells from donors, and found visible nodules on the spleen ten days later. Each nodule was a clone from a single cell and contained several lineages together, proving both multipotency and clonal origin. The number of nodules scaled linearly with the number of cells injected, which is the signature of a single-cell event. This spleen colony-forming unit assay remains the historical foundation of the field, though the modern gold standard is long-term multilineage reconstitution: transplant a limiting dilution of cells into a lethally irradiated recipient and show that donor-derived red cells, myeloid cells, B cells and T cells are all still present sixteen weeks later, and that marrow from that animal can rescue a second recipient.

In humans, the practical surface marker is CD34, a glycoprotein present on stem cells and early progenitors alike. CD34-positive cells make up roughly 0.5 to 2 per cent of marrow mononuclear cells, and true long-term stem cells are a small minority within that, perhaps one in ten thousand marrow cells or fewer. Refining the phenotype requires additional markers: human long-term stem cells are typically CD34 positive, CD38 negative, CD90 positive, CD45RA negative and CD49f positive. In mice the standard shorthand is LSK SLAM, meaning lineage-marker negative, Sca-1 positive, c-Kit positive, plus CD150 positive and CD48 negative.

The most counter-intuitive property is quiescence. Given the enormous output of the system, one might expect stem cells to divide constantly. They do the opposite. Label-retention studies suggest the deepest stem cells divide only every few weeks to months, and some estimates in humans put the interval at once every forty weeks or longer. Quiescence protects them: a non-dividing cell accumulates fewer replication errors and is less vulnerable to cytotoxic drugs that target dividing cells. This is precisely why chemotherapy depletes the circulating blood, which comes from rapidly dividing progenitors, but usually spares the stem cell pool, allowing recovery in two to three weeks. It is also why a small number of stem cells surviving a course of treatment can rebuild an entire haematological system.

sections.heading: The Marrow Niche and What Holds Stem Cells in Place
sections.body:
A stem cell is not autonomous. Its behaviour is dictated by the microenvironment around it, a concept formalised by Raymond Schofield in 1978 as the niche hypothesis. He proposed that stem cell identity is conferred by location, and that a cell displaced from its niche loses stemness. Four decades of imaging and genetic work have largely confirmed him, while substantially revising the anatomy he imagined.

The bone marrow niche is built around blood vessels. Marrow contains arterioles, which are narrow, thick-walled and associated with a low-oxygen, low-flow environment, and sinusoids, which are wide, thin-walled, fenestrated vessels through which mature cells enter the circulation. Most stem cells sit adjacent to sinusoids, in what is called the perivascular niche. The key supporting cells are specialised mesenchymal stromal cells, often identified in mice by expression of leptin receptor or by a marker called Nestin, together with sympathetic nerve fibres, macrophages, adipocytes and, at the bone surface, osteoblasts. An endosteal niche near bone was long thought dominant; current evidence suggests it matters more for lymphoid progenitors and for the deepest quiescent cells than for the bulk of the stem pool.

Two signalling molecules do most of the retention work. CXCL12, also called stromal-derived factor 1, is secreted abundantly by perivascular stromal cells and binds the receptor CXCR4 on stem cells, anchoring them. Stem cell factor, the ligand for the c-Kit receptor, supports their survival and is produced by the same cells. Deleting either from stromal cells, but not from osteoblasts, empties the stem pool, which is the cleanest genetic evidence for where the true niche lies. Adhesion molecules, especially VLA-4 binding VCAM-1, provide mechanical tethering.

This anchoring is directly exploitable. Plerixafor, a small molecule that blocks CXCR4, releases stem cells into the blood within hours. Given with or after granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, it is the standard way to mobilise stem cells for collection by apheresis, so that a donor gives blood through a machine rather than undergoing marrow harvest under anaesthesia. Roughly 70 to 80 per cent of transplants now use mobilised peripheral blood rather than marrow.

Oxygen tension matters too. Marrow is hypoxic by ordinary standards, with local oxygen partial pressures often between 10 and 30 mmHg, against about 100 in arterial blood. Stem cells stabilise hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha and rely heavily on glycolysis rather than oxidative phosphorylation, which limits the production of reactive oxygen species. Experimentally, forcing stem cells into oxidative metabolism drives them out of quiescence and exhausts them. Niche damage explains several diseases: in myelofibrosis, stromal cells are driven to deposit collagen and reticulin, physically strangling the marrow space, and in some leukaemias the malignant clone remodels the niche to favour itself while suppressing normal neighbours.

The niche is also under nervous control. Sympathetic nerve fibres running alongside marrow arterioles release noradrenaline in a circadian rhythm that rhythmically suppresses CXCL12 production, so stem cell release into the blood follows a daily cycle, peaking in humans in the early morning. Denervating the marrow abolishes both the rhythm and much of the response to mobilising drugs.

sections.heading: The Lineage Tree from Stem Cell to Blood Cell
sections.body:
The classical diagram of hematopoiesis is a branching tree. The long-term hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to a short-term stem cell with limited self-renewal, then to a multipotent progenitor with none. The multipotent progenitor was traditionally shown splitting into two great branches: the common myeloid progenitor, ancestor of red cells, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes, and the common lymphoid progenitor, ancestor of T cells, B cells and natural killer cells. From the common myeloid progenitor come the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor, which makes red cells and platelets, and the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor, which makes neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils and monocytes.

This tree is a useful teaching scaffold but is now known to be an idealisation. Single-cell sequencing and clonal barcoding work from around 2015 onward reframed the process as a continuum rather than a series of discrete branch points. Cells appear to drift gradually into lineage bias, with transcriptional priming of several programmes at once before one wins. The strict myeloid-lymphoid split has been particularly undermined: lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors retain myeloid potential, and a distinct megakaryocyte pathway appears to branch off almost immediately from the stem cell, bypassing the intermediate stages entirely, which fits the observation that platelet counts recover fast after transplantation. Individual stem cells also show durable, heritable bias, some producing predominantly myeloid output for the animal's lifetime, others balanced, others lymphoid-leaning.

Whichever topology is correct, the quantitative structure is not in dispute, and it is the more important lesson. Each step down the hierarchy trades potency for proliferative amplification. A single stem cell divides rarely; its progeny divide progressively faster and more often; and the terminal precursors divide four or five times in rapid succession before maturing. This produces enormous gain. One committed erythroid progenitor yields something on the order of 8 to 32 red cells; the whole chain from a single stem cell can generate perhaps a million mature cells. It is an amplifier, and the amplification is what allows a few tens of thousands of stem cells to supply trillions of blood cells.

The commitment decisions themselves are executed by transcription factors that act in mutually antagonistic pairs. GATA-1 drives erythroid and megakaryocytic fate while suppressing PU.1; PU.1 drives myeloid and lymphoid fate while suppressing GATA-1. Small initial fluctuations in their ratio are amplified into a stable all-or-nothing choice, a classic bistable switch. Other decisive factors include GATA-2 in early progenitors, C/EBP-alpha for granulocytes, EKLF for red cells, FLI1 and NF-E2 for platelets, PAX5 for B cells, and NOTCH1 signalling for T cells, which is why T cell development must occur in the thymus where the ligand is presented.

Whether the growth factors instruct these choices or merely permit them is a genuinely unsettled question. The instructive model holds that a cytokine actively directs an uncommitted cell down a path; the permissive or selective model holds that the cell chooses stochastically and the cytokine simply keeps the survivors alive. Careful single-cell imaging has produced evidence for both in different contexts, and the honest current position is that the two mechanisms coexist, with the balance differing by lineage and by how much demand the system is under.

sections.heading: Erythropoiesis: Building a Red Cell
sections.body:
Red cell production is the best-characterised branch, partly because its regulator was among the first hormones of the system to be found. The committed erythroid path begins with a burst-forming unit-erythroid, so named because in culture it forms a large scattered colony over about two weeks. This gives rise to the colony-forming unit-erythroid, a smaller, faster, exquisitely hormone-dependent cell. From there the recognisable morphological series runs: proerythroblast, basophilic erythroblast, polychromatophilic erythroblast, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte, and finally mature erythrocyte.

Across that series two things happen in parallel. The cell fills with haemoglobin, and it dismantles itself. Haemoglobin synthesis requires coordinated production of globin chains and of haem. Haem is built from glycine and succinyl-CoA in eight enzymatic steps that shuttle between mitochondrion and cytoplasm, beginning with ALA synthase 2, the rate-limiting erythroid enzyme, and ending with ferrochelatase inserting ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX. Faults in this pathway cause the porphyrias and the sideroblastic anaemias, the latter recognisable on marrow smear as ring sideroblasts, iron-laden mitochondria encircling the nucleus. Meanwhile the cytoplasm shifts from deep blue, reflecting abundant ribosomal RNA, through mottled grey-pink to salmon pink as ribosomes are lost and haemoglobin accumulates, which is exactly what the terms basophilic, polychromatophilic and orthochromatic describe.

The dismantling is equally remarkable. In mammals, and uniquely among vertebrates, the erythroblast expels its nucleus entirely, pinching it off enveloped in a rim of membrane, which is then engulfed by a central marrow macrophage. Erythroblasts cluster around such a macrophage in a structure called the erythroblastic island, first described by Marcel Bessis in 1958, where the macrophage supplies iron and consumes the discarded nuclei. The enucleated cell, still containing residual RNA and mitochondria, is a reticulocyte. It spends one to two days finishing its maturation, roughly one of those in the marrow and one in the blood, degrading remaining organelles by autophagy. Its residual RNA is what supravital stains such as new methylene blue precipitate into the visible reticulum that gives it its name.

The finished erythrocyte is a biconcave disc about 7 to 8 micrometres across and 2 micrometres thick, with no nucleus, no mitochondria and no ribosomes. It cannot synthesise protein or repair itself, which is why its lifespan is fixed. It generates ATP purely by anaerobic glycolysis, and the Rapoport-Luebering shunt within that pathway produces 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity and helps unload oxygen in tissues. Its shape gives a high surface-to-volume ratio for gas exchange and, crucially, deformability: it must squeeze through capillaries and through splenic sinusoidal slits narrower than itself, which the underlying spectrin-ankyrin membrane skeleton makes possible.

Defects in that skeleton confirm its importance. Mutations in ankyrin, spectrin or band 3 cause hereditary spherocytosis, in which the cell loses membrane surface and rounds up, becoming rigid and being trapped in the spleen. The whole erythroid sequence from committed progenitor to circulating red cell takes about seven days normally, and compresses to four or five under intense erythropoietin drive, at the cost of releasing immature reticulocytes into the blood.

sections.heading: Erythropoietin and the Oxygen Sensor
sections.body:
The rate of red cell production is governed almost entirely by one hormone, erythropoietin, and by an oxygen-sensing mechanism of unusual elegance. Erythropoietin is a glycoprotein of 165 amino acids, heavily glycosylated, produced predominantly by specialised interstitial fibroblasts in the kidney cortex, with roughly 10 to 15 per cent coming from the liver, which is the dominant source in the fetus. Normal plasma levels are around 4 to 30 milli-units per millilitre, but in severe anaemia they can rise a thousandfold.

The sensor works through prolyl hydroxylase enzymes. In the presence of adequate oxygen these enzymes, which require oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate as substrates, hydroxylate specific proline residues on hypoxia-inducible factor alpha subunits. The hydroxylated protein is recognised by the von Hippel-Lindau protein, tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed within minutes. When oxygen falls, hydroxylation stops, HIF-alpha escapes destruction, dimerises with HIF-beta and switches on the erythropoietin gene along with hundreds of others governing glycolysis and angiogenesis. The oxygen molecule is therefore a direct chemical substrate in the sensing reaction, which is why the response is fast and graded. This mechanism earned William Kaelin, Peter Ratcliffe and Gregg Semenza the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and it is now a drug target: the HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors, such as roxadustat and daprodustat, raise endogenous erythropoietin by tricking the sensor.

Erythropoietin acts on the colony-forming unit-erythroid and proerythroblast, which carry its receptor. Its principal effect is anti-apoptotic. In its absence these cells die by programmed cell death; in its presence they survive, proliferate and differentiate. Regulation therefore works largely by adjusting how many committed precursors are permitted to live, which allows red cell output to vary roughly tenfold. The response is not instant: because it takes about five days for a precursor to become a circulating red cell, a rise in erythropoietin shows up first as a reticulocyte increase at day three to five, and haemoglobin follows over weeks.

The clinical consequences are wide. Chronic kidney disease destroys the erythropoietin-producing cells, giving a normochromic normocytic anaemia that responds to recombinant erythropoietin, available since 1989. Recombinant erythropoietin is equally the classical blood-doping agent, and raising haematocrit above roughly 50 to 55 per cent thickens blood enough to raise thrombotic risk substantially. Trials in kidney patients found that correcting haemoglobin fully, to normal levels, increased strokes and deaths compared with partial correction, so guidelines deliberately target an incomplete correction, typically around 100 to 115 grams per litre. High-altitude residence raises erythropoietin through the same sensor; so does chronic lung disease, cyanotic heart disease and, rarely, an erythropoietin-secreting renal tumour.

Measuring the hormone is diagnostically useful in one particular situation. In a patient with a raised haematocrit, a suppressed erythropoietin level points to polycythaemia vera, where the marrow is autonomously overproducing and the feedback loop has correctly switched the hormone off, whereas a normal or raised level points to a secondary cause such as hypoxia or a tumour. That single measurement, combined with testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation, resolves most cases of unexplained polycythaemia without any need for a marrow biopsy.

sections.heading: Making Neutrophils and the Other Granulocytes
sections.body:
Granulocyte production, or granulopoiesis, is quantitatively the largest arm of hematopoiesis, producing on the order of 10 to 20 billion neutrophils per kilogram per day in an adult, rising several-fold under infectious stress. The morphological series runs myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band form, and finally segmented neutrophil. The dividing stages stop at the myelocyte; metamyelocytes onward mature without further division, a distinction that matters when interpreting a marrow.

The defining feature of the series is sequential granule formation, and the order is fixed. Azurophilic, or primary, granules form in the promyelocyte and contain myeloperoxidase, elastase, defensins and cathepsin G. Specific, or secondary, granules form in the myelocyte and contain lactoferrin, collagenase and the membrane-bound components of the NADPH oxidase. Tertiary or gelatinase granules and secretory vesicles form last. Because each granule type is made only during its own window, and because the granules are never replenished afterwards, a cell that misses its window is permanently deficient. Specific granule deficiency, caused by mutations in the transcription factor C/EBP-epsilon, is a rare but instructive illness in which neutrophils look pale and function poorly for life.

The marrow holds a large reserve. At any moment there are roughly ten times as many mature and near-mature neutrophils stored in the marrow as circulate in the blood, and about half the circulating pool is marginated, meaning loosely adherent to vessel walls rather than freely flowing. This explains several everyday observations. Exercise, adrenaline or acute stress demarginate cells and can double the measured count within minutes without any new production. Corticosteroids raise the count both by demargination and by mobilising the marrow reserve, and simultaneously reduce migration into tissues, which is why a patient on steroids may show a high white count while being less able to fight infection. Severe acute infection releases immature band forms and occasionally metamyelocytes, the classical left shift.

Regulation runs on granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, or G-CSF, produced by endothelium, macrophages and fibroblasts in response to inflammatory signals, principally interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 in a feedback loop keyed to the number of neutrophils being consumed in tissues. Recombinant G-CSF, marketed as filgrastim from 1991 and later as pegylated forms, shortens the neutropenic window after chemotherapy from around ten days to five or six and is one of the more consequential supportive-care drugs in oncology. GM-CSF acts more broadly across myeloid lineages.

Eosinophils, driven principally by interleukin-5 and involved in parasitic and allergic responses, and basophils, the rarest granulocyte at under one per cent of white cells, follow parallel maturation programmes from the same granulocyte-monocyte progenitor. Monocytes leave the marrow after only a day or two, circulate briefly and then take up residence in tissues as macrophages and dendritic cells, though many tissue macrophages are in fact self-renewing populations seeded in embryonic life rather than replenished from the marrow at all.

sections.heading: Platelets and the Megakaryocyte
sections.body:
Platelet production is the strangest process in the marrow, because the parent cell does something no other human cell does routinely: it replicates its DNA many times without dividing. The megakaryocyte undergoes endomitosis, entering the cell cycle and duplicating its chromosomes but aborting cytokinesis, so it accumulates a single lobulated polyploid nucleus containing 16N, 32N or occasionally 64N or 128N complements against the normal 2N. It becomes the largest cell in the marrow, 50 to 100 micrometres across, visible on a smear at low power. The polyploidy is not a curiosity; it scales up the machinery for protein synthesis so a single cell can furnish thousands of platelets.

While polyploidising, the megakaryocyte builds a vast internal reservoir of membrane, the demarcation membrane system, which will become the surface of its future platelets, and packs alpha granules with von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, platelet factor 4 and growth factors, and dense granules with ADP, ATP, serotonin and calcium. It then extends long branching cytoplasmic processes, called proplatelets, through the endothelium of a marrow sinusoid and directly into the flowing blood. Shear forces from the bloodstream progressively fragment these into individual platelets, a process filmed by intravital microscopy in living mice in 2007 and now the accepted mechanism. Each megakaryocyte releases roughly one to three thousand platelets, then its bare nucleus is consumed by macrophages. A small fraction of megakaryocytes reach the lung and shed platelets there, so the lungs contribute meaningfully to platelet output.

The finished platelet is an anucleate disc about 2 to 3 micrometres across, with no nucleus but retaining messenger RNA and some capacity for protein synthesis. It circulates for eight to ten days. Roughly a third of the total platelet mass is sequestered in the spleen at any moment, in reversible equilibrium with the circulation, which is why splenomegaly of almost any cause lowers the platelet count without any production defect, and why splenectomy raises it.

The regulating hormone is thrombopoietin, produced constitutively by the liver at a steady rate. Its regulation is beautifully simple and works without any sensor of platelet number. Platelets and megakaryocytes carry the thrombopoietin receptor MPL, bind the hormone and destroy it. When platelet mass is high, more hormone is cleared and the free concentration falls; when platelets are consumed, less is cleared and free hormone rises, driving production. It is regulation by sink rather than by measurement. A refinement discovered around 2015 is that ageing platelets lose sialic acid from their surface glycans, are captured by the Ashwell-Morell receptor in the liver, and that this capture signals hepatocytes to make more thrombopoietin. Thrombopoietin receptor agonists such as romiplostim and eltrombopag exploit this axis to raise counts in immune thrombocytopenia and aplastic anaemia.

sections.heading: Lymphocytes and the Two-Stage Education System
sections.body:
Lymphocyte production differs from every other lineage in one fundamental way: the cells are not finished when they leave the marrow. They must be tested, and most of them fail. B cells and T cells each generate their antigen receptor by cutting and rejoining gene segments at random, a process called V(D)J recombination, driven by the enzymes RAG1 and RAG2 and completed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase adding random nucleotides at the joins. The combinatorial arithmetic yields a theoretical repertoire well in excess of 10 to the 11th distinct receptors. This randomness is the whole point, since it lets the immune system recognise pathogens it has never encountered, but it guarantees that many receptors will be useless and some will attack the body itself.

B cells complete this in the marrow. The series runs pro-B, pre-B, immature B, then transitional and mature B cell, under the control of the transcription factor PAX5 and signals through the interleukin-7 receptor. At the pre-B stage the cell tests its newly rearranged heavy chain by pairing it with a surrogate light chain; if the assembly signals correctly, the cell proliferates and proceeds, if not, it dies or tries the other chromosome. Immature B cells that bind self-antigen strongly are either deleted, rendered anergic, or given a second chance through receptor editing, in which RAG genes are reactivated to rearrange a new light chain. Perhaps 75 per cent or more of newly made B cells die in the marrow before ever reaching the circulation.

T cell precursors leave the marrow unfinished and migrate to the thymus, a gland in the anterior mediastinum that is proportionally largest in childhood and involutes steadily from puberty. There they undergo the two-step selection that gives the system its specificity. In positive selection, in the thymic cortex, a thymocyte must bind self-MHC molecules with at least weak affinity or it dies by neglect, which ensures the surviving repertoire can actually see antigen presented on the body's own molecules. In negative selection, in the medulla, a thymocyte that binds self-peptide too strongly is deleted. Medullary thymic epithelial cells perform an extraordinary trick here, ectopically expressing thousands of tissue-restricted proteins, insulin and thyroglobulin among them, under the control of the AIRE gene, so that developing T cells are shown the whole body in miniature. Mutations in AIRE cause the autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome APS-1, a natural experiment confirming the mechanism.

Roughly 95 to 98 per cent of thymocytes die during this process. The survivors emerge as naive CD4 or CD8 single-positive T cells. Natural killer cells, by contrast, complete development in the marrow, use germline-encoded receptors rather than rearranged ones, and need no thymic education. Failure at any of these steps produces recognisable disease: absent RAG function causes severe combined immunodeficiency, thymic aplasia in DiGeorge syndrome leaves T cells absent despite normal marrow, and Bruton tyrosine kinase mutations block B cells at the pre-B stage.

sections.heading: Growth Factors, Cytokines and Nutritional Requirements
sections.body:
Hematopoiesis depends on a layered set of chemical signals and on a supply of specific raw materials, and failure of either produces anaemia or cytopenia that looks similar at the bedside but demands opposite treatment.

The signalling layer divides into early-acting and lineage-specific factors. Stem cell factor and FLT3 ligand act at the top of the hierarchy, maintaining the stem and early progenitor pool, and interleukin-3 and GM-CSF act broadly across myeloid lineages. Then come the specific regulators: erythropoietin for red cells, thrombopoietin for platelets, G-CSF for neutrophils, interleukin-5 for eosinophils, and interleukin-7 for lymphoid progenitors. Almost all of these signal through receptors that lack intrinsic kinase activity and instead recruit Janus kinases, principally JAK2, which phosphorylate STAT transcription factors. This shared wiring explains why one mutation, JAK2 V617F, which locks the kinase in the on position, can cause three different diseases depending on cellular context: polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis. It was identified in 2005 and is present in over 95 per cent of polycythaemia vera cases. It also explains why JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib help in myelofibrosis.

The nutritional layer has four principal requirements. Iron is needed in quantity, about 20 to 25 milligrams per day for haemoglobin synthesis, of which only 1 to 2 milligrams comes from the diet and the rest from recycling senescent red cells by macrophages. Absorption is regulated by hepcidin, a liver peptide that blocks the iron exporter ferroportin; inflammation raises hepcidin, locking iron inside macrophages, which is the mechanism of anaemia of chronic disease. Iron deficiency gives small pale cells, a low mean corpuscular volume typically below 80 femtolitres, with low ferritin and raised transferrin.

Vitamin B12 and folate are required for DNA synthesis, specifically for thymidylate production. Deficiency slows nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic maturation proceeds normally, producing large cells with immature-looking nuclei, the state called megaloblastic anaemia, with a mean corpuscular volume often above 100 and characteristically hypersegmented neutrophils showing six or more nuclear lobes. B12 absorption requires intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells and an intact terminal ileum; autoimmune destruction of those cells causes pernicious anaemia. The critical clinical trap is that folate alone will correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency while allowing the associated subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord to progress irreversibly, so B12 must always be excluded or replaced first. Copper deficiency, sometimes from excess zinc supplementation or bariatric surgery, mimics myelodysplasia. Vitamin B6 deficiency, classically from isoniazid, produces a sideroblastic picture that responds to pyridoxine.

The two layers interact therapeutically. Giving erythropoietin to an iron-deficient patient produces a poor response and can precipitate functional iron deficiency, in which stores appear adequate but iron cannot reach the marrow fast enough to meet the stimulated demand. This is why intravenous iron accompanies these agents in dialysis patients, and why failure to respond should prompt a check of iron status before escalating the dose. Replacing iron in a truly deficient patient gives a reticulocyte rise within a week and roughly 10 grams per litre of haemoglobin every one to two weeks; failure suggests a wrong diagnosis, poor absorption, or continuing bleeding.

sections.heading: Reading a Full Blood Count
sections.body:
The full blood count, sometimes called the complete blood count, is the single most-ordered laboratory test in medicine and is essentially a production report from the marrow. Reading it well means treating each number as the net result of production, destruction and distribution.

Haemoglobin concentration in adults is roughly 130 to 175 grams per litre in men and 120 to 155 in women, with anaemia defined by the World Health Organization at below 130 and 120 respectively. Haematocrit, the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells, runs about three times the haemoglobin in grams per decilitre. The mean corpuscular volume, normally 80 to 100 femtolitres, is the primary sorting tool: low points to iron deficiency or thalassaemia, high to B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism or myelodysplasia, and normal to acute blood loss, kidney disease, chronic inflammation or a mixed picture. Red cell distribution width measures variability in size and rises early in iron deficiency, often before the volume falls, and is typically normal in thalassaemia trait, which is a useful discriminator.

The reticulocyte count is the most under-used number on the form and answers the essential question of whether the marrow is responding. Normally 0.5 to 2.5 per cent, or 25 to 100 times ten to the ninth per litre in absolute terms, it should rise several-fold within three to five days of any acute anaemia. A high reticulocyte count in an anaemic patient points to blood loss or haemolysis, meaning the marrow is working; a low or normal count points to a production defect, meaning the marrow is not. Always use the absolute count, since the percentage is inflated when the denominator of red cells is low.

The white count, normally 4 to 11 times ten to the ninth per litre, must be read as a differential. Neutrophils normally make up 40 to 75 per cent; below 1.5 defines neutropenia and below 0.5 is severe, with substantial infection risk that becomes urgent below 0.2. Lymphocytosis, monocytosis and eosinophilia each carry their own differential. Platelets run 150 to 400 times ten to the ninth per litre; spontaneous bleeding is unusual above 20 and surgery is generally safe above 50 to 80.

Certain patterns demand immediate attention. Pancytopenia, meaning all three lines low, suggests marrow failure, infiltration, megaloblastic anaemia or hypersplenism and warrants a marrow examination. Blasts on the film in any number are abnormal and suggest acute leukaemia. A very high white count with a full spectrum of immature myeloid forms suggests chronic myeloid leukaemia. Nucleated red cells together with teardrop-shaped red cells and immature myeloid cells constitute a leukoerythroblastic film, indicating that something is disrupting the marrow architecture, classically fibrosis or metastatic infiltration.

sections.heading: When Production Fails: The Marrow Failure States
sections.body:
Marrow failure means insufficient production of one or more lineages despite adequate raw materials and stimulus. The classification separates diseases of an empty marrow from diseases of a full but useless one, and the marrow biopsy is what distinguishes them.

Aplastic anaemia is the emptied marrow: pancytopenia with a hypocellular biopsy showing mostly fat where cells should be. Incidence is about two per million per year in Europe and North America and two to three times higher in East Asia. The great majority of acquired cases are immune-mediated, with cytotoxic T lymphocytes attacking the stem cell pool, which is why immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin plus ciclosporin achieves responses in around 60 to 70 per cent of patients, and why allogeneic transplant, curative in over 80 per cent of young patients with a matched sibling, works. Some cases follow drugs, notably chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, gold and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, some follow hepatitis, and some are inherited: Fanconi anaemia arises from defective DNA interstrand crosslink repair and is diagnosed by chromosome breakage testing, and dyskeratosis congenita from defective telomere maintenance.

Myelodysplastic syndromes are the full but useless marrow: a clonal stem cell disorder in which the marrow is usually hypercellular yet the blood counts are low, because the abnormal precursors die before maturing, a state called ineffective hematopoiesis. Median age at diagnosis is around 70. Diagnosis rests on dysplastic morphology, cytogenetics and blast percentage, and prognosis is scored by systems such as the revised International Prognostic Scoring System. Roughly a third progress to acute myeloid leukaemia. Treatment ranges from transfusion support and erythropoietin through hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine to transplantation.

Pure red cell aplasia isolates the defect to the erythroid line, with reticulocytes near zero. Parvovirus B19 is a classic cause because the virus uses the P antigen on erythroid precursors as its receptor and destroys them; in a healthy person this causes a transient dip, but in someone with a shortened red cell lifespan from sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis it produces a sudden aplastic crisis. Thymoma and large granular lymphocytic leukaemia are other causes.

Marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma or myeloma physically displaces hematopoiesis, and myelofibrosis replaces it with scar. Nutritional deficiencies, viral infections including HIV, and drugs may each suppress production. The practical rule is to establish the reticulocyte count and the marrow cellularity first, since together they separate destruction from production failure and an empty marrow from a dysplastic one, and almost all the subsequent reasoning follows from that fork.

Two conditions sit between categories and are worth knowing by name. Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria arises from an acquired PIGA mutation in a stem cell, stripping the anchors that hold complement-regulatory proteins on the cell surface and leaving red cells defenceless against complement. It causes haemolysis, dark morning urine and a striking tendency to thrombosis in unusual sites such as the hepatic veins, often alongside aplastic anaemia; it is diagnosed by flow cytometry and treated with complement inhibitors such as eculizumab. Large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, an indolent clonal T cell expansion, suppresses neutrophil production and is a commonly missed cause of chronic unexplained neutropenia.

sections.heading: Leukaemia and Clonal Hematopoiesis
sections.body:
Malignancy of the blood is hematopoiesis with its regulation broken, and its behaviour follows directly from which step in the hierarchy is damaged. Acute leukaemias arise when a progenitor acquires mutations that both block differentiation and drive proliferation. The result is a marrow crowded with blasts that cannot mature, and the patient presents with the consequences of failed normal production, meaning anaemia, infection and bleeding, often within weeks. Acute myeloid leukaemia is defined by twenty per cent or more blasts in blood or marrow, or by certain defining genetic abnormalities regardless of count. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer, peaking between ages two and five, with cure rates now above 85 per cent in children though considerably lower in adults.

The classic worked example of the mechanism is acute promyelocytic leukaemia, in which a translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 fuses the PML gene to the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene. The fusion protein binds retinoic acid response elements and recruits repressors, freezing maturation at the promyelocyte stage. Pharmacological doses of all-trans retinoic acid displace the repressor and force the cells to mature into neutrophils rather than killing them, converting what was once the most lethal leukaemia, because the abnormal promyelocytes release procoagulants and cause catastrophic bleeding, into one with cure rates above 90 per cent when combined with arsenic trioxide. It remains the cleanest proof that a differentiation block is the disease.

Chronic leukaemias reflect damage further down or a milder lesion. Chronic myeloid leukaemia is caused by the Philadelphia chromosome, a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Cells still mature, so the blood fills with functioning granulocytes at every stage. The 2001 approval of imatinib, designed specifically to occupy that kinase's ATP pocket, took ten-year survival from roughly twenty per cent to over eighty and became the template for targeted cancer therapy.

Between health and leukaemia lies clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, described around 2014 from large sequencing studies. Here a single stem cell clone carrying a mutation, most often in DNMT3A, TET2 or ASXL1, expands to make up more than two per cent of blood cells without any cytopenia or dysplasia. It is essentially absent under age forty, present in roughly ten per cent of people over seventy and perhaps twenty per cent over ninety. It carries a risk of progression to a blood cancer of only about half to one per cent per year, but, unexpectedly, it roughly doubles the risk of coronary heart disease, apparently because mutant macrophages are more inflammatory. It reframes ageing of the marrow as a gradual loss of clonal diversity rather than simple exhaustion.

sections.heading: Transplantation, Mobilisation and Marrow Rescue
sections.body:
Because the entire hierarchy descends from a transplantable cell, the whole organ can be replaced. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used to cure marrow failure, to replace a genetically defective marrow, and above all to permit doses of chemotherapy or radiation that would otherwise be lethal by supplying a rescue population afterwards.

The procedure has three parts. Conditioning is chemotherapy with or without total body irradiation, given to make space, to suppress the recipient's immune system so the graft is not rejected, and in cancer to kill residual disease. Myeloablative conditioning destroys the marrow irreversibly; reduced-intensity conditioning relies more on the graft's own immune attack and permits treatment of older patients. Infusion is then simply a bag of cells through a central vein, taking under an hour; the cells find their way to marrow by CXCR4-mediated homing to CXCL12, an extraordinary piece of self-assembly. Engraftment follows, conventionally defined as the first of three consecutive days with a neutrophil count above 0.5 times ten to the ninth per litre, usually at day 10 to 20, with platelets recovering later. Between conditioning and engraftment the patient is profoundly neutropenic and dependent on transfusion and antimicrobials.

Autologous transplant returns the patient's own previously collected cells and carries no immunological risk, but no anti-tumour benefit from the graft. Allogeneic transplant uses a donor matched at the human leukocyte antigen loci, ideally 10 out of 10 at HLA-A, B, C, DRB1 and DQB1. A sibling has a one in four chance of matching. Unrelated donor registries, which now hold over forty million volunteers worldwide, supply most of the rest, and umbilical cord blood and haploidentical family donors with post-transplant cyclophosphamide have largely solved the shortfall for patients of under-represented ancestry.

Allogeneic grafts bring both the central danger and the central benefit. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor T cells attack recipient skin, gut and liver, acutely in the first hundred days or chronically thereafter, affecting perhaps 30 to 50 per cent of recipients to some degree. The same alloreactivity produces the graft-versus-leukaemia effect, which is a major part of the cure. Removing donor T cells reduces the disease and increases relapse, a trade-off that has driven decades of research.

Sources of cells differ practically. Marrow harvest takes around a litre of marrow from the posterior iliac crests under general anaesthesia. Mobilised peripheral blood, obtained after four to five days of G-CSF with plerixafor if needed, engrafts faster but carries more chronic graft-versus-host disease. Cord blood is immediately available and tolerates mismatch better, but contains few cells and engrafts slowly. Gene therapy now uses the same platform, correcting a patient's own harvested stem cells ex vivo and returning them, with approved products for beta-thalassaemia and sickle cell disease.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Pitfalls and What To Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Several errors in reasoning about blood production recur often enough to be worth naming. The first is treating a number without asking whether it reflects production, destruction or distribution. A low platelet count in a patient with a large spleen may need no marrow investigation at all; a low platelet count with a normal spleen and a normal marrow suggests immune destruction. A high white count after a seizure or a sprint may be pure demargination. Always ask what the reticulocyte count is doing before treating anaemia, because it separates the two great categories in a single number.

The second is the megaloblastic trap already noted but worth restating precisely: giving folate to someone deficient in vitamin B12 will raise the haemoglobin and mask the diagnosis while the neurological damage, a demyelination of the dorsal and lateral columns causing loss of position sense, ataxia and eventually paralysis, continues and may become permanent. Check B12 before, or replace both.

The third is misreading iron studies during inflammation. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises in infection, inflammation and liver disease, so a normal or high ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency in a sick patient. Transferrin saturation, soluble transferrin receptor, or a trial of iron may be needed. Conversely, giving intravenous iron during active infection is generally avoided, since free iron favours bacterial growth.

The fourth concerns urgency. Febrile neutropenia, meaning a temperature at or above 38 degrees Celsius in a patient with a neutrophil count below 0.5, is a medical emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given within one hour of presentation, before any culture results, because untreated Gram-negative sepsis in this setting can be fatal within hours. Do not wait for confirmation. Similarly, a patient with a white count above roughly 100 with blasts may have leukostasis, with sludging in cerebral and pulmonary vessels, and needs urgent haematology input. Suspected acute promyelocytic leukaemia, suggested by a coagulopathy with blasts, warrants starting all-trans retinoic acid on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation, because the bleeding risk is front-loaded.

The fifth is forgetting that many marrow problems are iatrogenic or environmental and reversible. Methotrexate, trimethoprim, azathioprine, linezolid, alcohol, benzene and radiation all suppress production, as do zinc supplements taken to excess, through copper deficiency. Take a full drug and supplement history, including over-the-counter products.

Finally, know the limits of what can be done without a laboratory. Nothing in this account permits diagnosis by symptoms alone; pallor, fatigue and breathlessness are unreliable, and conjunctival or palmar pallor detects only severe anaemia. If a count is unavailable, the practical priorities are to stop any drug that might be responsible, correct obvious nutritional deficiency, avoid unnecessary bleeding risk such as aspirin or intramuscular injections, protect against infection, and seek testing as soon as it can be reached.

guides.title: Blood: Plasma, Cells and What It Carries
guides.summary: How blood is built and what it does: plasma and its proteins, red cells and gas transport, white cells and immunity, platelets and clotting, blood types, the marrow that makes it all, and the tests and diseases that reveal when it fails.

sections.heading: The River Inside: What Blood Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: An adult body holds about five liters of blood, roughly seven to eight percent of body weight, and it is the only tissue that visits every other tissue. Physiologists classify blood as a connective tissue: a population of cells suspended not in fibers but in a liquid matrix called plasma, and it earns the name by connecting everything — lungs to muscles, gut to liver, glands to their distant target organs, the hot metabolic core to the skin where heat escapes. Spin a tube of blood in a centrifuge and it separates into three layers that map its anatomy. The bottom layer is packed red cells; that fraction, called the hematocrit, runs about 40 to 54 percent of the volume in men and 36 to 48 percent in women. Above it sits a thin gray-white band called the buffy coat, less than one percent of the volume, containing the white blood cells and platelets. The straw-colored liquid filling the remaining 55 percent or so is plasma. Blood performs three families of work. The first is transport: oxygen from lungs to tissues and carbon dioxide back; glucose, fats and amino acids from the gut and liver to the cells that burn or store them; hormones from glands to targets; and wastes such as urea to the kidneys and bilirubin to the liver for disposal. The second is regulation: blood carries heat from working muscle to the skin, buffers acids and bases to hold pH inside the narrow band of 7.35 to 7.45, and trades water and salts with the tissues to keep fluid balance steady. The third is protection: white cells patrol for microbes, antibodies and complement proteins circulate as chemical weaponry, and platelets with clotting factors stand ready to seal any breach in a vessel wall. The stakes are absolute. The brain stores almost no fuel and loses consciousness within about ten seconds if its blood flow stops; permanent damage begins within four to six minutes. Losing 30 to 40 percent of blood volume — roughly 1.5 to 2 liters — drops blood pressure into shock, and losing half is usually fatal without transfusion. The modern picture of a closed circuit dates to the English physician William Harvey, who showed in 1628 that the heart pumps a fixed volume around and around rather than the liver continuously brewing new blood, as the ancient Greek physician Galen had taught for 1,400 years. At rest the heart drives the entire five liters through the circuit about once a minute — a cardiac output near five liters per minute — and during hard exercise that can rise fivefold. Whole blood is three to five times as viscous as water, mostly because of the red cells, and that thickness is itself physiologically important: it sets the resistance the heart must pump against. Everything that follows in this guide is an unpacking of those layers in the centrifuge tube — what the liquid is, what each cell type does, and what the whole system carries.

sections.heading: Plasma: The Golden Liquid Fraction
sections.body: Plasma is about 92 percent water, and the eight percent dissolved in it amounts to a complete inventory of what the body is moving at any moment. The largest solute class is protein, about seven to eight grams per deciliter, discussed in its own right later; everything else is present in smaller but exquisitely regulated amounts. The electrolytes are the charged minerals that make plasma a salt solution close to a third the saltiness of seawater: sodium at 135 to 145 millimoles per liter, potassium at 3.5 to 5.0, calcium near 2.2 to 2.6, chloride at 96 to 106, and bicarbonate at 22 to 26. These narrow ranges are defended fiercely because nerves and muscle fire by moving these very ions across membranes; a potassium of 7 can stop the heart, and a sodium that falls fast below 120 swells the brain. Fuel travels here too. Fasting glucose runs 70 to 100 milligrams per deciliter, held steady between meals by the liver; fats, insoluble in water, ride packaged inside lipoprotein particles; amino acids from digested protein stream toward the liver and muscles. Dissolved gases, vitamins, trace metals bound to carrier proteins, and hormones at concentrations as low as parts per trillion complete the outbound cargo. The return freight is waste: urea from protein breakdown at 7 to 20 milligrams per deciliter of blood urea nitrogen, creatinine from muscle turnover near 0.6 to 1.3, and yellow bilirubin from retired red cells, all destined for the kidneys or liver. Total solute concentration, the osmolality, sits near 285 to 295 milliosmoles per kilogram, and water shifts between blood and tissue whenever it drifts. A distinction worth learning: plasma is the liquid from blood kept unclotted with an anticoagulant; serum is what remains after blood has been allowed to clot, which is plasma minus fibrinogen and the other consumed clotting factors. Laboratories choose one or the other depending on the test. Plasma volume is a managed quantity. The kidneys adjust salt and water excretion hour by hour under hormonal instruction — antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary concentrates the urine when plasma osmolality rises, and aldosterone from the adrenal glands retains sodium when volume falls. Drink a liter of water and plasma dilutes within half an hour; the kidneys excrete the excess over the next few hours. Hemorrhage triggers the reverse: vessels constrict, the kidneys hoard salt and water, and fluid moves in from the tissues, restoring plasma volume within 12 to 72 hours long before the lost red cells are replaced — which is why the blood is temporarily dilute after a major bleed. Plasma is also a medicine. Donated plasma, frozen within hours as fresh frozen plasma, supplies clotting factors to bleeding patients; fractionation plants separate donated plasma into albumin, immunoglobulins and factor concentrates, an industry processing tens of millions of liters a year. That golden supernatant in the centrifuge tube is, quite literally, the body's logistics network in liquid form.

sections.heading: Plasma Proteins: Albumin, Globulins and Fibrinogen
sections.body: Dissolve seven to eight grams of protein in every deciliter of plasma and you get about 200 grams of working protein in circulation, nearly all of it manufactured by the liver, and its three classical fractions — albumin, globulins and fibrinogen — divide the labor. Albumin is roughly 60 percent of the total, kept between 3.5 and 5.0 grams per deciliter, and the liver synthesizes 10 to 15 grams of it every day. Its first job is osmotic. Capillary walls leak water and small solutes freely but hold back protein, so albumin generates the colloid osmotic pressure, about 25 millimeters of mercury, that pulls water back into the bloodstream against the outward push of blood pressure. The nineteenth century physiologist Ernest Starling formalized this balance, and its failure explains a hallmark sign: when albumin falls below roughly 2.5 grams per deciliter — from liver failure, from protein loss through diseased kidneys in nephrotic syndrome, or from severe malnutrition as in kwashiorkor — water stays in the tissues and the ankles, belly and face swell with edema. Albumin's second job is carriage. It is the plasma's general-purpose taxi, binding fatty acids, the unconjugated bilirubin from red cell breakdown, about half of circulating calcium, thyroid hormone in transit, and a long list of drugs from warfarin to ibuprofen; two highly protein-bound drugs can compete for seats and displace each other into sudden potency. The globulins split into alpha, beta and gamma bands on electrophoresis, the laboratory technique that spreads serum proteins along a strip by charge. Alpha and beta globulins are mostly specialist transporters and enzymes: transferrin ferries iron, ceruloplasmin carries copper, haptoglobin scavenges hemoglobin spilled from ruptured red cells, and alpha-1 antitrypsin restrains tissue-digesting enzymes, its inherited deficiency causing emphysema in young adults. The gamma fraction is the immunoglobulins — antibodies — and is the one fraction not made by the liver but by plasma cells of the immune system; a tall narrow spike in the gamma band is a classic laboratory signature of myeloma, a cancer of a single antibody-producing clone. Fibrinogen, present at 200 to 400 milligrams per deciliter, is the soluble precursor of the fibrin mesh that turns a platelet plug into a durable clot, and it is consumed in clotting, which is why serum lacks it. Beyond these constants, the liver retunes its output during illness. Within a day or two of significant infection, injury or inflammation, acute-phase proteins surge — C-reactive protein can rise a hundredfold in 48 hours, and fibrinogen and ferritin climb — while albumin production is dialed down. Clinicians exploit this: an elevated C-reactive protein flags active inflammation, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate rises because extra fibrinogen makes red cells stack and settle faster in a tube. Read together, a protein electrophoresis strip is a one-page report on the liver's factory, the immune system's arsenal and the body's current state of siege.

sections.heading: Red Blood Cells: Design of an Oxygen Courier
sections.body: The red blood cell, or erythrocyte, is the most numerous cell in the body — four and a half to five and a half million in every microliter of blood, twenty to thirty trillion in total, roughly a quarter of all the cells you own — and it is a masterpiece of subtraction. During its manufacture the mammalian red cell ejects its nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes and nearly every other organelle, leaving a flexible bag filled almost solid with hemoglobin, about 270 million molecules per cell. What remains is a biconcave disc about 7.5 micrometers across and 2 micrometers thick at the rim, dimpled in the middle. The shape is not decorative. Compared with a sphere of equal volume, the disc carries about 40 percent more surface area, shortening the distance any oxygen molecule must diffuse to reach hemoglobin; no point inside the cell is more than about a micrometer from the membrane. The shape also buys deformability. Capillaries narrow to 3 micrometers, less than half the cell's diameter, and the red cell folds and slides through like a soft parachute, its membrane anchored to a springy protein lattice of spectrin and ankyrin just beneath the surface. Inherited defects in that lattice produce hereditary spherocytosis, in which rounded, rigid cells are culled early by the spleen and mild anemia with jaundice results. Having discarded its mitochondria, the red cell cannot use the oxygen it carries — an elegant conflict-of-interest rule — and runs entirely on anaerobic glycolysis, sipping glucose to make the small amount of ATP needed to run its ion pumps and keep its membrane supple. A side branch of that same glycolysis produces 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, a small molecule that tunes hemoglobin's grip on oxygen. Lacking a nucleus, the cell cannot repair itself, and its working life is about 120 days, roughly 250 kilometers of travel through the circulation. Aging cells lose flexibility and surface signals; macrophages in the spleen and liver recognize and dismantle them at about two million cells per second, matching the marrow's production rate exactly in health. The salvage operation is thrifty: the iron is stripped from heme, loaded onto transferrin and shipped back to the marrow for reuse; the globin protein is broken to amino acids; and the ring of the heme molecule becomes biliverdin and then yellow bilirubin, which the liver conjugates and excretes in bile — the pigment that colors bruises as they age, stool brown, and the skin yellow in jaundice when the pathway backs up. Two routine numbers summarize the red cell mass: hemoglobin concentration, normally about 13.5 to 17.5 grams per deciliter in men and 12 to 15.5 in women, and the hematocrit described earlier. A third, mean corpuscular volume, sizes the average cell at 80 to 100 femtoliters and is the first fork in the road when a clinician investigates anemia: small cells suggest iron problems, large cells point toward vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

sections.heading: Hemoglobin and the Oxygen Cascade
sections.body: Hemoglobin is the molecule that makes blood red and vertebrate life at scale possible. Oxygen dissolves poorly in water — plain plasma at body temperature holds only about 0.3 milliliters of oxygen per deciliter — while whole blood carries about 20 milliliters per deciliter, a nearly seventyfold amplification supplied by hemoglobin. Each hemoglobin molecule is a four-part machine: two alpha and two beta protein chains in the adult form called hemoglobin A, each chain cradling a heme group, a flat ring with a single ferrous iron atom at its center. Each iron binds one oxygen molecule, so one hemoglobin carries four, and one gram of hemoglobin binds 1.34 milliliters of oxygen; at 15 grams per deciliter the arithmetic yields blood's 20-milliliter capacity. The subtlety is in how the four sites cooperate. When one heme binds oxygen, the protein shifts shape from a low-affinity tense state to a high-affinity relaxed state, making the next binding easier — work for which Max Perutz, who solved hemoglobin's structure in 1959 after 22 years of X-ray crystallography, shared a Nobel Prize. Cooperativity gives the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve its S shape, and the S shape is the whole trick: at the lung's oxygen pressure of about 100 millimeters of mercury, hemoglobin loads to 97 percent saturation, yet at the 40 millimeters typical of resting tissue it unloads a quarter of its cargo, and at the 20 millimeters of hard-working muscle it gives up most of the rest. The midpoint of the curve, the P50, sits near 27 millimeters of mercury and slides with conditions. Acid, carbon dioxide and heat — precisely the exhaust of active tissue — shift the curve rightward so hemoglobin releases oxygen exactly where it is needed most, an effect the Danish physiologist Christian Bohr described in 1904. The red cell's own 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate does the same, and rises within days at high altitude to sweeten unloading. Fetal hemoglobin, built with gamma chains instead of beta, binds 2,3-BPG poorly and therefore holds oxygen more tightly, letting the fetus siphon oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta. The system's vulnerabilities follow from its chemistry. Carbon monoxide binds the same iron site about 240 times more avidly than oxygen, so even 0.1 percent carbon monoxide in air converts half of hemoglobin into useless carboxyhemoglobin — and it also locks the remaining sites into high affinity so they will not release what they hold, which is why carbon monoxide poisoning suffocates at the tissue level while the skin stays deceptively pink. Oxidize the iron from ferrous to ferric and you get methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen at all; certain drugs and nitrites push this conversion faster than the red cell's repair enzyme can reverse it. And when more than about 5 grams per deciliter of hemoglobin sits deoxygenated in surface capillaries, lips and nail beds turn visibly blue — the sign called cyanosis.

sections.heading: Carrying Carbon Dioxide and Guarding pH
sections.body: Every minute at rest the tissues produce about 200 milliliters of carbon dioxide, and blood must haul it to the lungs without letting it acidify the body, because carbon dioxide dissolved in water forms carbonic acid. The cargo travels in three forms. About seven percent rides simply dissolved in plasma. Roughly 23 percent binds to the amino groups of proteins, chiefly hemoglobin itself, forming carbamino compounds — and conveniently, deoxygenated hemoglobin binds carbon dioxide better than oxygenated hemoglobin does, so the act of dropping off oxygen in the tissues increases capacity for the return freight, a reciprocity described by the Scottish physiologist John Scott Haldane. The remaining 70 percent converts to bicarbonate inside the red cell, where the enzyme carbonic anhydrase — one of the fastest enzymes known, processing on the order of a million reactions per second — combines carbon dioxide with water into carbonic acid, which instantly splits into a hydrogen ion and a bicarbonate ion. Hemoglobin soaks up the hydrogen ion, and the bicarbonate is exported to plasma in exchange for a chloride ion drawn inward, the so-called chloride shift. At the lungs every step runs backward: bicarbonate re-enters the cell, reforms carbon dioxide, and diffuses out into the alveolar air to be exhaled. This chemistry doubles as the body's principal pH buffer. The ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide sets blood pH according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, and with bicarbonate near 24 millimoles per liter and arterial carbon dioxide pressure near 40 millimeters of mercury, the result is the normal arterial pH of about 7.40, defended within 7.35 to 7.45. The genius of the system is that each side of the ratio has its own control knob. The lungs adjust carbon dioxide within seconds to minutes: breathe twice as hard and carbon dioxide pressure falls, raising pH — which is why panic hyperventilation causes tingling lips and lightheadedness, as the sudden alkalinity lowers ionized calcium and excites nerves. The kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days, excreting acid and regenerating bicarbonate. Disorders are named for the side that moves first: respiratory acidosis when failing lungs let carbon dioxide accumulate, respiratory alkalosis from overbreathing, metabolic acidosis when acids accumulate — as in diabetic ketoacidosis or when oxygen-starved tissues pour out lactic acid — and metabolic alkalosis, classically from prolonged vomiting of stomach acid. Each primary disturbance summons compensation from the other organ: a patient with metabolic acidosis breathes deep and fast, the pattern called Kussmaul respiration, blowing off carbon dioxide to drag pH back toward normal. The tolerances are tight. Below a pH of roughly 6.8 or above 7.8, enzymes denature, cardiac muscle fails and survival is rare; most of clinical acid-base medicine is the art of reading the bicarbonate, the carbon dioxide and the pH together to deduce which organ failed first and how far the other has gone to cover for it.

sections.heading: White Blood Cells: The Mobile Defense Force
sections.body: White blood cells, or leukocytes, are the only complete cells in blood — nucleus, mitochondria and all — and blood is not their workplace so much as their highway. A healthy adult carries 4,500 to 11,000 of them per microliter, outnumbered by red cells roughly 700 to one, yet this small force is the body's entire mobile defense. The census, called a differential count, recognizes five types, and their normal proportions are worth memorizing because departures from them are diagnostic clues. Neutrophils make up 50 to 70 percent; lymphocytes 20 to 40 percent; monocytes 2 to 8 percent; eosinophils 1 to 4 percent; and basophils under 1 percent — generations of students have kept the order straight with the mnemonic "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas." Structurally the five divide into granulocytes — neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils, whose cytoplasm is packed with chemical-loaded granules and whose nuclei are lobed — and the agranulocytes, lymphocytes and monocytes, with cleaner cytoplasm and rounder nuclei. Functionally they divide differently: into the innate immune system, the fast, hard-wired responders that treat every threat by category, and the adaptive immune system, the lymphocytes, which learn specific enemies and remember them for decades. What makes leukocytes remarkable as blood cells is that they leave the blood. Summoned by chemical distress signals from infected or injured tissue, a white cell rolls along the vessel wall, gripping adhesion molecules that inflamed endothelium displays like flags, stops, and then squeezes bodily between the wall's cells — a maneuver called diapedesis — before crawling through the tissue up the chemical gradient toward the trouble, a guided migration called chemotaxis. At any moment far more white cells are in tissues, marrow reserves and vessel-wall margins than in the circulating blood; the blood count samples only the traffic, not the army. That is why the count moves so informatively. A count above 11,000, leukocytosis, most often means bacterial infection — neutrophils pour in from marrow reserves within hours, and desperate marrow even ships immature "band" forms, a sign clinicians call a left shift — but hard exercise, steroids and stress hormones also lift the count by shaking marginated cells into the stream. A count below 4,500, leukopenia, is more ominous, appearing when chemotherapy, radiation, certain drugs or marrow disease suppress production, or when overwhelming sepsis consumes cells faster than they can be replaced. Some viral infections invert the usual pattern, suppressing neutrophils while lymphocytes surge. The absolute neutrophil count is watched most closely of all: below 500 per microliter, a state called severe neutropenia, ordinary skin and gut bacteria become lethal threats, and a fever in such a patient is treated as an emergency requiring immediate antibiotics, because the patient has, in effect, no first line of defense left at all.

sections.heading: Neutrophils, Macrophages and the Innate First Response
sections.body: When a splinter breaches the skin, the counterattack begins within minutes, and its shock troops are neutrophils. These short-lived cells — hours to a few days in circulation — are professional killers built for expendability. Arriving first at any bacterial invasion, a neutrophil engulfs microbes by phagocytosis, wrapping its membrane around the target and sealing it in an internal bubble, then kills what it has swallowed with a chemical arsenal: an oxygen-consuming "respiratory burst" generates reactive oxygen species, and the enzyme myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorous acid — literally the active chemistry of household bleach, brewed inside a cell. Neutrophils also fight after death: they can extrude their own DNA as sticky webs called neutrophil extracellular traps, or NETs, which snare bacteria in a mesh laced with antimicrobial proteins. The thick yellow-white fluid of pus is largely spent neutrophils, dead bacteria and liquefied tissue — the debris field of this battle. Behind the shock troops come the monocytes, the largest blood cells at 15 to 20 micrometers, which circulate for a day or two and then enter tissues and transform into macrophages — "big eaters" — long-lived cells that can consume hundreds of bacteria apiece, clear the dead neutrophils, and remodel the damage. Many tissues keep resident macrophages permanently on station under local names: Kupffer cells lining the liver's blood channels, alveolar macrophages patrolling the lung's air sacs, microglia in the brain, osteoclasts dissolving old bone. Macrophages are also the intelligence service of immunity: after digesting an invader they display its protein fragments on their surface and present them to lymphocytes, converting a street fight into a targeted campaign. The remaining granulocytes are specialists. Eosinophils, staining brick-red with the dye eosin, are armed against enemies too large to swallow — parasitic worms — which they attack by docking on the surface and discharging granule proteins; in the parasite-scarce modern world they are noticed mainly when allergic disease or asthma recruits them into mischief. Basophils, and their tissue-dwelling cousins the mast cells, carry granules of histamine that dilate vessels and make them leaky; they are central players in allergy, and their overwrought systemic discharge is anaphylaxis. The coordinated result of all this cellular work is inflammation, whose four cardinal signs the Roman writer Celsus recorded in the first century: rubor, calor, dolor and tumor — redness, heat, pain and swelling — each with a mechanism, as widened vessels bring more warm blood, leaky capillaries let protein-rich fluid swell the tissue, and chemical mediators such as prostaglandins and bradykinin sensitize nerve endings. Fever completes the picture: molecules called pyrogens, including bacterial fragments and the messenger interleukin-1, reset the hypothalamic thermostat upward, and moderate fever measurably accelerates immune cell function while slowing many microbes. It is a system tuned for overwhelming force, and much of medicine consists of restraining it when it fires at the wrong target.

sections.heading: Lymphocytes: Memory and Precision
sections.body: Lymphocytes are the reason you catch measles once. Small, round and unassuming under the microscope, they carry the immune system's two deepest inventions — specificity and memory — and they come in three principal kinds. B lymphocytes, matured in the bone marrow, are antibody factories in waiting. Each B cell displays a receptor of one unique shape, generated by randomly shuffling gene segments during development, a mechanism worked out by Susumu Tonegawa in the 1970s; across the whole B cell population the body holds a library of billions of shapes, prepared in advance for molecules it has never met. When a B cell's receptor happens to fit an invader's surface, and it receives confirmation from a helper T cell, it multiplies furiously — the process of clonal selection — and its descendants become plasma cells secreting up to 2,000 antibody molecules per second. Antibodies, also called immunoglobulins, work by binding: they clump microbes, coat them for easier eating by phagocytes, block the sites viruses use to enter cells, and trigger the complement protein cascade that punches holes in bacterial membranes. Five classes divide the work — IgM, the bulky first responder of a new infection; IgG, the durable workhorse that also crosses the placenta to protect a newborn; IgA, guarding the wet surfaces of gut and airway and delivered in breast milk; IgE, the anti-parasite class hijacked in allergy; and IgD, mostly a receptor on young B cells. T lymphocytes, schooled in the thymus, work in cells rather than fluids. Helper T cells, marked by the surface protein CD4, are the orchestra conductors: they recognize enemy fragments presented by macrophages and dendritic cells and then license B cells, energize killers and summon phagocytes with chemical messengers called cytokines — which is why HIV, a virus that specifically infects and destroys CD4 cells, collapses the whole defense when untreated. Cytotoxic T cells, marked CD8, inspect the peptide fragments that every nucleated cell continuously displays in surface holders called MHC molecules; a cell showing viral peptides is ordered to self-destruct. Natural killer cells, a third lineage, apply the inverse test, executing cells that have suspiciously stopped displaying MHC — a common trick of viruses and tumors. After victory, most of the expanded clone dies away, but a cadre of memory cells persists for years or decades, and a second meeting with the same microbe triggers a response so fast and massive that illness often never begins. Vaccination is the deliberate manufacture of that memory without the disease, a practice Edward Jenner began in 1796 with cowpox against smallpox — and which ended smallpox itself, declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980 after a global campaign. Immunity's precision has a price: lymphocyte clones that react against the body's own tissues normally are deleted or suppressed, and when that tolerance fails, the result is autoimmune disease, from type 1 diabetes to lupus.

sections.heading: Platelets and the First Seconds of Hemostasis
sections.body: Blood must stay liquid inside vessels yet solidify instantly at a breach, and the resolution of that contradiction is called hemostasis. Its first responders are platelets: not cells but cell fragments, 2 to 4 micrometers across, budded off in their thousands from giant bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes, which extend arms into the marrow's blood channels and let the flow shear platelets away. A healthy count runs 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter, each platelet living 8 to 10 days, with about a third of the total held in reserve in the spleen. In an intact vessel platelets cruise inert, actively pacified by the endothelium — the single-cell lining of every vessel — which releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin and wears surface enzymes that dismantle platelet-activating signals. Injury flips the switch. Torn endothelium exposes collagen, the structural protein of the vessel wall, and a plasma protein called von Willebrand factor instantly bridges collagen to receptors on passing platelets, snagging them against the current like burrs. Adhesion transforms the platelet: it throws out spiky pseudopods, dumps granules of ADP and serotonin, and synthesizes thromboxane A2 — and ADP with thromboxane recruits and activates more platelets in an accelerating chain reaction. Activation also flips the platelet's surface receptor GPIIb/IIIa into a sticky conformation that grabs fibrinogen, and because each fibrinogen molecule has two ends, it bridges platelets into a growing aggregate. Within three to seven minutes of a small cut — the clinical "bleeding time" — the pile of interlinked platelets forms a plug that stops blood in vessels up to about a millimeter across. Meanwhile the injured vessel itself constricts, smooth muscle clamping down within seconds in response to injury reflexes and the serotonin and thromboxane just released, reducing flow through the breach by half or more while the plug assembles. This platelet phase is where two of medicine's most consumed drugs act. Aspirin permanently disables the enzyme cyclooxygenase that platelets need to make thromboxane A2; since platelets cannot synthesize new protein, one low dose blunts aggregation for the fragment's whole 8-to-10-day life, the basis of low-dose aspirin after heart attack. Clopidogrel and its relatives block the ADP receptor instead. The cost of both is a modestly longer bleeding time and easier bruising.
