Counts matter as much as function: below about 50,000 platelets per microliter surgery becomes hazardous, and below 10,000 spontaneous bleeding can occur — pinpoint skin hemorrhages called petechiae, gum and nose bleeding, and, most feared, bleeding into the brain, which is why very low counts are treated with platelet transfusion. A platelet plug alone, though, is soft, and arterial pressure would soon push through it. Durability requires weaving the plug through with insoluble protein cable — fibrin — and that is the work of the coagulation cascade, an enzymatic amplifier waiting in the plasma.

sections.heading: The Coagulation Cascade and Clot Retirement
sections.body: Coagulation is a chain of enzymes activating enzymes, and its architecture is an amplifier: a few trigger molecules at the top yield a burst of millions of fibrin strands at the bottom within minutes. The classical scheme numbers the clotting factors with Roman numerals I through XIII, nearly all synthesized by the liver, four of them — II, VII, IX and X — requiring vitamin K for a finishing chemical step that lets them grip calcium. In the modern, cell-based understanding, clotting begins when injury exposes tissue factor, a protein abundant on cells outside the vessel but hidden from blood, which captures circulating factor VII and ignites the sequence; the older laboratory division into an "extrinsic" pathway (tested by prothrombin time, PT) and an "intrinsic" pathway (tested by activated partial thromboplastin time, aPTT) survives because those two tests still localize which factors are missing. All routes converge on factor X, which with its partner factor V converts prothrombin into thrombin — the cascade's master enzyme. Thrombin snips soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that self-assemble into strands; factor XIII then cross-links the strands covalently, and the mesh nets platelets and red cells into a firm clot. Thrombin also feeds back to accelerate its own production and further activate platelets, an autocatalytic loop that converts a trickle into an explosion — and every enzymatic step requires calcium and assembles on the phospholipid surface that activated platelets helpfully expose, confining the explosion to the wound. Balance is everything. Antithrombin circulates to strangle stray thrombin — the drug heparin works by supercharging it a thousandfold — while proteins C and S shut down the cascade's amplifiers; inherited shortages of these brakes, or the common factor V Leiden mutation that resists them, tilt carriers toward unwanted clots. Warfarin, derived from a compound discovered after cattle bled to death eating spoiled sweet clover in the 1920s, blocks vitamin K recycling and so cripples factors II, VII, IX and X; its dose is tracked with the standardized prothrombin time called the INR. Newer oral drugs inhibit factor Xa or thrombin directly. Deficiency diseases map the cascade: hemophilia A, an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII carried through Queen Victoria's descendants into the Russian, Spanish and German royal houses, and hemophilia B, a deficiency of factor IX, both produce deep joint and muscle bleeds and are treated today with recombinant factor replacement. Once a vessel heals, the clot must go. Retraction comes first — platelet motors pull the fibrin net tighter, squeezing out serum and drawing the wound edges together — and then fibrinolysis: plasminogen woven into the clot is converted by tissue plasminogen activator into plasmin, an enzyme that dices fibrin into fragments. Medicine borrows this too, infusing recombinant tPA within the first hours of ischemic stroke or heart attack to dissolve the offending clot while it is still fresh.

sections.heading: Blood Types and the Rules of Transfusion
sections.body: Transfusion killed as often as it cured until 1901, when the Austrian physician Karl Landsteiner mixed blood samples from his laboratory colleagues and discovered why: human red cells come in incompatible surface types. The ABO system rests on sugar chains projecting from the red cell membrane. Type A cells carry the A sugar, type B the B sugar, type AB both, and type O neither — the letter O from the German "ohne," meaning without. The dangerous half of the system is in the plasma: by a few months of age, everyone manufactures IgM antibodies against whichever A or B sugars their own cells lack, apparently primed by similar sugars on ordinary gut bacteria. A type A person therefore carries anti-B antibody, type O carries both anti-A and anti-B, and type AB carries neither. Transfuse type A red cells into a type B recipient and the recipient's anti-A antibodies coat the incoming cells within minutes, activating complement and rupturing them inside the vessels — an acute hemolytic reaction producing fever, back pain, red-brown urine from spilled hemoglobin, kidney failure and, in perhaps one in ten severe cases, death. This is why type O red cells, bare of both sugars, serve as the near-universal red cell donation, and why type AB individuals, with no anti-A or anti-B, can receive any ABO red cells — while for plasma the logic inverts, AB plasma being the universal donor because it contains neither antibody. The second system that matters at the bedside is Rh, centered on the D antigen, a membrane protein carried by about 85 percent of people, who are called Rh-positive. Unlike ABO antibodies, anti-D does not preexist; an Rh-negative person makes it only after exposure to Rh-positive cells. The classic tragedy unfolds in pregnancy: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is sensitized by fetal cells that leak across at delivery, and her IgG anti-D — the class that crosses the placenta — attacks the red cells of the next Rh-positive fetus, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn, historically a major killer of infants. Since 1968 this has been almost abolished by RhoGAM, an injection of ready-made anti-D given to Rh-negative mothers around 28 weeks and at delivery, which mops up fetal cells before her immune system can notice them and form its own permanent antibody. Some three dozen other blood group systems exist — Kell, Duffy, Kidd and the rest — that occasionally complicate matters for repeatedly transfused patients who accumulate antibodies against them. Practice therefore layers safeguards: the laboratory types every recipient for ABO and Rh, screens their plasma for irregular antibodies, and crossmatches donor cells against recipient plasma before release. In uncontrolled emergency hemorrhage, when there is no time even for typing, the universal choice is O-negative red cells. ABO frequencies vary by ancestry, but O and A are everywhere the common types, and AB-negative, at well under one percent, the rarest.

sections.heading: Where Blood Comes From: The Marrow Factory
sections.body: Every blood cell descends from a single self-renewing ancestor, the hematopoietic stem cell, and a few hundred thousand of them, resident in the bone marrow, sustain a production line of staggering throughput: on the order of 500 billion blood cells manufactured per day, every day, for a lifetime — red cells at about two million per second, plus the entire white cell and platelet supply. In the fetus the work migrates — yolk sac first, then liver and spleen, then bone — and in adults active red marrow retreats to the axial skeleton: pelvis, sternum, ribs, vertebrae, skull, and the upper ends of the long bones, which is why marrow samples are taken from the hip. The stem cell's daughters commit stepwise to lineages: one branch toward the myeloid family — red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes — the other toward lymphocytes. Each branch answers to its own hormonal throttle. For red cells the throttle is erythropoietin, or EPO, a hormone made by oxygen sensing cells in the kidney; when tissue oxygen falls, EPO rises and the marrow lifts output. This is the loop behind altitude acclimatization — weeks at elevation raise hematocrit measurably — behind the anemia of kidney failure, when the EPO source itself is destroyed, and behind blood doping in sport, where injected EPO builds an illegally elevated red cell mass. Thrombopoietin, made in the liver, governs platelets; G-CSF drives neutrophil production and is injected to rescue chemotherapy patients from neutropenia. Building a red cell from a committed precursor takes about seven days, during which the cell fills with hemoglobin and finally ejects its nucleus; it enters the blood as a reticulocyte, still carrying ribosome remnants for a day or two, and the reticulocyte count is the marrow's live production gauge — high after bleeding as the factory compensates, inappropriately low when the factory itself is the problem. Production has three non-negotiable raw materials. Iron is the heme metal: the body owns only 3 to 4 grams, two-thirds of it inside hemoglobin, absorbs a mere 1 to 2 milligrams a day in the duodenum, and recycles 20 to 25 milligrams daily from retired red cells — a nearly closed loop policed by the liver hormone hepcidin, which locks iron gates shut during inflammation. Vitamin B12 and folate are the DNA-synthesis vitamins; without them dividing precursors stall and enlarge. B12 absorption is famously baroque — it must bind intrinsic factor, a protein from the stomach's parietal cells, to be absorbed in the final stretch of the small intestine — and the autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia, fatal before 1926, when George Minot and William Murphy showed that eating liver, later found to be a B12 reservoir, cured it. The liver stores several years of B12, so deficiency creeps in slowly; folate stores last only months.

sections.heading: The Cargo Manifest: Nutrients, Hormones, Heat and Waste
sections.body: Think of the circulation as a logistics company with one truck fleet and thousands of clients, and the manifest becomes legible. Fuel delivery is the steadiest contract. Glucose is held near 70 to 100 milligrams per deciliter fasting by an elegant push-pull: after a meal the pancreas releases insulin, which orders muscle and fat to take glucose up and the liver to bank it as glycogen; between meals glucagon reverses the flow, and the liver can pour out glucose for a day or so before turning to manufacturing it afresh from amino acids. The brain, consuming about 120 grams of glucose daily and storing essentially none, is the client the system exists to protect — confusion begins when glucose falls below roughly 55 milligrams per deciliter and coma below 40. Fat, being oil in a watery medium, ships in specialized containers called lipoproteins, named by density: chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut; VLDL exports triglyceride from the liver; LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues — the "bad" particle, because excess LDL infiltrates artery walls and seeds atherosclerotic plaque; HDL runs the return service, ferrying cholesterol back to the liver, which is why higher HDL correlates with cleaner arteries. A standard lipid panel is simply a count of these containers. Hormones are the mail: chemical letters posted by glands into the blood, diluted into concentrations of nanograms or picograms per deciliter, and read only by cells bearing the matching receptor. Some travel dissolved; many — thyroid hormone, cortisol, sex steroids — ride bound to carrier proteins, with only the free fraction biologically active, a nuance that complicates laboratory interpretation. Waste hauling runs continuously. Protein metabolism yields ammonia, which the liver detoxifies into urea for the kidneys to excrete; muscle sheds creatinine at so steady a rate that its blood level serves as the standard gauge of kidney function; the spent heme of dead red cells travels as bilirubin to the liver for export in bile. During hard exercise, muscle exports lactate, which the liver retrieves and rebuilds into glucose — the Cori cycle, a loop between organs stitched entirely through the bloodstream. Blood also carries heat. Water's high heat capacity makes blood an excellent coolant: it collects roughly 100 watts of resting metabolic heat — ten times that in heavy exercise — from the core and delivers it to the skin, where flow is the control valve. Skin perfusion can swing from about 250 milliliters per minute in cold to several liters per minute in heat, which is why faces flush with exertion and fingers blanch in winter, and why alcohol's artificial skin flush feels warm while actually dumping core heat. Finally, the fleet carries whatever medicine adds: every swallowed drug that survives the liver's first inspection is distributed by plasma, much of it seated on albumin, and the entire science of dosing — peaks, troughs, half-lives — is the study of this traffic.

sections.heading: When Blood Fails: Anemias, Cancers and Clotting Gone Wrong
sections.body: Anemia — too little hemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen — is the most common blood disorder on Earth, affecting on the order of two billion people, and its symptoms are the sound of an engine starved of air: fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, pale skin and conjunctivae, a pounding or racing heart as the pump compensates with volume for what each deciliter lacks. The causes sort usefully by cell size. Small pale cells point to iron deficiency, the world leader, driven by menstrual and gastrointestinal blood loss and by diets poor in absorbable iron — and in anyone without an obvious source, especially an older adult, it demands a search for hidden bleeding, because a slowly oozing colon cancer classically announces itself this way. Large cells point to B12 or folate deficiency, where DNA synthesis lags and precursors balloon; B12 lack adds a neurological dimension — numb feet, unsteady gait — that folate lack spares. Normal-sized cells in insufficient number accompany chronic disease, kidney failure with its lost erythropoietin, or a failing marrow. Two great inherited anemias deserve their own lines. Sickle cell disease arises from a single substitution in the beta-globin gene — valine for glutamate at position six — that lets deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerize into stiff rods, warping red cells into fragile crescents that jam small vessels, producing excruciating vaso-occlusive crises, strokes in children and a lifespan of sickled cells of merely 10 to 20 days; the mutation persists because carrying one copy confers meaningful protection against falciparum malaria, and it is common wherever malaria was. Thalassemias, the other Mediterranean and Asian legacy, are quantitative failures to produce enough globin chains at all. Blood's cancers are the clonal escape of its own production lines. Leukemias flood marrow and blood with a malignant white cell clone — acute forms with immature blasts that kill in weeks untreated, chronic forms that smolder for years; chronic myeloid leukemia carries a signature chromosome fusion, BCR-ABL, and became the proof that a cancer can be switched off by a designed molecule when the inhibitor imatinib entered practice in 2001. Lymphomas are lymphocyte cancers massed in nodes; myeloma is the malignant plasma cell eroding bone and spilling one useless antibody. Marrow failure — aplastic anemia — empties all three cell lines at once. Clotting fails in both directions. Hemophilia and von Willebrand disease bleed; the thrombophilias clot, loading veins with thrombi that break loose as pulmonary emboli. And in the worst crises of sepsis and obstetrics, disseminated intravascular coagulation ignites clotting everywhere at once until the factors and platelets are consumed and the patient simultaneously clots and bleeds — the system's two failure modes at the same catastrophic moment.

sections.heading: Reading Your Own Blood: Tests, Donation and Warning Signs
sections.body: The complete blood count, or CBC, is the most ordered laboratory test in medicine, and reading one is a learnable skill. Its backbone is three numbers and their supporting cast: hemoglobin (roughly 13.5 to 17.5 grams per deciliter for men, 12 to 15.5 for women) with hematocrit alongside; the white cell count (4,500 to 11,000 per microliter) with its differential percentages; and platelets (150,000 to 450,000). The red cell indices refine the story — mean corpuscular volume classifies an anemia as small-celled, normal or large-celled before any further test is drawn — and the reticulocyte count asks whether the marrow is responding. A basic metabolic panel reads the plasma itself: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, glucose, and the kidney pair of urea nitrogen and creatinine; liver enzymes and bilirubin extend it; ferritin reports iron stores, and hemoglobin A1c summarizes three months of glucose control by measuring how much sugar has bonded to hemoglobin over the red cell's 120-day life. Three habits make lay reading safer. First, judge trends, not single values — a hemoglobin of 12.9 means one thing as a stable baseline and another as the latest point in a year-long slide. Second, expect a scatter of trivial flags; reference ranges are drawn to contain 95 percent of healthy people, so one in twenty healthy results falls outside by construction. Third, let the laboratory interpret nothing dangerous alone: a few findings warrant a professional call the same day, notably any new hemoglobin below about 10, a neutrophil count below 1,000, platelets below 50,000, or a potassium outside 3.0 to 6.0. Blood donation is the system's civic dimension: a standard whole-blood donation of about 470 milliliters — under a tenth of blood volume — is tolerated because plasma volume refills within 24 to 48 hours, though the donated red cells take four to six weeks to replace, setting the customary 8-to- 12-week minimum between donations. Donated units are separated into red cells, platelets and plasma, so one donation can serve several patients; with red cells storable about 42 days and platelets only five to seven, the supply is perpetually perishable, and a few percent of the eligible population donating carries entire health systems. Finally, the warning signs that blood itself is failing deserve memorizing. Unexplained bruising, pinpoint red skin spots, bleeding gums or nosebleeds that will not stop suggest platelet or clotting failure. Progressive exhaustion with pallor suggests anemia; recurrent fevers and infections suggest white cell failure; drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss and painless swollen nodes are lymphoma's classic triad. A warm, swollen, tender calf — especially after immobility — suggests deep vein thrombosis, and if breathlessness or chest pain joins it, the concern becomes pulmonary embolism: an emergency, not an appointment. For external bleeding the first aid is unchanged for a century: firm, direct, uninterrupted pressure, and for a limb wound that soaks through everything, a tourniquet and the fastest possible route to help.

guides.safetyNote: This guide is educational and cannot diagnose. Uncontrolled bleeding, chest pain with breathlessness, one-sided limb swelling, or sudden severe pallor and fainting are emergencies: apply firm direct pressure to external bleeding and seek professional medical care immediately.

guides.title: The Coronary Circulation
guides.summary: A full account of the heart's own blood supply: the anatomy of the coronary arteries and veins, why the heart perfuses itself in diastole, how flow is regulated and measured, and how atherosclerosis, spasm and thrombosis turn that supply into the world's commonest cause of death.

sections.heading: The Pump That Cannot Drink From Its Own Reservoir
sections.body: Roughly five litres of blood pass through the chambers of the heart every minute, yet almost none of it feeds the heart muscle. The walls of the left ventricle are one to one and a half centimetres of dense working muscle, far too thick for oxygen to diffuse inward from the blood in the cavity, and the pressures and turbulence inside a beating ventricle make any such arrangement useless anyway. The heart therefore has its own dedicated arterial supply, branching off the aorta within the first two centimetres of its course, before any other organ takes a share. That system is the coronary circulation, and understanding it is the single most useful piece of anatomy and physiology a non-specialist can learn, because its failure is the commonest cause of death in most of the world. The name comes from the Latin corona, a crown or wreath, because the two main arteries encircle the base of the heart in a rough ring lying in the grooves between the atria and the ventricles, with branches running down the front and back of the ventricles like the pendant strings of a garland. It is an elegant arrangement with several unusual properties. It is a high-priority circulation, taking its supply first. It is largely an end-artery system in practice, meaning that although small connections exist between territories, they are usually too small to rescue a region if its own artery is suddenly blocked. And, uniquely among major circulations, it is squeezed shut by the very organ it supplies each time that organ contracts, so that the heart is largely perfused during the relaxation phase between beats. These features explain almost everything about coronary disease. Because each region has essentially one supplier, an occlusion produces a sharply demarcated area of dying muscle rather than a diffuse impairment. Because the muscle already extracts most of the oxygen delivered to it at rest, it cannot compensate for a supply problem by extracting more, and must instead be given more flow. Because flow happens in diastole, a fast heart rate is dangerous in a way it is not for other organs, since speeding up shortens diastole disproportionately and cuts the perfusion window at exactly the moment demand is highest. And because the innermost layer of the ventricular wall is both the most compressed and the hardest working, ischaemic damage starts there and spreads outward, which is why time is the decisive variable in a heart attack. None of this is only of interest to cardiologists. Recognising the symptom pattern, understanding why chest discomfort on exertion means something different from chest discomfort at rest, and knowing why minutes matter after an occlusion are practical knowledge with a measurable effect on survival.

sections.heading: Where the Coronary Arteries Begin: The Aortic Sinuses
sections.body: The aortic valve has three semilunar cusps, each shaped like a shallow pocket. Behind each cusp the aortic wall bulges outward into a small chamber called an aortic sinus, or sinus of Valsalva after the eighteenth-century Bolognese anatomist Antonio Maria Valsalva. These bulges are not decorative. During ejection they hold the opened cusps clear of the aortic wall so that the valve leaflets do not seal against it, and they create small eddies of blood behind each cusp that help snap the valve shut cleanly when ventricular pressure falls. Two of the three sinuses carry an arterial opening, called an ostium. The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior sinus and the right coronary artery from the anterior sinus; the third, the right posterior sinus, has no artery and is called the non-coronary sinus. The ostia sit typically in the upper third of each sinus, near or slightly above the level of the free edge of the cusp. The exact height matters clinically, because a modern transcatheter aortic valve implanted too high can push a native calcified leaflet across an ostium and obstruct it, a rare but catastrophic complication. The position also creates the mechanism by which the coronary circulation is filled. During systole, when the ventricle is contracting and the aortic valve is open, blood is rushing past the ostia at high velocity, the cusps are swung back toward them, and the myocardium is squeezing its own intramural vessels. Filling is therefore poor. When the ventricle relaxes and aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, the valve snaps shut, the column of blood in the aorta rebounds against the closed cusps and settles into the sinuses, and that reservoir of pressurised blood is driven into the coronary ostia. The elastic recoil of the aorta, the windkessel effect, sustains this pressure across diastole. This is why a stiff, non-compliant aorta and a low diastolic blood pressure both impair coronary perfusion, and it is one reason aortic regurgitation, in which diastolic pressure collapses because blood leaks backward into the ventricle, can cause angina in someone with entirely normal coronary arteries. Variation is common and mostly harmless. The right coronary artery frequently arises slightly higher than the left. Separate ostia for the conus branch occur in perhaps half of hearts. More consequential anomalies exist: an artery arising from the wrong sinus and then running between the aorta and pulmonary trunk can be compressed during exertion, which is a recognised cause of sudden death in young athletes and is one of the findings that pre-participation cardiac screening is looking for. A single coronary artery supplying the whole heart from one ostium occurs in roughly one in two thousand people. Because the ostia are the first branches off the aorta, they are also involved in aortic dissection, and a dissection flap that shears across a coronary ostium produces an infarction as its presenting event, most often inferior because the right ostium is the more commonly affected.

sections.heading: The Left Coronary System: Left Main, LAD and Circumflex
sections.body: The left coronary artery begins as the left main stem, a short trunk usually between five and fifteen millimetres long and about four to five millimetres in diameter, running behind the pulmonary trunk before dividing. In roughly a third of hearts it trifurcates rather than bifurcates, giving an intermediate branch called the ramus intermedius that supplies territory between the two main divisions. The left anterior descending artery, universally abbreviated LAD, runs down the front of the heart in the anterior interventricular groove, the surface furrow overlying the septum, and usually curls around the apex to supply a variable amount of the inferior wall. It has two families of branches. Diagonal branches, often numbered first and second, run leftward across the front wall of the left ventricle. Septal perforators dive directly backward into the interventricular septum, and they are functionally important because the septum contains the bundle of His and the proximal bundle branches; septal infarction is therefore a common cause of new conduction block. The LAD typically supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior two thirds of the septum, and the apex, which together represent something like forty to fifty percent of the left ventricular mass. That is why proximal LAD occlusion is nicknamed the widow-maker: it removes the single largest territory in one stroke. The left circumflex artery, abbreviated LCx, turns leftward into the left atrioventricular groove, wrapping around toward the back of the heart under the left atrial appendage. Its main branches are the obtuse marginal arteries running down the lateral free wall of the left ventricle. It supplies the lateral wall and, depending on dominance, a variable share of the posterior and inferior walls. In a minority of people it also supplies the sinoatrial node. Two anatomical points have outsized clinical weight. First, significant narrowing of the left main stem threatens both the LAD and the circumflex simultaneously, jeopardising the majority of the working myocardium, which is why left main disease has historically been an indication for surgical bypass rather than watchful waiting. Second, branch points are where atherosclerosis preferentially develops, because at a bifurcation the flow along the outer wall of the daughter vessel is slow, disturbed and oscillatory rather than smoothly laminar. Endothelial cells sense the frictional drag of flowing blood, called shear stress, and low or oscillating shear stress switches them into an inflamed, permeable, pro-coagulant state. Plaque location is therefore predictable from fluid mechanics, and the proximal LAD just past the first diagonal is the single commonest site in the body. For the same reason, interventional cardiologists treat bifurcation lesions as a distinct technical problem: a stent placed across a branch point can shift plaque into the side branch and occlude it, and the outer wall of the daughter vessel is exactly where restenosis recurs. Length matters as well as position, since an LAD that wraps the apex means one proximal lesion places an unusually large mass of muscle at risk.

sections.heading: The Right Coronary Artery and the Question of Dominance
sections.body: The right coronary artery emerges from the anterior aortic sinus and runs into the right atrioventricular groove, the furrow between right atrium and right ventricle, curving around the right border of the heart toward the back. Its first branch is usually the conus artery, supplying the right ventricular outflow tract, which sometimes has its own separate ostium. Next, in about sixty percent of people, comes the sinoatrial nodal artery, which runs backward to supply the natural pacemaker at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. Acute marginal branches then descend across the free wall of the right ventricle. The right coronary artery's territory is the right ventricle, much of the right atrium including in most people the sinus node, and, when it reaches far enough around, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and the posterior third of the septum. This last question is what cardiologists mean by dominance, and the terminology is confusing because it does not refer to size or importance but to a single specific branch: the posterior descending artery, which runs forward along the posterior interventricular groove. Whichever artery supplies the posterior descending artery is called dominant. In roughly eighty-five percent of people it comes from the right coronary artery, which is right dominance. In about seven or eight percent it comes from the left circumflex, which is left dominance. In the remainder both contribute, described as codominant or balanced. Dominance has real consequences. In a right-dominant heart, the atrioventricular nodal artery usually arises from the right coronary artery at the crux, the point where the atrioventricular and interventricular grooves meet on the back of the heart. That is the anatomical reason why inferior myocardial infarction so often comes with bradycardia, heart block or a vagally mediated picture of nausea, vomiting and hypotension: the same occlusion that is killing inferior muscle is also starving the conducting tissue and irritating richly vagal territory. In left dominance, the circumflex assumes that role and the left coronary system supplies an unusually large fraction of the heart, so left main disease is even more dangerous. Right ventricular infarction accompanies perhaps a third to half of inferior infarcts, and it changes management sharply. A stunned right ventricle cannot generate enough pressure to fill the left, so cardiac output becomes critically dependent on venous return. Nitrates and diuretics, which reduce venous return and are staples of left-sided heart failure management, can cause abrupt profound hypotension in this setting. The correct treatment is usually intravenous fluid to raise filling pressure and urgent restoration of flow. This is why clinicians record additional right-sided chest electrodes when the standard tracing shows an inferior pattern.

sections.heading: The Microcirculation, the Myocyte and the Venous Return
sections.body: The named arteries visible on an angiogram are only the plumbing at the surface. They are epicardial conduit vessels running on the outside of the heart under a layer of fat, and in health they contribute perhaps five percent of the total resistance to flow. Their job is delivery, not regulation. Control lives in the vessels too small to see. From each epicardial artery, penetrating branches dive perpendicularly through the wall toward the cavity and divide into arterioles of roughly one hundred micrometres down to ten, and it is here, in vessels narrower than a human hair, that the bulk of coronary resistance sits and is actively adjusted. These feed a capillary bed of extraordinary density: cardiac muscle carries roughly three to four thousand capillaries per square millimetre of cross-section, approximately one capillary alongside every muscle fibre, with diffusion distances of only about ten micrometres. Skeletal muscle may have one capillary for every three or four fibres. The cell being supplied is a cardiac myocyte, roughly one hundred micrometres long and twenty across, with mitochondria occupying thirty to forty percent of its volume against perhaps two percent in a fast skeletal fibre. It is almost purely aerobic, burning free fatty acids for around sixty to seventy percent of its energy with glucose and lactate making up the rest, and it stores enough high-energy phosphate for only a handful of beats. Supply must therefore match demand continuously through some two and a half billion contractions, and contraction of an affected segment falters within about ten to fifteen seconds of occlusion. Disease confined to these small vessels, called coronary microvascular dysfunction, can produce genuine ischaemia with entirely normal large arteries on an angiogram; it is common in women and in diabetes, and such patients were for many years wrongly told their pain was not cardiac. Venous return follows three routes. Around sixty to seventy percent of left ventricular drainage runs through epicardial veins accompanying the arteries, the great cardiac vein alongside the left anterior descending and the middle cardiac vein alongside the posterior descending, converging into the coronary sinus, a channel some two centimetres long in the posterior atrioventricular groove that opens into the right atrium beside the inferior vena cava. This is a working highway in modern cardiology, the route for pacing leads in cardiac resynchronisation therapy and for retrograde cardioplegia in surgery. Anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle directly into the right atrium. Strangest are the Thebesian veins, tiny channels draining some myocardium directly into the cardiac chambers including the left ventricle, so that already-deoxygenated blood mixes with freshly oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. With the bronchial circulation this forms the normal anatomical right-to-left shunt, and it is why arterial blood in a healthy person is about ninety-seven or ninety-eight percent saturated rather than a full hundred.

sections.heading: Why the Heart Feeds Itself Between Beats
sections.body: The defining peculiarity of coronary physiology is that contraction of the heart obstructs its own blood supply. The penetrating arteries and arterioles run through the thickness of the ventricular wall, and when that wall contracts it generates tissue pressure that squeezes them. In the left ventricle, cavity pressure rises to around 120 millimetres of mercury in systole while aortic pressure is essentially the same, so the driving pressure across intramural vessels approaches zero. In the deepest layers, flow during systole can fall to nothing and in early contraction there is measurable backflow. The result is that left coronary flow is predominantly diastolic. Roughly eighty percent of left ventricular perfusion occurs during relaxation, and a tracing of flow in the left anterior descending artery shows a sharp dip during systole and a large peak at the start of diastole, which is the mirror image of what flow does in almost every other artery in the body. The right coronary artery behaves differently, because right ventricular pressure only reaches about twenty-five millimetres of mercury; the compressive effect is mild and right coronary flow continues fairly evenly throughout the cycle. Right ventricular ischaemia is therefore uncommon except when right-sided pressures are pathologically high, as in pulmonary hypertension. The practical expression of all this is coronary perfusion pressure, usefully approximated as aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Three things degrade it. A low diastolic blood pressure reduces the driving head. A raised end-diastolic pressure, as in heart failure or severe aortic regurgitation, raises the back pressure the arteries must push against. And tachycardia shortens diastole: at a heart rate of 60 the cardiac cycle lasts one second with roughly two thirds of it in diastole, but at 150 the whole cycle is 0.4 seconds and diastole is compressed far more than systole, so perfusion time per minute falls sharply just as demand climbs. This is the mechanism behind one of the most reliable therapeutic principles in cardiology: slowing the heart with a beta-blocker both cuts oxygen demand and lengthens the window for supply. Layering matters too. The subendocardium, the innermost quarter of the wall, is the most compressed, faces the highest wall stress, and shortens the most, so its oxygen demand is highest while its perfusion window is shortest. It compensates in health by keeping its arterioles more dilated than the outer layers, which means it has less reserve left when trouble comes. Every consequence follows from this: ischaemia begins in the subendocardium, a partial supply shortfall produces subendocardial injury with ST depression on the electrocardiogram, and infarction spreads as a wavefront from the inner surface outward toward the epicardium over several hours.

sections.heading: The Numbers: Flow, Demand and Oxygen Extraction
sections.body: Quantities make coronary physiology intelligible in a way that description alone does not. At rest, total coronary blood flow in an adult is approximately 225 to 250 millilitres per minute, which is about four to five percent of a cardiac output of five litres per minute. Expressed per unit tissue, that is roughly 0.7 to 1.0 millilitres per minute per gram of myocardium, which is among the highest specific flows in the body, exceeded only by the kidney. The heart weighs about 300 grams and represents around 0.4 percent of body mass, so it takes some ten times its proportional share of the circulation. Myocardial oxygen consumption at rest is around 8 to 10 millilitres of oxygen per 100 grams of tissue per minute, roughly twenty times the consumption of resting skeletal muscle, and it can rise to 70 or more during heavy exercise. The determinants of that demand are worth memorising because every anti-anginal drug works by altering one of them: heart rate, contractility, and wall stress. Wall stress follows the law of Laplace, where stress is proportional to chamber pressure multiplied by radius and divided by twice the wall thickness. This explains several observations at once. A dilated ventricle costs more oxygen at the same pressure. High blood pressure raises demand directly. And hypertrophy, by increasing wall thickness, initially reduces stress per unit muscle, which is why it develops, though it eventually becomes counterproductive because thicker muscle outgrows its capillary supply. The decisive number is oxygen extraction. Most tissues extract about twenty-five percent of the oxygen delivered to them, leaving mixed venous blood around seventy-five percent saturated. The myocardium extracts sixty-five to seventy-five percent at rest, so blood in the coronary sinus is only about thirty percent saturated with an oxygen tension near 20 millimetres of mercury, the lowest of any major venous drainage in the body. The heart is already running its extraction near maximum before any demand is placed upon it. The consequence is stark and it is the central fact of ischaemic heart disease. Because extraction cannot meaningfully increase, any rise in oxygen demand must be met almost entirely by a rise in blood flow. A healthy coronary circulation can increase flow four to fivefold, to something like a litre per minute, by dilating its arterioles. If disease has already consumed part of that dilating capacity to maintain resting flow, the ability to meet extra demand is correspondingly reduced, and exertion, cold, emotion, a large meal or a fast arrhythmia will produce a supply gap. Two clinical corollaries follow directly from the extraction figure. Giving supplemental oxygen to someone with normal blood oxygen saturation cannot meaningfully increase myocardial oxygen delivery, and trials have found routine oxygen in uncomplicated infarction to be of no benefit and possibly harmful, which reversed decades of reflex practice. And severe anaemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, which lower the oxygen content of arterial blood rather than the flow, can precipitate angina in arteries that would otherwise cope.

sections.heading: How Flow Is Regulated: Autoregulation and Metabolic Control
sections.body: The coronary circulation matches supply to demand automatically and with remarkable precision. Several mechanisms operate together, and their relative importance is still genuinely debated. Autoregulation is the capacity to hold flow roughly constant despite changes in perfusion pressure. Over a range of about 60 to 140 millimetres of mercury, coronary flow varies little, because a rise in pressure causes the arterioles to constrict and a fall causes them to dilate. Part of this is myogenic: vascular smooth muscle depolarises and contracts when stretched, an intrinsic property described by Bayliss in 1902. Below roughly 60 millimetres of mercury the vessels are already maximally dilated and flow falls in direct proportion to pressure, which is why profound hypotension causes myocardial ischaemia even with normal arteries. Metabolic control is the dominant mechanism day to day, and it is elegantly simple in principle: the products of hard work dilate the vessels supplying the working tissue. Falling oxygen tension itself is a stimulus. Adenosine, produced when ATP is broken down faster than it is regenerated, was for decades taught as the principal mediator, and it is certainly a potent coronary vasodilator, but experiments blocking adenosine receptors leave most of the response intact, so the modern view is that adenosine is one contributor among several rather than the master switch. ATP-sensitive potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle appear to be more important; when cellular energy charge falls these channels open, potassium leaves the cell, the membrane hyperpolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels close and the muscle relaxes. Blocking these channels substantially blunts metabolic dilation. The endothelium, the single-cell lining of every vessel, is the other major controller and is the component that fails first in disease. Endothelial cells respond to increased shear stress from faster flow, and to signals such as acetylcholine and bradykinin, by producing nitric oxide from L-arginine via the enzyme endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Nitric oxide diffuses into the adjacent smooth muscle, activates soluble guanylate cyclase, raises cyclic GMP and causes relaxation. This produces flow-mediated dilation, so that when the small vessels open, the large conduit arteries upstream widen to accommodate the increased flow. Prostacyclin and endothelium-derived hyperpolarising factor act similarly; endothelin-1 acts oppositely as a powerful constrictor. Neural and hormonal influences are comparatively minor and are largely overridden by metabolic demand. Sympathetic stimulation acts on alpha receptors to constrict and beta-2 receptors to dilate, but the dominant effect of adrenaline in exercise is indirect: it drives the heart harder, metabolic demand rises, and the metabolic vasodilators overwhelm any direct constriction. This override is called functional sympatholysis. Endothelial failure inverts one of these responses in a way that is diagnostically useful. Acetylcholine normally dilates a coronary artery by stimulating nitric oxide release, but where the endothelium is damaged the drug reaches the smooth muscle directly and causes constriction instead. Paradoxical constriction to acetylcholine is therefore a marker of endothelial dysfunction, and it is measurable long before any narrowing is visible, which places endothelial injury at the beginning of the disease rather than as a consequence of it.

sections.heading: Coronary Flow Reserve and Measuring What a Narrowing Actually Does
sections.body: A narrowing visible on an image is not the same thing as a narrowing that matters, and the gap between the two has driven a large part of modern cardiology. The physics is governed by Poiseuille's law, in which resistance to laminar flow through a tube is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius. Halving a vessel's diameter therefore increases its resistance sixteenfold. Because the arterioles downstream can compensate by dilating, resting flow is maintained almost unchanged until the narrowing becomes severe: experimentally, resting flow does not fall appreciably until diameter stenosis exceeds about 85 to 90 percent. What falls much earlier is the reserve. Maximal achievable flow begins to decline once diameter stenosis passes roughly 50 percent, and by around 70 percent the reserve is usually insufficient to meet the demands of moderate exertion. This is precisely why someone can have a substantially diseased artery and feel entirely well at rest yet develop chest discomfort walking uphill, and why the first symptom of coronary disease in a sedentary person is sometimes an infarction rather than angina, because they never asked the artery for a flow it could not supply. Coronary flow reserve is the formal expression of this: the ratio of maximal flow, obtained by giving a potent vasodilator such as adenosine or regadenoson, to resting flow. In healthy young arteries it is typically between 3.5 and 5. A value below about 2.0 is regarded as clearly abnormal. Its limitation is that it measures the whole pathway, so a low value cannot distinguish a blockage in the large artery from disease in the microvessels, and it varies with resting haemodynamics. Fractional flow reserve solves the first of those problems and has changed practice. A pressure-sensing guide wire is passed across the narrowing, maximal hyperaemia is induced so that microvascular resistance is minimised and fixed, and the pressure distal to the lesion is divided by the pressure in the aorta. The resulting ratio estimates the fraction of normal maximal flow that still gets through. A value of 0.80 or below is the accepted threshold for a lesion that is causing ischaemia. The FAME trials showed that stenting guided by this measurement, rather than by the eye, produced fewer stents and better outcomes, which is a rare and instructive result: doing less, better. Instantaneous wave-free ratio measures a similar quantity during a specific quiet portion of diastole without needing a vasodilator drug, with a threshold of 0.89. The broader lesson is that the visual severity of a narrowing on an angiogram correlates only moderately with its physiological effect, because angiography shows a two-dimensional silhouette of the lumen and cannot see lesion length, eccentricity, the state of the vessel wall, or how much muscle lies downstream.

sections.heading: Collateral Circulation: The Body's Own Bypass Grafts
sections.body: Human coronary arteries are often described as end arteries, meaning each territory has a single supplier with no meaningful alternative route. This is true enough as a working approximation, but it understates a real and clinically important capacity. Most hearts contain pre-existing collateral channels: small, thin-walled anastomoses, typically 20 to 200 micrometres across, connecting the distal branches of one artery to those of another. In a normal heart these carry negligible flow because there is no pressure difference across them; both ends sit at the same pressure. They are, in effect, dormant bypass routes with the taps closed. A stenosis changes that. Pressure distal to the narrowing falls, a gradient appears across the collateral, and flow begins. That flow itself is the stimulus for growth. The mechanism, called arteriogenesis, is distinct from the sprouting of new capillaries in response to hypoxia, which is angiogenesis. Increased shear stress on the endothelium of the collateral channel activates it, monocytes adhere and infiltrate, they release growth factors and proteases that digest the surrounding matrix, and the vessel remodels outward, acquiring a smooth muscle coat and enlarging perhaps ten to twentyfold in diameter. Since resistance falls with the fourth power of radius, a twentyfold increase in diameter transforms a functionally irrelevant channel into a substantial conduit. The critical variable is time. Arteriogenesis takes weeks to months, so collaterals develop well in gradual progressive narrowing and not at all when a previously healthy artery is suddenly occluded by a rupturing plaque. This produces one of the paradoxes of coronary disease: a person with long-standing severe stable narrowing may have a well-developed collateral network and survive a complete occlusion with modest damage, while a younger person with only a mild plaque that ruptures unexpectedly may sustain a large infarct because nothing had ever prompted collateral growth. It is also why patients with a long history of stable angina sometimes have better outcomes after occlusion than the shortness of their symptom history would suggest. Attempts to induce collateral growth deliberately have been disappointing. Trials of injected growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor and fibroblast growth factor, and of gene and cell therapies, have repeatedly produced encouraging early results that did not survive rigorous randomised testing, and no such treatment is standard care. The one intervention with reasonable supporting evidence is regular endurance exercise, which appears to promote collateral development through repeated episodes of increased flow and shear stress, alongside its many other benefits. External counterpulsation is used in some centres for refractory angina on a similar rationale, with modest and contested evidence. Collateral supply is measurable. During a brief balloon occlusion in the catheter laboratory, the pressure recorded beyond the balloon divided by aortic pressure gives a collateral flow index; values above roughly 0.25 indicate a network sufficient to prevent ischaemia. Human variation is wide and partly genetic, and the reason one person survives an occlusion that kills another is often this, rather than anything about the plaque itself.

sections.heading: How a Coronary Artery Narrows: The Biology of Atherosclerosis
sections.body: Atherosclerosis is not a passive accumulation of fat in a pipe. It is a chronic inflammatory disease of the artery wall, driven by lipid retention, and it begins decades before symptoms. The first step is endothelial dysfunction. Regions of low or oscillating shear stress, notably at branch points and along inner curves, plus the effects of smoking, high blood pressure, high blood sugar and circulating LDL particles, reduce nitric oxide production and make the endothelium permeable and adhesive. Low-density lipoprotein particles cross into the intima, the layer beneath the endothelium, and are trapped there by binding to proteoglycans in the matrix. Retention, not merely entry, is the key event, and it is concentration-dependent, which is the mechanistic reason lowering LDL cholesterol reduces events across the whole range of achievable values. Trapped LDL is chemically modified, chiefly by oxidation. Modified LDL is recognised as foreign. The endothelium expresses adhesion molecules, monocytes stick and migrate into the intima, and there they become macrophages that ingest modified LDL through scavenger receptors. Unlike the normal LDL receptor, scavenger receptors are not switched off by cholesterol loading, so the macrophage keeps eating until it becomes a lipid-laden foam cell. Clusters of foam cells form a fatty streak, visible in the aortas of many teenagers and in a substantial minority of young adults. Foam cells die, releasing their lipid into a growing extracellular necrotic core, and secrete cytokines that sustain the inflammation. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, change phenotype and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over the core. Two features of plaque growth are counterintuitive. First, for much of its life a plaque grows outward rather than inward, a process described by Seymour Glagov in 1987: the artery remodels its outer wall so the lumen is preserved until plaque occupies roughly forty percent of the vessel's cross-sectional area. A large, dangerous, inflamed plaque can therefore produce a near-normal angiogram, which is why angiography underestimates disease burden and why intravascular ultrasound or CT sees more. Second, the plaques that cause heart attacks are frequently not the tightest ones. Studies tracking lesions over time have repeatedly found that a majority of infarctions arise from plaques that were less than fifty percent obstructive beforehand. Calcification appears later, partly a genuine ossification process involving bone-forming proteins. Its meaning is dual: coronary calcium on a CT scan is an excellent overall marker of plaque burden and future risk, yet a heavily calcified plaque is itself relatively stable. Statins increase calcification while reducing events, which is not a contradiction but a sign of stabilisation. The timescale is decades. Autopsy studies of young soldiers killed in Korea and Vietnam found established coronary lesions in a substantial fraction of men in their early twenties, and the PDAY study documented fatty streaks and raised lesions in adolescents. Risk factors do not initiate a disease in middle age; they accelerate one already under way, which is the argument for treating cholesterol and blood pressure as cumulative lifetime exposures rather than as a problem that begins at fifty.

sections.heading: Ischaemia and Angina: What a Supply Gap Feels Like
sections.body: Ischaemia means inadequate blood supply for the tissue's current needs. It is a relationship, not a fixed state: the same artery can be entirely adequate at rest and grossly inadequate on a staircase. The consequences unfold in a fixed order, known as the ischaemic cascade, and knowing the order explains why different tests detect disease at different stages. Within seconds of a supply shortfall, perfusion becomes uneven between layers and regions, which is what a nuclear perfusion scan detects. Metabolism shifts to anaerobic glycolysis; lactate is produced rather than consumed, intracellular pH falls, and high-energy phosphate stores deplete. Because relaxation is an active process requiring energy to pump calcium back into storage, diastolic dysfunction appears next: the affected segment becomes stiff. Then systolic function fails, producing a visible regional wall motion abnormality, which is what stress echocardiography looks for. Only after these does the electrocardiogram change, classically ST-segment depression when ischaemia is confined to the inner layer. Chest discomfort, if it comes at all, comes last. This ordering is why a normal resting electrocardiogram excludes very little, and why a person can have substantial ischaemia with no pain at all, which is called silent ischaemia and is particularly common in diabetes because of autonomic neuropathy affecting the afferent nerves. Stable angina is the classic presentation. It is typically a heavy, tight, squeezing or pressing sensation behind the breastbone rather than a sharp pain, often described by a clenched fist against the chest. It radiates to the jaw, neck, shoulders, either arm or the back. It is brought on reproducibly by a predictable amount of exertion, by cold air, by emotional stress or by a heavy meal, and it is relieved within a few minutes by rest or by sublingual nitrate. The referral pattern is anatomical: cardiac afferent fibres enter the spinal cord at the same segments, roughly the first to fourth thoracic levels, as somatic nerves from the chest wall and arm, and the brain misattributes the source. This is also why angina can present as jaw ache, epigastric discomfort or arm heaviness with no chest symptom at all. Presentations are frequently atypical in women, in older people and in people with diabetes, in whom breathlessness, unusual fatigue, nausea or sudden sweating may be the only feature. The historical framing of these as atypical has caused real harm through under-recognition and delayed treatment. Unstable angina describes a decisive change in that pattern: angina that appears at rest, that is new and severe, or that is escalating in frequency, duration or ease of provocation. It signals a plaque that has become active rather than a fixed narrowing, and it is a medical emergency rather than an outpatient problem.

sections.heading: Plaque Rupture, Thrombosis and Myocardial Infarction
sections.body: A heart attack is usually not a slow narrowing finally closing off. It is a sudden thrombotic event on a plaque that may have been modest in size, and it happens over minutes. The vulnerable lesion is a thin-cap fibroatheroma: a large soft necrotic lipid core covered by a fibrous cap thinner than about 65 micrometres, heavily infiltrated by macrophages, with few smooth muscle cells and little collagen. Inflammatory cells secrete matrix metalloproteinases that digest the collagen holding the cap together while the smooth muscle cells that would replace it are dying. When the cap tears, the highly thrombogenic contents of the core, particularly tissue factor, are exposed to flowing blood. Platelets adhere via von Willebrand factor, activate, aggregate, and the coagulation cascade generates thrombin and a fibrin mesh. A vessel can go from patent to occluded in minutes. This mechanism accounts for perhaps sixty to seventy percent of infarctions. Most of the remainder are caused by plaque erosion, in which the endothelium is denuded over a fibrous plaque without a cap tear, a mechanism that appears commoner in women, in smokers and in younger patients. What happens next depends on whether the occlusion is complete and sustained. A totally occluding thrombus causes full-thickness ischaemia, which produces ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram and is called STEMI. A partially occluding or intermittently occluding thrombus, or one with good collateral supply, causes subendocardial injury with ST depression or T-wave inversion, and if muscle dies this is a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Both are diagnosed as infarction by a rise and fall in cardiac troponin, a structural protein of the contractile apparatus released when myocytes die, detectable with high-sensitivity assays within one to three hours. The territory affected can be read from the electrocardiogram, because each set of electrodes looks at a particular wall. Changes in leads II, III and aVF indicate the inferior wall, usually right coronary territory. Changes in V1 to V4 indicate the anterior wall and septum, the left anterior descending. Changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6 indicate the lateral wall, typically the circumflex. Tall R waves with ST depression in V1 and V2 can indicate a true posterior infarct. Necrosis begins about twenty to thirty minutes after complete occlusion and advances as a wavefront from the subendocardium outward, a phenomenon demonstrated by Reimer and Jennings in the 1970s. Roughly half the territory at risk is dead within two to three hours and most of it within six. This is the entire basis of the clinical maxim that time is muscle. Infarction has a distinct daily rhythm, clustering in the hours after waking, when blood pressure, heart rate, sympathetic tone and platelet reactivity all rise together and fibrinolytic activity is at its lowest. This is also why the first dose of the day matters and why sudden unaccustomed exertion in the early morning carries disproportionate risk in someone with established disease.

sections.heading: When the Arteries Look Normal: Spasm, Dissection and Microvascular Disease
sections.body: Not all coronary disease is atherosclerotic plaque, and a substantial minority of patients with genuine myocardial ischaemia or infarction have angiographically unobstructed arteries. Recognising these conditions matters because the treatments differ and sometimes directly conflict. Vasospastic angina, described by Myron Prinzmetal in 1959 and also called variant angina, is intense focal spasm of an epicardial artery caused by hyperreactive smooth muscle. Characteristically it strikes at rest, often between midnight and early morning, exercise tolerance is preserved, and the electrocardiogram during an episode shows transient ST elevation that resolves completely. It is more prevalent in Japanese populations and is provoked by smoking, cocaine, amphetamines and certain drugs. Calcium channel blockers and long-acting nitrates are the mainstay. Non-selective beta-blockers can worsen it by leaving alpha-mediated constriction unopposed, which is the reverse of standard angina advice. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection occurs when a tear or bleed within the vessel wall creates a false lumen that compresses the true one. It disproportionately affects women under fifty, accounts for a meaningful share of infarctions in that group and of pregnancy-associated infarction, and is associated with fibromuscular dysplasia and with intense physical or emotional stress. Crucially, most cases heal spontaneously over weeks and stenting can extend the dissection, so conservative management is usually preferred, the opposite of the reflex for atherothrombotic infarction. Coronary microvascular dysfunction involves the arterioles and capillaries, which cannot be seen on an angiogram. It may be structural, with remodelling and rarefaction, or functional, with impaired endothelium-dependent dilation or increased constriction. It is diagnosed by measuring coronary flow reserve or an index of microvascular resistance, and it carries a genuinely increased risk of adverse events. It is common in women, in diabetes, in hypertensive heart disease and after successful stenting. Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries, abbreviated MINOCA, is an umbrella diagnosis applying to perhaps five to six percent of infarctions, requiring a search for the underlying cause: plaque disruption without obstruction, spasm, dissection, embolism, or a mimic such as myocarditis or takotsubo syndrome. Structural anomalies complete the picture. Anomalous origin of a coronary artery from the opposite sinus with a course between the aorta and pulmonary trunk can cause exertional sudden death in young people. Myocardial bridging, in which a segment of artery tunnels beneath muscle and is compressed in systole, is found in perhaps a quarter of hearts at autopsy and is usually benign, since compression occurs in systole when little flow happens anyway, though a long deep bridge can occasionally cause symptoms. Kawasaki disease in childhood leaves coronary aneurysms in a minority of untreated cases, and those aneurysms can thrombose or stenose decades later in an adult with no other risk factors. Coronary embolism, from a mechanical valve, infective endocarditis, atrial fibrillation or a paradoxical clot crossing a patent foramen ovale, accounts for a small share of infarctions. Arteritis in Takayasu disease or systemic lupus can involve the ostia. Finally, supply-demand infarction without any acute plaque event, formally type 2 myocardial infarction, is common in critically ill patients with sepsis, severe anaemia, tachyarrhythmia or respiratory failure, and it is treated by correcting the precipitant rather than by angiography.

sections.heading: Restoring Flow: Drugs, Stents, Bypass and Their Limits
sections.body: Treatment of coronary disease pursues two separate goals that are often confused: relieving symptoms by improving the supply and demand balance, and preventing death and infarction by stabilising the disease. Different treatments serve different goals, and assuming that opening a narrowing does both is one of the commonest misconceptions in medicine. Medical therapy addresses both. Antiplatelet drugs, chiefly aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1 and thus platelet thromboxane production for the platelet's whole eight to ten day life, reduce thrombotic events. Lipid-lowering therapy, statins first and where needed ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor, lowers LDL and demonstrably reduces infarction and death, with benefit proportional to the absolute LDL reduction achieved. Beta-blockers slow the heart, cutting demand and lengthening diastolic perfusion time. Nitrates dilate veins, reducing preload and wall stress, and dilate epicardial arteries and collaterals; they relieve symptoms but have never been shown to prolong life. Calcium channel blockers reduce afterload and relieve spasm. Blood pressure control, smoking cessation, diabetes management and regular exercise are not adjuncts but among the most effective interventions available. Percutaneous coronary intervention threads a catheter, usually from the radial artery at the wrist, to the lesion, inflates a balloon and deploys a drug-eluting stent that scaffolds the vessel open while releasing an antiproliferative drug to suppress the scar-tissue overgrowth that caused restenosis in bare-metal stents. In acute ST-elevation infarction it is unambiguously life-saving, and the target is a door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes, or under 120 minutes from first medical contact if transfer is required, with clot-busting fibrinolytic therapy given within 30 minutes where timely intervention is impossible. In stable angina the evidence is very different: the COURAGE and ISCHEMIA trials found that adding stenting to good medical therapy improved symptoms but did not reduce death or infarction. This is consistent with the biology, since the plaque most likely to rupture is often not the one being stented. Coronary artery bypass grafting routes blood around blockages using conduits, and the choice of conduit dominates the long-term result. The left internal mammary artery grafted to the left anterior descending artery has patency above ninety percent at ten years and is the single most durable component of cardiac surgery. Saphenous vein grafts, taken from the leg, are more prone to their own atherosclerosis, with roughly half occluded by ten years. Surgery generally outperforms stenting in left main disease, in complex three-vessel disease and in diabetes. Every option has limits. Stents can thrombose, particularly if antiplatelet therapy is stopped early. Restenosis still occurs in a small percentage. Grafts fail. Revascularisation treats a lesion; it does not treat the disease, which continues in every artery unless the underlying drivers are addressed.

sections.heading: Recognition, Emergencies and What Actually Changes Outcomes
sections.body: The most consequential decisions in coronary disease are made by people who are not clinicians, in the first minutes of an event, and they are frequently made badly. Median delay between symptom onset and seeking help is commonly measured in hours, and it is the largest single modifiable cause of avoidable damage. The pattern that should trigger emergency action is discomfort in the chest, which may be described as pressure, heaviness, tightness, burning or squeezing rather than pain, lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going, possibly spreading to the jaw, neck, shoulders, either arm, the back or the upper abdomen, and accompanied by breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea, light-headedness or a sense of impending doom. Symptoms that are new at rest, or markedly worse than a previously stable pattern, are as significant as severe ones. In women, older people and those with diabetes, breathlessness, sudden profound fatigue or nausea may be the only presentation. Discomfort that is sharp and stabbing, reproduced exactly by pressing on the chest wall, or that lasts only seconds, is less likely to be cardiac, but no rule is reliable enough to be used to talk yourself out of calling for help. Correct immediate action is short. Call the emergency ambulance number, not a relative, and not a taxi: ambulances carry defibrillators and can transmit an electrocardiogram ahead so the receiving hospital activates its team before arrival. Do not drive yourself, because a cardiac arrest at the wheel endangers others as well. Stop all activity and sit or lie down. Unless there is a known allergy or a clinician has advised otherwise, chew a standard 300 milligram aspirin tablet, or two to four low-dose tablets, since chewing speeds absorption and this single measure produces a measurable reduction in mortality. If the person has prescribed sublingual nitrate, take it as directed. If they collapse and are unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing, begin chest compressions immediately at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute and a depth of five to six centimetres, and send someone for an automated external defibrillator, because survival from cardiac arrest falls by roughly seven to ten percent for every minute without defibrillation. Over the long run the interventions that most reduce coronary events are unglamorous and cumulative: not smoking, sustained blood pressure and LDL control, physical activity of roughly 150 minutes a week at moderate intensity, weight and glucose management, sleep, and treatment adherence. None of them produces the drama of a stent, and collectively they prevent far more deaths. Two limits are worth stating honestly. Risk prediction at the level of the individual remains imprecise: the scores in routine use estimate population risk well but cannot tell a particular person whether a particular plaque will rupture, and a substantial number of infarctions occur in people classified as low or intermediate risk. And restoring flow to dead muscle does not restore the muscle; it salvages what is still alive at the moment the artery opens. Everything that determines outcome therefore happens before the hospital doors, in prevention over decades and in the minutes after symptoms begin.

guides.safetyNote: This guide is educational and is not a substitute for medical assessment. Chest discomfort lasting more than a few minutes, occurring at rest, or accompanied by breathlessness, sweating, nausea or faintness is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number immediately, do not drive yourself to hospital, and unless allergic or advised otherwise chew a 300 mg aspirin. Symptoms are frequently atypical in women, older adults and people with diabetes, and may be only breathlessness, fatigue or nausea. Never start, stop or change prescribed cardiac medication, including beta-blockers, antiplatelet drugs or statins, without medical advice; stopping antiplatelet therapy early after a stent can cause fatal stent thrombosis.

guides.title: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries: Vascular Anatomy
guides.summary: A comprehensive account of the structure of blood vessels: the three-layered wall plan, how elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins each differ, how exchange and return actually work, and how the system fails and is assessed.

sections.heading: Why the Vascular Tree Matters
sections.body: Almost every cell in the human body sits within about 100 micrometres of a blood vessel, and that distance is not an accident of growth but the fundamental constraint the whole circulatory system exists to satisfy. Oxygen moves through tissue only by diffusion, and diffusion is punishingly slow over distance: the time taken roughly quadruples when the distance doubles. Beyond about a tenth of a millimetre from a source, a metabolically active cell cannot get oxygen fast enough to survive. A single-celled organism has no problem, and a flatworm a millimetre thick can still manage by soaking oxygen in through its surface. A seventy-kilogram mammal cannot. The solution evolution arrived at is a branching plumbing network that carries oxygen in bulk, at speed, to within diffusion distance of every cell, and then hands over to diffusion for the final short hop. Everything else about vascular anatomy follows from that division of labour. The estimated total length of the network is often quoted at around 100,000 kilometres, though this figure deserves honest scepticism: it is an extrapolation from capillary densities counted in small tissue samples, and published estimates range from roughly 60,000 to over 100,000 kilometres depending on the assumptions. What is not in doubt is the geometry. The aorta is a single tube about 2.5 to 3 centimetres across; a capillary is 5 to 10 micrometres across, barely wider than the red cell that must squeeze through it. Yet because there are billions of capillaries, their combined cross-sectional area is on the order of 4,500 to 5,000 square centimetres against the aorta's 4 or 5. Blood therefore slows from about 40 centimetres per second in the aorta to under half a millimetre per second in a capillary, which buys roughly one to two seconds of transit time. That second is the entire window in which oxygen leaves, carbon dioxide enters, glucose is delivered and waste collected. The vessels are not passive pipes. They generate the pressure gradients that drive flow, they redistribute cardiac output minute by minute according to which organs need it, they manufacture and release hormones, they decide whether blood clots or stays fluid, and they control which white cells leave the bloodstream and where. Understanding the vascular tree therefore means understanding four things simultaneously: a mechanical structure, a hydraulic circuit, a secretory organ, and a regulated barrier. Nearly every major cause of death in wealthy countries — heart attack, stroke, aortic rupture, pulmonary embolism, the complications of diabetes and kidney failure — is a disease of these vessels rather than of the organs they supply. The organs die downstream of a vascular failure. A heart attack is not usually a disease of heart muscle; it is a coronary artery that closed. A stroke is not usually a disease of brain tissue; it is a cerebral vessel that blocked or burst. Diabetic blindness, diabetic kidney failure and the diabetic foot are all one disease of small vessels expressing itself in three organs. Vascular anatomy is therefore the shortest route to understanding why bodies fail.

sections.heading: The Closed Loop: Systemic and Pulmonary Circuits
sections.body: Human circulation is a closed double loop driven by a single four-chambered pump, an arrangement correctly described by the English physician William Harvey in 1628 in his short book De Motu Cordis. Harvey's argument was quantitative rather than anatomical: he estimated the volume the heart ejects per beat, multiplied by the beat rate, and showed the body could not possibly manufacture that much blood from food, so the same blood must be circulating. He could not see the connection between arteries and veins; capillaries were only observed by Marcello Malpighi in frog lung in 1661, using the newly available microscope. The systemic circuit begins at the left ventricle, which ejects oxygenated blood into the aorta at a mean pressure of about 93 millimetres of mercury in a healthy adult, conventionally written as a peak of 120 and a trough of 80. Blood passes through arteries, arterioles and capillaries in every organ except the lungs' own gas-exchange tissue, then collects into venules and veins and returns to the right atrium at a pressure of roughly zero to five millimetres of mercury. The pulmonary circuit takes over: the right ventricle pushes deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk at about 25 over 8 millimetres of mercury, a fifth of systemic pressure, because the lungs are close, short and offer little resistance. Blood returns oxygenated through four pulmonary veins to the left atrium. This is the one place where the naming convention inverts: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. The words artery and vein describe direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content. An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein returns it. The two circuits are in series, which has a rigid consequence: over any sustained period the two ventricles must eject exactly the same volume per minute, roughly five litres at rest, or blood would progressively accumulate in one circuit and drain the other. Even a one percent sustained mismatch would flood the lungs within minutes. Within the systemic circuit, however, the organ beds are arranged in parallel rather than in series. Kidneys, brain, gut, muscle and skin each hang off the aorta as a separate branch, so every organ receives blood at the same starting pressure and freshly oxygenated, and one bed can be constricted or dilated without changing what its neighbours receive. The important exceptions are the portal systems, where two capillary beds sit in series so that the second bed receives blood already processed by the first. The share of cardiac output each organ claims at rest is uneven and instructive: the liver and gut together take about a quarter, the kidneys a fifth despite weighing only 300 grams, the brain about 15 percent, resting skeletal muscle 15 to 20 percent, and the coronary circulation 4 to 5 percent. These proportions are not fixed. Heavy exercise can raise cardiac output fivefold to around 25 litres a minute and simultaneously redirect the split, so muscle receives 80 percent or more of a much larger total while gut and kidney flow is halved — a redistribution performed entirely by the arterioles of each bed.

sections.heading: The Three-Layered Wall Plan
sections.body: Every blood vessel larger than a capillary is built to the same three-layer template, and the differences between an aorta, a radial artery, an arteriole and a vein are almost entirely differences in the relative thickness and composition of these three coats. The innermost layer is the tunica intima. Its defining component is a single continuous sheet of flattened endothelial cells sitting on a basement membrane, oriented with their long axes parallel to the direction of flow. Beneath the endothelium lies a thin subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue, and in arteries the intima is bounded on its outer side by the internal elastic lamina, a fenestrated sheet of elastin that is conspicuous in muscular arteries and appears wavy in histological sections because the vessel has relaxed after death. The middle layer, the tunica media, is the muscular and elastic bulk of the wall. It contains smooth muscle cells arranged circumferentially or in a shallow helix, so that when they contract the lumen narrows, together with elastin and collagen fibres that the same smooth muscle cells secrete. In arteries the media is thick and is the dominant layer; in veins it is thin. The outer layer is the tunica adventitia, sometimes called the tunica externa, made mainly of longitudinally arranged collagen type I with some elastin, blending into the surrounding connective tissue and tethering the vessel in place.
