In veins the adventitia is the thickest layer. Two mechanical laws govern how these layers are apportioned. The law of Laplace states that for a thin-walled cylinder the circumferential wall tension equals pressure multiplied by radius, so a large high-pressure vessel needs far more tensile material than a small one. Wall stress, the tension spread through the wall's thickness, is pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, which is why the body thickens vessel walls when pressure rises chronically. A capillary can survive with a wall one cell thick precisely because its radius is minute, roughly 4 micrometres, despite a pressure of 25 or 30 millimetres of mercury. Elastin and collagen divide the mechanical work between them: elastin is compliant and bears load at normal pressures, stretching to perhaps 150 percent of its resting length and recoiling without energy loss, while collagen is roughly a thousand times stiffer and lies slack until the vessel is stretched substantially, at which point it engages and prevents further expansion. This is why the pressure–volume curve of an artery is J-shaped, soft at first and abruptly stiff. Elastin is essentially not replaced after adolescence; the elastin in an adult aorta was laid down in childhood and slowly fragments across a lifetime, which is the structural basis of the arterial stiffening that raises systolic pressure with age.

sections.heading: Elastic Conducting Arteries and the Windkessel Effect
sections.body: The largest arteries — the aorta, the brachiocephalic trunk, the common carotids, the subclavians, the pulmonary trunk and the common iliacs — are classed as elastic or conducting arteries, and their job is not primarily to distribute blood but to smooth it. The human aortic media contains roughly 40 to 70 concentric fenestrated sheets of elastin, called elastic lamellae, with a thin layer of smooth muscle and collagen sandwiched between each pair. The whole unit of one lamella plus its associated muscle is a lamellar unit, and across mammals the tension borne per lamellar unit is remarkably constant at around 2 newtons per metre, so a species with higher blood pressure simply builds more lamellae. In section these vessels look pink and wavy under an elastin stain, with muscle almost hidden between the sheets. The functional consequence is called the Windkessel effect, after the German word for the air chamber in an old hand-pumped fire engine. A piston pump alone produces violently pulsatile flow; an air chamber downstream absorbs the stroke by compressing, then pushes back during the pause, converting spurts into a steady jet. The aorta does exactly this. During systole, the roughly 70 millilitres ejected by the left ventricle cannot all pass immediately into the periphery, so the aorta distends and stores perhaps half of it, absorbing the energy in stretched elastin. During diastole, when the aortic valve has closed and the heart is filling, the stretched aorta recoils and continues to drive blood forward. The result is that flow at the capillaries is nearly continuous rather than intermittent, and diastolic pressure is maintained at around 80 millimetres of mercury rather than collapsing towards zero. This matters enormously for the coronary arteries, which perfuse the heart muscle almost entirely during diastole because systolic contraction squeezes them shut; without diastolic pressure the heart could not feed itself. It also spares the small vessels from pressure spikes. The Windkessel is estimated to reduce the work the left ventricle must do by roughly a third compared with a rigid pipe of the same resistance. When the aorta stiffens with age, or with the medial calcification of chronic kidney disease and diabetes, the reservoir fails. The stroke volume must be accommodated by pressure rather than volume, so systolic pressure climbs while diastolic falls, widening the pulse pressure. Isolated systolic hypertension of 170 over 70 in an eighty-year-old is a stiffness problem, not a resistance problem, and it is the single commonest blood pressure pattern in old age. Pulse wave velocity, measured between the carotid and femoral arteries, quantifies it directly: about 5 metres per second in a healthy young adult, over 12 in a stiff elderly aorta, and each metre per second of increase carries measurable added cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: Muscular Arteries and the Control of Tone
sections.body: As the elastic arteries branch, elastin gives way to smooth muscle and the vessels become muscular or distributing arteries. These are the named arteries a surgeon or anatomist works with: the radial, brachial, femoral, popliteal, splenic, renal, coronary and cerebral arteries, generally between about 0.5 and 10 millimetres across. Their media may contain up to 40 layers of circumferential smooth muscle with comparatively little elastin, bounded by a prominent internal elastic lamina on the inside and a thinner external elastic lamina on the outside. Under the microscope these two crisp elastic sheets sandwiching a solidly muscular media are the signature that identifies a muscular artery at a glance. Their function is to route blood: by contracting or relaxing they change the fraction of cardiac output that reaches a given region, and they hold their calibre against pressure rather than ballooning. Smooth muscle tone is set by the intracellular calcium concentration, and the contractile mechanism differs from skeletal muscle in an important way. Calcium binds calmodulin, the complex activates myosin light chain kinase, and phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain permits cross-bridge cycling. Relaxation requires myosin light chain phosphatase to remove that phosphate, and the RhoA/Rho-kinase pathway inhibits the phosphatase, allowing a vessel to stay contracted at a given calcium level — a phenomenon called calcium sensitisation that is a major target of research in hypertension. Because smooth muscle can sustain tension with slow cross-bridge cycling, it holds tone for hours at a fraction of the energy cost skeletal muscle would incur. Four influences set that tone at any moment. Sympathetic nerve fibres release noradrenaline onto alpha-1 receptors to constrict, with a background firing rate that means most vessels are partly constricted at rest, so withdrawal of sympathetic traffic is itself a dilating signal. Circulating hormones act next: angiotensin II, vasopressin and endothelin constrict; adrenaline constricts through alpha receptors in skin and gut but dilates through beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle. Local metabolites dilate — falling oxygen, rising carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, potassium, adenosine and lactate all relax the muscle, which is the elegant mechanism of active hyperaemia whereby a working tissue orders its own blood supply. Finally the endothelium releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin to dilate, and endothelin-1 to constrict. Superimposed on all of this is the myogenic response, described by William Bayliss in 1902: stretch a vessel by raising the pressure inside it and the smooth muscle contracts in reply, so flow stays roughly constant across a wide pressure range. This autoregulation holds cerebral blood flow nearly constant between mean arterial pressures of roughly 60 and 150 millimetres of mercury, and it is why standing up does not black you out.

sections.heading: Arterioles: Where Resistance Lives
sections.body: Arterioles are the smallest arterial vessels, generally under 100 to 300 micrometres across, with a media of only one to three layers of smooth muscle wrapped around a lumen that may be no wider than the wall is thick. They are physiologically the most important vessels in the body, because they are where the pressure of the arterial system is dissipated and where the distribution of cardiac output is decided. The reason is the fourth-power relationship in Poiseuille's law, derived independently by the French physician Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille around 1840 and the German engineer Gotthilf Hagen. For steady laminar flow of a uniform fluid through a rigid tube, flow equals pi times the pressure difference times the radius to the fourth power, divided by eight times the viscosity times the length. Resistance is therefore proportional to one over the radius to the fourth. Halve a vessel's radius and resistance rises sixteenfold; narrow it by only 19 percent and resistance doubles. No other biological control lever has this gain. A modest, energetically cheap contraction of a thin muscular cuff can shut a tissue's blood supply almost completely, and modest relaxation can open it wide. In consequence, mean pressure falls only a little across the large arteries — from about 93 to perhaps 85 millimetres of mercury by the time blood reaches a small artery — and then collapses across the arterioles to around 35 millimetres of mercury at the arterial end of a capillary. Roughly half of total systemic vascular resistance sits in these vessels, which is why they are called the resistance vessels and why blood pressure drugs overwhelmingly act on them. The same drop also protects the fragile capillaries downstream, which would rupture at arterial pressure. Arterioles are also where the pulse is extinguished; blood arrives at the capillary bed almost non-pulsatile, and a visibly pulsating capillary bed, such as the nail-bed pulsation known as Quincke's sign, is abnormal and suggests aortic regurgitation. Textbooks classically describe terminal arterioles feeding metarterioles, which carry scattered smooth muscle cells forming precapillary sphincters that open and close individual capillaries in a cycle called vasomotion, so that only a fraction of capillaries carry flow at rest. That picture came largely from mesenteric and bat-wing preparations, and the existence of a discrete anatomical sphincter in most human tissues is genuinely contested; recent imaging work supports sphincter-like structures in the brain but not everywhere. What is not disputed is the functional fact that capillary perfusion is intermittent and locally regulated, and that a resting muscle may perfuse a quarter of its capillaries while exercise recruits nearly all of them, shortening diffusion distances and multiplying exchange surface.

sections.heading: Capillaries: Three Structural Types
sections.body: A capillary is the minimum possible blood vessel: a tube of endothelial cells rolled into a cylinder about 5 to 10 micrometres in internal diameter, resting on a basement membrane, with no smooth muscle and no adventitia. In the narrowest capillaries a single endothelial cell wraps entirely around the lumen and joins itself, and the wall may be only a quarter of a micrometre thick. Red blood cells, which are about 7 to 8 micrometres across at rest, must deform into a bullet or parachute shape to pass, and this deformation is useful: it wipes the cell membrane close against the endothelium and shortens the diffusion path for oxygen almost to zero. Scattered along the outside of capillaries and sharing their basement membrane are pericytes, contractile branching cells that wrap the vessel, stabilise it, contribute to blood–brain barrier function and can constrict capillaries; they are densest in the central nervous system and retina, where they may equal endothelial cells in number, and sparse in skeletal muscle. Capillaries come in three structural grades, and knowing which type a tissue has predicts what can leave the blood there. Continuous capillaries are the commonest. Their endothelial cells form an unbroken sheet joined by tight junctions and adherens junctions, with a complete basement membrane; the only routes out are dissolved gases and lipid-soluble molecules crossing the cell membrane directly, water and small solutes slipping through intercellular clefts about 4 nanometres wide, and vesicular transcytosis. Muscle, skin, lung, connective tissue and fat use them. The extreme version is found in the central nervous system, where the tight junctions are unusually elaborate, transcytosis is actively suppressed and the vessel is enveloped by astrocyte end-feet: this is the blood–brain barrier, and it is a property of the capillary endothelium, not a separate membrane. Fenestrated capillaries have circular pores 60 to 100 nanometres wide punched through the thinnest parts of the endothelial cell, usually spanned by a thin diaphragm except in the kidney glomerulus, where they are open. The basement membrane remains continuous, so large proteins are still held back, but water and small solutes cross freely. They occur exactly where high-volume filtration or rapid absorption is required: the renal glomerulus and peritubular capillaries, the intestinal villi, the choroid plexus and all endocrine glands, whose hormones must reach the circulation quickly. Discontinuous capillaries, better called sinusoids, are the leakiest. They are wide, often 30 to 40 micrometres, irregularly shaped, with large intercellular gaps and an incomplete or absent basement membrane, and blood moves through them slowly. Liver, spleen, bone marrow and the adrenal cortex have them, allowing whole cells to cross — newly made blood cells leaving the marrow, or plasma proteins pouring out of hepatocytes.

sections.heading: Exchange at the Capillary: Diffusion, Bulk Flow and Starling Forces
sections.body: Two entirely different processes move material across a capillary wall, and confusing them is the commonest conceptual error in this subject. Diffusion is responsible for essentially all nutrient and gas exchange. It is driven by concentration gradients, needs no energy, and is enormously effective over the short distances involved. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are lipid-soluble and simply pass through the endothelial cell membranes anywhere on the surface, so their exchange is limited only by blood flow, not by the wall; this is why oxygen delivery is described as flow-limited. Water-soluble molecules such as glucose, amino acids and ions must use the intercellular clefts and specific transporters, and permeability falls steeply with molecular size. The volume diffusing is large: on the order of 80,000 litres of water cross the body's capillary walls each day, almost all of it moving out and back in again with no net effect. Bulk flow, by contrast, moves negligible amounts of nutrient but determines the distribution of fluid between blood and tissue, and it is governed by the balance the British physiologist Ernest Starling described in 1896. Four pressures act. Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out and falls along the capillary from roughly 35 millimetres of mercury at the arterial end to about 15 at the venous end. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes it and is small, in most tissues slightly negative, perhaps minus 1 to minus 3 millimetres of mercury. Plasma colloid osmotic pressure, generated almost entirely by albumin at around 40 grams per litre, pulls fluid back in with a force of about 25 to 28 millimetres of mercury. Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure pulls outward at maybe 5 to 8. The net filtration pressure is the difference, multiplied by a filtration coefficient reflecting the wall's leakiness and surface area. The classical teaching that fluid filters out at the arterial end and is reabsorbed at the venous end has been substantially revised. The revised Starling principle, developed since the 1990s largely by Charles Michel and Fitz-Roy Curry, recognises that the effective osmotic gradient is sensed across the endothelial glycocalyx, and that the protein concentration immediately beneath that layer, not in the general interstitium, is what counts. In most tissues under steady conditions there is net filtration along the whole capillary length with little reabsorption, and the filtered fluid is returned by lymphatics rather than by the capillary. Roughly 2 to 4 litres a day return through the thoracic duct, and when that fails, oedema results. Three clinical patterns follow directly from the four pressures. Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure or a leg vein blocked by clot, drives filtration and produces pitting oedema in the dependent parts. Reduced plasma albumin — from liver failure, protein-losing kidney disease or severe malnutrition, typically once albumin falls below about 20 grams per litre — removes the inward pull and produces generalised swelling, including the puffy face and distended abdomen of severe childhood malnutrition. Increased permeability, as in burns, sepsis or anaphylaxis, lets protein itself escape so the oncotic gradient collapses on both sides; a large burn can lose litres of plasma into the tissues within hours.

sections.heading: Venules, Veins and the Capacitance Reservoir
sections.body: Blood leaving capillaries enters postcapillary venules, vessels 10 to 50 micrometres across whose walls are still essentially endothelium with pericytes and no muscle. These unglamorous vessels do something no other segment does: they are the site of inflammation. Histamine, bradykinin and other mediators cause postcapillary venule endothelial cells to contract and pull apart at their junctions, opening gaps that let plasma protein and then white cells escape, which is why an inflamed tissue swells. Leukocyte rolling on selectins, firm adhesion via integrins and ICAM-1, and diapedesis between or through endothelial cells all happen here, because the low shear stress of venular flow allows a rolling cell to catch. As venules merge they acquire smooth muscle and become veins, whose walls are thin relative to their diameter, with a modest media and a thick collagenous adventitia. A vein alongside its companion artery is easy to identify in section: a larger, often collapsed lumen and a much thinner wall, while the artery is round and thick. The venous identity is capacitance. At any moment roughly 60 to 70 percent of total blood volume — about 3 to 3.5 litres of an adult's 5 litres — sits in the systemic veins and venules, against perhaps 13 percent in systemic arteries, 7 percent in capillaries, 9 percent in the pulmonary circulation and 7 percent in the heart chambers. Veins are about 20 to 30 times more compliant than arteries of the same calibre, meaning a given volume change produces a far smaller pressure change, so they can accept or release large volumes almost silently. This makes the venous system the body's blood reservoir. Sympathetic constriction of veins, particularly in the splanchnic bed of the gut and in the spleen, can shift several hundred millilitres into the active circulation within seconds — a transfusion from the body's own stores that is a first-line response to haemorrhage and to standing up. The distinction between stressed and unstressed volume is worth grasping: unstressed volume is the blood merely filling the veins at zero distending pressure and contributes nothing to filling the heart, while stressed volume distends them and generates the mean systemic filling pressure of roughly 7 millimetres of mercury that actually drives venous return. Venoconstriction converts unstressed into stressed volume. This is also why drugs like nitroglycerin, which dilate veins preferentially, relieve angina: they pool blood peripherally, reduce the volume returning to the heart, and so reduce the work and oxygen demand of the left ventricle. Compliance also explains why veins look so different from arteries in life. An artery cut across stays open because its thick muscular wall holds a circular shape; a vein collapses into a flattened ribbon unless blood is holding it open, and a vein under low filling pressure adopts an elliptical cross-section until it rounds out. It is also the basis of the jugular venous pulse, examined with the patient reclined at 45 degrees: the height of blood visible in the internal jugular vein above the sternal angle reads out right atrial pressure, normally no more than 3 or 4 centimetres, and rises in fluid overload and right heart failure.

sections.heading: Valves, the Muscle Pump and Venous Return
sections.body: Getting blood back to the heart from the feet is a genuine engineering problem, because the pressure available to do it is tiny. By the time blood reaches a venule the pressure is about 15 millimetres of mercury, and the right atrium sits near zero, so the entire driving gradient for venous return is perhaps 12 to 15 millimetres of mercury — less than a tenth of what pushed blood out of the heart. Standing makes it far worse. A column of blood from the heart to the ankle is roughly 120 centimetres tall, and since blood has a density close to water, that column exerts a hydrostatic pressure of about 90 millimetres of mercury at the ankle. Venous pressure in a motionless standing person's foot vein therefore reaches around 90 to 100 millimetres of mercury, and capillary pressure rises with it, pushing fluid into the tissues. Standing still for twenty minutes can move several hundred millilitres of plasma out of the circulation into the legs, and standing rigidly to attention for long enough reliably causes fainting — an entirely mechanical failure of venous return, not a failure of nerve. Three mechanisms defeat the problem. First, veins of the limbs contain valves: paired semilunar pockets formed as folds of the intima and reinforced with elastin, arranged so that they open under flow toward the heart and balloon shut under any backward flow. They are numerous in the leg veins and largely absent in the great veins of the trunk, the head and neck, where posture cannot generate a reversed column. Second, the skeletal muscle pump: the deep veins run inside the muscle compartments of the calf and thigh, so every contraction squeezes them flat and, because the valves permit only one direction, ejects their contents upward. The calf is often called the peripheral heart, and a single vigorous contraction can move 60 to 100 millilitres. Rhythmic walking drops foot venous pressure from about 90 to around 25 millimetres of mercury within a dozen steps. Third, the respiratory pump: inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and simultaneously raises intra-abdominal pressure as the diaphragm descends, so the pressure gradient between abdomen and thorax steepens and blood is drawn upward with each breath. This is why venous return rises during inspiration and why a patient in circulatory difficulty is helped by lying flat with the legs raised — that manoeuvre alone can shift roughly 300 to 500 millilitres centrally. Failure of any of these produces recognisable disease. Incompetent valves cause venous hypertension in the leg, dilated tortuous superficial veins, brown haemosiderin staining of the skin above the ankle and eventually venous ulceration; compression stockings work by supporting the vein wall so the remaining valve cusps can meet.

sections.heading: The Endothelium as a Distributed Organ
sections.body: It is tempting to treat the endothelium as a lining, an inert non-stick surface. That view was demolished in 1980 when Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki in Brooklyn discovered that acetylcholine relaxed a rabbit aortic ring only if the endothelium was intact; if the inner surface was accidentally rubbed during preparation, the same drug caused contraction. They inferred a diffusible substance and called it endothelium-derived relaxing factor. Over the following seven years it was identified as nitric oxide, a gas, and Furchgott, Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the work. The endothelium is now understood as an organ in its own right, with a combined mass of about a kilogram in an adult and a surface area of several thousand square metres, distributed as a single-cell film through every tissue. Its outputs are numerous and mostly paired in opposition. It synthesises nitric oxide from L-arginine using endothelial nitric oxide synthase, activated by the shear stress of flowing blood and by acetylcholine, bradykinin and histamine; nitric oxide diffuses into the underlying smooth muscle, raises cyclic GMP and relaxes it, while also inhibiting platelet adhesion and smooth muscle proliferation. It makes prostacyclin, another vasodilator and antiplatelet agent, from arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenase, and this is the pathway aspirin acts on. Against these it makes endothelin-1, the most potent vasoconstrictor known in the body, and it houses angiotensin-converting enzyme, especially on pulmonary capillaries, which generates the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II and destroys the vasodilator bradykinin. It controls coagulation in both directions: healthy endothelium presents heparan sulphate, thrombomodulin and tissue plasminogen activator to keep blood fluid, while injured endothelium exposes tissue factor, releases von Willebrand factor from its Weibel–Palade bodies and displays adhesion molecules, committing to clot. It controls inflammation by deciding which selectins and integrin ligands to display. And it is regionally specialised: brain endothelium builds a barrier, liver sinusoidal endothelium is a sieve, high endothelial venules in lymph nodes are cuboidal and exist to admit lymphocytes. Coating the luminal surface is the glycocalyx, a hydrated mesh of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans and adsorbed plasma proteins between about 0.5 and 2 micrometres deep, which excludes red cells from the vessel edge, senses shear stress and forms the true permeability barrier to protein. Endothelial dysfunction — reduced nitric oxide availability, a prothrombotic pro-inflammatory surface, a degraded glycocalyx — precedes visible atherosclerosis by decades and is the earliest measurable vascular abnormality in smoking, diabetes and hypertension. It can be measured non-invasively by flow-mediated dilatation: a blood pressure cuff on the forearm is inflated above systolic pressure for five minutes, and on release the surge of flow through the brachial artery should raise shear stress enough to trigger nitric oxide release and dilate the vessel by 5 to 10 percent on ultrasound; a blunted response predicts future cardiovascular events. Exercise raises shear stress repeatedly and upregulates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, one reason activity lowers blood pressure independently of weight, while a single cigarette measurably impairs the response for an hour or more.

sections.heading: Named Arteries: A Practical Map of the Body
sections.body: The arterial tree has a recognisable and largely predictable plan worth learning as a map. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, gives off the left and right coronary arteries immediately above the aortic valve from the sinuses of Valsalva, arches over the left main bronchus and supplies three great branches from that arch: the brachiocephalic trunk, which splits into right common carotid and right subclavian; then the left common carotid; then the left subclavian. Each common carotid divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into an external carotid, supplying face and scalp, and an internal carotid, which enters the skull and supplies the front two-thirds of the brain. Each subclavian gives off a vertebral artery, which ascends through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and joins its fellow to form the basilar artery supplying the brainstem and the back of the brain. In the skull base the internal carotids and the basilar are linked by communicating arteries into the circle of Willis, an anastomotic ring that in principle allows blood to reach any part of the brain if one feeding vessel blocks, although the ring is complete and symmetrical in fewer than half of people. Beyond the first rib the subclavian becomes the axillary artery, then the brachial artery in the arm, which divides at the elbow into radial and ulnar arteries; these reconnect in the palm as the superficial and deep palmar arches, which is why a hand can survive loss of one forearm artery. The descending aorta supplies intercostal arteries in the chest, then in the abdomen the coeliac trunk at the twelfth thoracic vertebra for stomach, liver and spleen, the superior mesenteric artery at the first lumbar vertebra for small bowel and right colon, paired renal arteries at about the first to second lumbar level, and the inferior mesenteric artery at the third for the left colon and rectum. At the fourth lumbar vertebra, roughly level with the navel, the aorta bifurcates into common iliac arteries; each divides into an internal iliac for the pelvis and an external iliac which passes under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery. That continues as the popliteal behind the knee and divides into anterior tibial, posterior tibial and fibular arteries, ending as the dorsalis pedis on the top of the foot. Two categories deserve emphasis. End arteries, such as the central retinal artery and the arteries supplying spleen and kidney segments, have no useful anastomoses, so occlusion means infarction of everything downstream. Richly anastomotic beds — the palmar arches, the bowel mesentery, the shoulder — tolerate occlusion far better. Anatomical variation is the rule rather than the exception. The aortic arch has the standard three-branch pattern in only about 70 to 80 percent of people; a common origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid, the bovine arch, occurs in perhaps 15 percent. The coronary circulation is right-dominant in roughly 85 percent of hearts, which is why a right coronary occlusion so often produces an inferior heart attack. Before any operation the individual's actual anatomy is imaged rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Named Veins, Portal Systems and Anastomoses
sections.body: Venous anatomy is more variable than arterial anatomy and is organised in two parallel systems in the limbs. Deep veins accompany the arteries, usually as paired venae comitantes wrapped around a smaller artery so that arterial pulsation helps massage venous blood along, and they carry roughly 90 percent of the return from the leg. Superficial veins run in the subcutaneous fat with no companion artery. In the leg these are the great saphenous vein, which begins in front of the medial malleolus at the ankle, ascends the medial calf and thigh and drains into the femoral vein at the groin, and the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus draining into the popliteal vein. The great saphenous is the longest vein in the body and, being expendable and thick-walled, is the classic graft harvested for coronary artery bypass. Perforating veins connect superficial to deep, with valves directing flow inward; when these fail, the muscle pump's pressure is transmitted outward to the skin veins and varicosities follow. In the arm the cephalic vein runs on the lateral side and the basilic on the medial, connected at the elbow by the median cubital vein, the standard site for taking blood. All the return from below the diaphragm collects in the inferior vena cava, which lies to the right of the aorta and pierces the diaphragm at the eighth thoracic vertebra; the head, neck and arms drain via the internal jugular and subclavian veins, which join as brachiocephalic veins to form the superior vena cava. A portal system is a segment where blood passes through two capillary beds in series without returning to the heart between them, and the body has two important ones. The hepatic portal vein, formed behind the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, carries all the nutrient-laden, potentially toxin-laden blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas into the liver sinusoids before it reaches the general circulation. This is what allows the liver first refusal on everything absorbed, and it is the reason many swallowed drugs are largely destroyed before they act, the so-called first-pass effect. The hypophyseal portal system carries releasing hormones the few millimetres from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary in concentrated form. Portosystemic anastomoses, where portal and systemic veins meet, are normally trivial but become dangerous when liver disease raises portal pressure: blood is forced through them, distending veins at the lower oesophagus into varices that can bleed catastrophically, around the umbilicus as caput medusae, and in the rectum. Elsewhere in the body venous anastomoses are generally generous, which is why a single vein can usually be sacrificed, and why deep vein thrombosis often produces surprisingly little swelling until a major segment is involved.

sections.heading: Development, Angiogenesis and Remodelling
sections.body: Blood vessels are among the first organs to form. In the third week of human development, mesodermal cells in the yolk sac and embryo condense into blood islands; the outer cells become angioblasts and flatten into endothelium, the inner ones become the first blood cells, and the islands fuse into a primitive plexus. This de novo formation of vessels from precursor cells is called vasculogenesis and depends critically on vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF-A, signalling through the receptor VEGFR-2. Losing even a single copy of the Vegfa gene in a mouse is lethal in the embryo, a rare example of true haploinsufficiency and a measure of how tightly dosed the system is. Once a plexus exists, all later growth is angiogenesis: new vessels sprouting from existing ones. A VEGF gradient released by hypoxic tissue selects one endothelial cell to become a tip cell, which extends filopodia and migrates up the gradient without dividing. The tip cell expresses the ligand DLL4, which activates Notch in its neighbours and suppresses their tip behaviour, so they become stalk cells that proliferate and form the lumen behind. This lateral inhibition is what prevents every cell sprouting at once and turning the vasculature into a useless tangle. Blocking DLL4 experimentally produces dense, hyperbranched, non-functional networks. New tubes are stabilised by recruiting pericytes and smooth muscle through platelet-derived growth factor B and the angiopoietin–Tie2 system, and vessels carrying no flow regress. Arterial and venous identity is specified genetically before flow begins, not by pressure as was long assumed: arterial endothelium expresses ephrin-B2 and Notch targets, venous endothelium expresses EphB4 and the nuclear receptor COUP-TFII, and swapping these swaps the vessel's behaviour. Flow then refines the anatomy through remodelling. Endothelial cells sense shear stress and signal the vessel to adjust its calibre so that shear returns to a set point of roughly 15 dynes per square centimetre, meaning a vessel carrying more flow enlarges and an under-used one shrinks. This explains why the feeding artery to an arteriovenous fistula created for dialysis enlarges dramatically over weeks, and why a collateral vessel bypassing a slowly narrowing artery can grow from a hair-thin channel into a useful conduit — the process called arteriogenesis, which is driven by shear and inflammation rather than hypoxia. In adults angiogenesis is otherwise largely switched off except in wound healing, the menstrual cycle and placental development. Its pathological reactivation drives tumour growth, diabetic retinopathy and wet macular degeneration, which is why anti-VEGF antibodies and traps injected into the eye have transformed the treatment of those retinal diseases since around 2006. The same principle underlies the anti-angiogenic approach to cancer proposed by Judah Folkman in 1971, who argued that a solid tumour cannot grow beyond one or two millimetres without recruiting its own blood supply. Drugs blocking VEGF do slow some tumours, but the clinical benefit has been more modest than the theory promised, partly because tumours switch to alternative growth factors. One further quirk resolves at birth: the fetal circulation bypasses the lungs through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, and these normally close within days of the first breath.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: Atherosclerosis, Aneurysm, Thrombosis, Varicosity
sections.body: Atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima of large and medium arteries and remains the leading cause of death worldwide. It begins with endothelial dysfunction at sites of disturbed, low or oscillatory shear stress — arterial branch points, the outer wall of bifurcations, the coronary arteries — where the protective shear-driven nitric oxide signal is weak. Low-density lipoprotein particles enter the intima, are retained by binding to proteoglycans and become oxidised; monocytes are recruited, become macrophages, engulf the modified lipid and turn into foam cells, producing the fatty streak visible even in the aortas of many teenagers. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, proliferate and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. Two quite different clinical events follow. Gradual luminal narrowing causes demand ischaemia — stable angina on exertion, or intermittent claudication in the legs — and usually needs about 70 percent diameter stenosis before flow reserve is exhausted. Far more dangerous is plaque rupture or erosion, in which a thin inflamed cap tears, exposing tissue factor to the blood and producing an occlusive thrombus in minutes; this causes most heart attacks and many strokes, and the culprit plaque is frequently one that was not severely narrowing beforehand. An aneurysm is permanent dilatation to more than 1.5 times normal diameter, caused by destruction of medial elastin and collagen by matrix metalloproteinases. The abdominal aorta below the renal arteries is the commonest site; normal diameter is around 2 centimetres and 3 centimetres defines an aneurysm. Rupture risk is governed by Laplace's law, so it climbs steeply with diameter — roughly 1 percent per year below 5 centimetres but on the order of 10 to 20 percent per year above 6 — which is why repair is generally offered around 5.5 centimetres in men. Aortic dissection is different: blood tears into the media through an intimal defect and splits the wall along its length, classically producing sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, and it is immediately life-threatening. Venous thrombosis follows Virchow's triad, described in the 1850s: stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Immobility, long flights, surgery, pregnancy, cancer and inherited clotting defects such as factor V Leiden all contribute. A calf or thigh vein clot may embolise to the pulmonary arteries. Chronic venous insufficiency from valve failure produces varicose veins, ankle swelling, brown pigmentation and ulcers. Vasculitis, in which the vessel wall itself is attacked by immune mechanisms, is a smaller but important category — giant cell arteritis in the temporal artery of people over fifty can cause irreversible blindness within days and is treated with steroids before the biopsy result returns. Two further failure modes deserve naming. Arterial spasm without structural disease produces Raynaud's phenomenon, in which cold or stress closes the digital arteries and the fingers turn white, then blue, then red on rewarming. Microvascular disease, meaning damage to arterioles and capillaries rather than named arteries, is the quieter and in some ways more destructive process: sustained hyperglycaemia thickens capillary basement membranes and destroys pericytes, the mechanism behind diabetic retinopathy, diabetic kidney disease and the loss of protective sensation in the feet.

sections.heading: Reading the Vascular System at the Bedside
sections.body: Vascular examination needs no equipment beyond fingers, a watch and, ideally, a blood pressure cuff, and it yields more information than most people expect. Pulses are felt where an artery crosses a bone close to the skin. The standard points are the radial at the wrist on the thumb side, the brachial medial to the biceps tendon in the elbow crease, the carotid between the larynx and the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the femoral at the mid-inguinal point, the popliteal deep in the back of the flexed knee, the posterior tibial just behind and below the inner ankle bone, and the dorsalis pedis on the top of the foot lateral to the big toe's extensor tendon. Around 8 to 10 percent of healthy people have no palpable dorsalis pedis as a normal variant, so its absence alone means little; absence of both foot pulses is significant. Never press both carotids at once, and press gently: the carotid sinus baroreceptor can be stimulated into a reflex slowing of the heart. Assess rate, rhythm, volume and symmetry, and compare sides — a blood pressure difference greater than about 20 millimetres of mercury between arms suggests obstruction or dissection. The ankle–brachial index is the single most useful bedside vascular number: measure systolic pressure at the ankle and at the arm and divide. Values of 1.00 to 1.40 are normal, 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease, and below 0.40 suggests critical limb ischaemia. Values above 1.40 mean incompressible calcified vessels and are themselves a warning. The six signs of acute arterial occlusion are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and perishing cold; a limb with the last three has hours at most before muscle necrosis becomes irreversible.
steps: Protect yourself first: put on gloves or use a plastic bag as a barrier if blood contact is possible.
Expose the wound. Cut or move clothing away so you can see exactly where blood is coming from; a soaked trouser leg hides the source.
Apply firm direct pressure with the flat of your fingers over the bleeding point, using a clean pad if available and bare hands if not. Press hard, and on a point rather than vaguely over an area.
Hold continuously for at least ten uninterrupted minutes by the clock. Lifting the pad to check destroys the forming clot and is the commonest reason pressure appears to fail.
If blood soaks through, add more dressing on top and press harder; do not remove the original layer.
Raise the injured limb above the level of the heart if that does not cause severe pain, since it lowers local pressure.

For bright red blood spurting in time with the pulse from an arm or leg that pressure does not stop within a few minutes, apply a tourniquet 5 to 7 centimetres above the wound, never over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops completely, write the time on the casualty, and do not loosen it.
Keep the person lying flat and warm, watch for pale clammy skin, rising pulse and confusion as signs of major blood loss, and get professional help as fast as possible.

guides.safetyNote: This guide describes anatomy and physiology for education. It is not a substitute for clinical training or medical care. Suspected arterial bleeding, a cold pulseless limb, a tearing chest or back pain, or a sudden painful swollen leg are emergencies: control obvious bleeding with firm direct pressure, and seek professional help immediately.

guides.title: Blood Pressure Regulation and the Baroreflex
guides.summary: A comprehensive account of what arterial blood pressure is, the physical factors that set it, and how the body regulates it over seconds, minutes and days, centred on the baroreflex and extending to the hormonal and renal systems and their clinical failures.
guides.safetyNote: This guide is educational and explains normal and abnormal physiology; it is not medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose yourself or to start, stop, or adjust any medication. Very high or very low blood pressure, fainting, or symptoms such as chest pain, severe headache, or confusion require prompt professional medical care.

sections.heading: What Blood Pressure Is
sections.body:
Blood pressure is the force that circulating blood exerts against the walls of the arteries, and it is the pressure that drives blood through the tissues so that every cell receives oxygen and nutrients and has its wastes carried away. It is measured in millimetres of mercury, a unit inherited from the mercury column of the original sphygmomanometer, and a normal adult reading is conventionally written as around one hundred and twenty over eighty. The two numbers name the extremes of a pressure that rises and falls with every heartbeat. The higher figure, the systolic pressure, is the peak reached when the left ventricle contracts and ejects blood into the aorta. The lower figure, the diastolic pressure, is the trough that remains while the heart relaxes and refills between beats, sustained by the elastic recoil of the large arteries.

Because pressure is pulsing rather than steady, physiologists often use a single averaged value called the mean arterial pressure, which is the average pressure over a whole cardiac cycle and the pressure that actually determines tissue perfusion. Since the heart spends more of each cycle in diastole than in systole, the mean is not the simple average of the two numbers but lies closer to the diastolic value, and it is estimated as the diastolic pressure plus one third of the difference between systolic and diastolic, the difference itself being called the pulse pressure. For a typical one hundred and twenty over eighty reading the mean arterial pressure is therefore about ninety-three millimetres of mercury.

Blood pressure is not one fixed number even in a healthy person; it varies continuously with posture, activity, emotion, breathing, and the time of day, typically dipping during sleep and rising in the early morning. This variability is not a flaw but the visible sign of an active control system constantly adjusting the circulation to circumstance. Standard measurement uses an inflatable cuff around the upper arm, inflated above systolic pressure to stop flow and then slowly released while a listener or a sensor detects the return and disappearance of flow sounds, called Korotkoff sounds after the Russian physician Nikolai Korotkov, who first described them in 1905, whose onset marks systolic and whose muffling or disappearance marks diastolic pressure. Accurate readings require a correctly sized cuff, a supported arm at heart level, and a rested subject, because pain, a full bladder, talking, or a recent coffee can all raise the figure. Understanding what the numbers mean and how they are obtained is the necessary first step before asking how the body holds them within a life-sustaining range.

sections.heading: The Physical Determinants: Flow, Resistance, and Cardiac Output
sections.body:
Arterial pressure is not regulated directly; the body controls it by adjusting a small number of underlying physical quantities, and understanding those quantities is essential to understanding every reflex that follows. The governing relationship is an analogue of Ohm's law from electricity: pressure equals flow multiplied by resistance. In the circulation, mean arterial pressure is set by the cardiac output, the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute, multiplied by the total peripheral resistance, the overall opposition the vessels present to that flow. Raise either factor and pressure rises; lower either and it falls. Almost every physiological and pharmacological influence on blood pressure acts through one of these two levers.

Cardiac output is itself the product of heart rate and stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat. Heart rate is set moment to moment by the balance of sympathetic nerve traffic, which speeds the heart, and parasympathetic vagal traffic, which slows it. Stroke volume depends on how full the ventricle is before it contracts, called preload, on the force of contraction, called contractility, and on the pressure the ventricle must push against to eject, called afterload. Preload rises with venous return, so anything that returns more blood to the heart, such as increased blood volume or the squeezing of veins by muscle activity, increases stroke volume, a principle formalised as the Frank-Starling mechanism, in which a more stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully.

Total peripheral resistance is dominated by the small arteries and arterioles, whose muscular walls can constrict or dilate. Here the physics is unforgiving: by Poiseuille's law the resistance of a vessel varies inversely with the fourth power of its radius, so halving a vessel's radius multiplies its resistance sixteenfold. This extreme sensitivity is precisely why the arterioles are the body's chief pressure-control valves; tiny changes in their calibre, driven by sympathetic nerves and by local and hormonal signals, produce large changes in resistance and hence in pressure while barely altering the total blood delivered. Blood viscosity and vessel elasticity also contribute, the stiffening of arteries with age widening pulse pressure by reducing the cushioning of each ejection.

A final determinant is the total volume of blood in the system and its distribution. Roughly two thirds of the blood sits at any moment in the highly distensible veins, which act as a reservoir; constricting them shifts blood toward the heart and raises filling. Because pressure emerges from output times resistance, and output and resistance are each built from these sub-factors, the regulatory systems have several independent handles to pull, and the reflexes described next work by turning heart rate, contractility, arteriolar tone, and venous capacity up or down in coordinated fashion.

sections.heading: The Timescales of Regulation
sections.body:
The body defends its arterial pressure with several overlapping control systems that differ chiefly in how fast they act and how long they can be sustained, and it is helpful to sort them by timescale before examining any one in detail. No single mechanism does everything; each covers a range of speeds, and they hand off to one another as a disturbance persists, so that pressure is guarded from the first second after a change of posture to the slow adjustments of chronic disease.

The fastest responses operate within seconds and are neural reflexes carried by the autonomic nervous system. Chief among them is the baroreflex, driven by stretch sensors in the great arteries, which corrects a sudden fall or rise in pressure almost immediately by changing heart rate, cardiac contractility, and the tone of arterioles and veins. Alongside it act the chemoreceptor reflexes, which respond to blood gas changes, and the central nervous system ischaemic response, a powerful emergency reaction to severe brain underperfusion. These neural systems are quick but they fatigue and reset; they buffer transients superbly but cannot hold a corrected pressure indefinitely.

Over minutes to hours a second tier engages, largely hormonal and involving shifts of fluid between compartments. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system responds to falling pressure and reduced kidney perfusion by generating angiotensin, a potent constrictor, and aldosterone, which promotes salt and water retention. Antidiuretic hormone, released when pressure or blood concentration warrants, conserves water and at high levels constricts vessels. Stress-relaxation of the vessel walls and the movement of fluid across capillary walls between blood and tissue also help match the volume of blood to the capacity of the circulation over this intermediate period.

The slowest and ultimately dominant control operates over hours to days and belongs to the kidney, which sets the long-term level of blood pressure by adjusting the total volume of body fluid through the balance of salt and water intake against excretion. This renal-body fluid mechanism, emphasised in the influential analysis of Arthur Guyton in the mid-twentieth century, has in principle an unlimited ability to correct a sustained pressure error, because as long as a mismatch exists the kidney keeps changing fluid volume until balance is restored. The practical lesson of this layered arrangement is that fast neural reflexes such as the baroreflex are exquisite at smoothing the moment-to-moment turbulence of daily life but are not the arbiters of a person's average pressure over weeks and years; that role falls to the hormonal and renal systems. Keeping the timescales distinct prevents the common error of expecting the baroreflex to explain chronic hypertension, which it does not.

sections.heading: The Baroreceptors: Where Pressure Is Sensed
sections.body:
The baroreflex begins with sensors that measure arterial pressure, and these are not pressure gauges in the engineering sense but stretch receptors, nerve endings embedded in the walls of certain arteries that fire more rapidly as the vessel wall is distended. Because a higher pressure stretches the wall further, the firing rate of these endings encodes the prevailing pressure, and it encodes not only the steady level but the rate of change and the pulsatility, so the nervous system receives a rich, continuously updated signal about the state of the circulation.

The two most important groups sit at strategic points near the heart and brain. The carotid sinus is a slight dilation at the origin of the internal carotid artery on each side of the neck, positioned to monitor the pressure of blood heading to the brain. Its receptors are exquisitely sensitive, and their afferent signals travel along a small branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, the ninth cranial nerve, sometimes called the sinus nerve of Hering. The aortic arch carries a second population of stretch receptors that monitor pressure in the central systemic circulation, and their signals travel along the vagus nerve, the tenth cranial nerve. Both sets are called high-pressure or arterial baroreceptors to distinguish them from the low-pressure stretch receptors in the atria and great veins that sense the filling of the venous side.

These receptors are most responsive within the normal operating range of pressure, around the usual mean arterial pressure, where the relationship between pressure and firing is steepest, so that a small change in pressure produces the largest change in signal and hence the promptest correction. At very low pressures the receptors fall silent, and at very high pressures their response saturates. They are also rate-sensitive, firing more during the rising phase of each pulse than a static pressure would predict, which lets the system respond to the sharpness as well as the height of a pressure change. A clinically important property is adaptation: if a new pressure is held steady for a period, the receptors gradually adjust their firing toward a baseline, a resetting that is central to why the baroreflex cannot by itself set long-term pressure.

The carotid sinus is accessible enough that gentle external pressure on the neck can stimulate it, and carotid sinus massage is used cautiously by clinicians to slow a racing heart, exploiting exactly this reflex; the same sensitivity explains why a tight collar or sudden neck pressure can occasionally cause faintness in susceptible people. From these sensors a continuous stream of nerve impulses flows toward the brainstem, where the information is integrated and the corrective response is generated, the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Central Integration in the Brainstem
sections.body:
The signals from the baroreceptors do not act directly on the heart and vessels; they are first delivered to and processed by the brainstem, where the corrective response is computed and dispatched. The primary destination is a region of the medulla oblongata called the nucleus of the solitary tract, often abbreviated NTS, which is the first central relay for almost all visceral sensory information, including that from the arterial baroreceptors and the chemoreceptors. The afferent fibres of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves terminate here, and the NTS acts as the integrating hub that reads the incoming firing rate as a measure of current pressure.

From the NTS the information is distributed to other medullary centres that command the two arms of the autonomic outflow. When baroreceptor firing is high, signalling that pressure is high, the NTS excites neurons in a region called the caudal ventrolateral medulla, which in turn inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla, the principal source of the excitatory drive to the sympathetic nervous system. The net effect is that high pressure reduces sympathetic outflow. Simultaneously, high baroreceptor firing excites the cardiac vagal neurons in the nucleus ambiguus and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, increasing parasympathetic drive to the heart. The arrangement is a classic negative feedback loop: a rise in pressure quietens the sympathetic system and activates the parasympathetic, both of which act to bring pressure back down, while a fall in pressure does the opposite.

This brainstem circuitry is not sealed off from the rest of the nervous system. Higher centres, including the hypothalamus and regions of the cortex and limbic system, feed into it, which is why anticipation, fear, pain, exercise, and emotion can override or bias the reflex, raising pressure and heart rate before any actual change in circulation has occurred. The hypothalamic defence reaction, mobilising the body for exertion or threat, deliberately resets the baroreflex so that it defends a higher pressure appropriate to activity rather than fighting the useful rise. Breathing also modulates the loop, producing the familiar respiratory sinus arrhythmia in which heart rate quickens on inspiration and slows on expiration.

Because the medulla is the meeting point of these pathways, damage there, from stroke, tumour, or trauma, can devastate cardiovascular control, producing wild swings of pressure or a dangerous loss of regulation. The precise wiring of the medullary centres was worked out through decades of animal experiments and remains an active field, but the essential logic is settled and elegant: a single stream of stretch information is transformed, within a few small nuclei, into coordinated commands that raise or lower pressure by acting oppositely on the two branches of the autonomic nervous system.

sections.heading: The Efferent Response: Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Action
sections.body:
Once the brainstem has judged that pressure is too high or too low, it acts through the two divisions of the autonomic nervous system, whose opposing effects on the heart and vessels are the muscles of the reflex. The sympathetic division is the pressure-raising arm. Its nerves release noradrenaline onto the heart and blood vessels, and the adrenal medulla adds adrenaline to the bloodstream, so that sympathetic activation produces a suite of coordinated effects that all tend to raise arterial pressure at once.

On the heart, sympathetic stimulation acting through beta-one adrenergic receptors increases the rate of firing of the sinoatrial node, so the heart beats faster, and increases the force of each contraction, so stroke volume rises; together these raise cardiac output. On the arterioles, sympathetic nerves acting through alpha-one adrenergic receptors cause vasoconstriction, narrowing the vessels and raising total peripheral resistance. On the veins, the same constriction reduces the venous reservoir and squeezes blood back toward the heart, increasing preload and thus, through the Frank-Starling mechanism, stroke volume once more. A rise in pressure needing correction downward is met simply by withdrawing this sympathetic drive, allowing rate, contractility, and vessel tone to fall.

The parasympathetic division, carried to the heart by the vagus nerve, is the pressure-lowering arm, but its reach is narrower. Vagal fibres release acetylcholine onto the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, acting through muscarinic receptors to slow the heart rate sharply and, to a lesser extent, reduce atrial contractility. The vagus has little direct effect on the arterioles of the systemic circulation, so parasympathetic control of pressure works chiefly by changing heart rate. Because vagal effects are fast, mediated by rapidly acting potassium channels, the parasympathetic system can slow the heart within a single beat, giving the baroreflex its remarkable speed on the downward side.

The two divisions are usually reciprocally controlled, so that when pressure falls the sympathetic drive rises while the vagal drive falls, and both changes push pressure up, whereas when pressure rises the reverse occurs. This push-pull arrangement gives fine and rapid control across the normal range. The pharmacology of these pathways is the basis of much cardiovascular medicine: beta-blockers oppose the sympathetic effect on the heart, alpha-blockers oppose the vasoconstriction, and drugs that mimic or block acetylcholine alter vagal tone. Understanding which receptor and which target a signal acts upon makes the otherwise bewildering array of blood-pressure drugs intelligible, since each intervenes at a specific point in this efferent limb, either blunting the pressure-raising sympathetic actions or reinforcing the pressure-lowering parasympathetic ones.

sections.heading: The Baroreflex in Action: Standing and Bleeding
sections.body:
The abstract loop becomes concrete in two everyday and life-threatening scenarios that the baroreflex is built to handle: the simple act of standing up, and the emergency of blood loss. Both begin with a fall in central arterial pressure, and both are corrected by the same reflex arithmetic of increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic outflow.

When a person stands from lying or sitting, gravity immediately pulls perhaps half a litre of blood downward into the veins of the legs and abdomen. Venous return to the heart drops, filling falls, and by the Frank-Starling mechanism stroke volume and therefore cardiac output decline, so pressure at the level of the carotid sinus begins to fall within a second or two. The baroreceptors fire less, the medulla detects the reduced signal, and it responds by raising sympathetic drive and lowering vagal drive. Heart rate quickens, the heart contracts more forcefully, the arterioles constrict to raise resistance, and the veins constrict to push blood back toward the heart. Within a few heartbeats pressure is restored, usually so smoothly that the person notices nothing. When this reflex is sluggish or inadequate, the person feels light-headed on standing and may faint, a condition called orthostatic hypotension.

Haemorrhage poses the same problem more severely and for longer. Losing blood reduces the total volume in the circulation, lowering venous return, filling, cardiac output, and pressure. The baroreflex responds with maximal sympathetic activation: the heart races, the arterioles clamp down, especially in the skin, gut, and non-essential beds, and the veins constrict to mobilise their reserve, all working to keep pressure and brain perfusion adequate despite the shortfall. The pallor, cold clammy skin, and rapid weak pulse of a bleeding patient are the visible signature of this intense sympathetic compensation, and they can hold pressure nearly normal until perhaps a quarter of the blood volume is lost, after which the reflex is overwhelmed and pressure collapses. This is why a falling blood pressure in trauma is an ominous late sign rather than an early one.

These examples also reveal the reflex's limits. It buffers a change but does not by itself replace lost volume; in standing, the longer-term correction comes from fluid shifts and, if the upright posture is sustained, from the hormonal systems, while in haemorrhage the definitive treatment is to stop the bleeding and restore volume. The baroreflex buys time, holding perfusion of the brain and heart while slower and more durable mechanisms, or a clinician, address the underlying cause. This buying of time is the whole purpose of a fast reflex, and it is exactly the response that a tilt-table test probes, deliberately standing a patient upright under monitoring to unmask a sluggish or paradoxical reaction and so investigate unexplained dizziness and fainting.

sections.heading: Baroreflex Sensitivity and Resetting
sections.body:
The baroreflex is not a fixed circuit but an adjustable one, and two properties, its sensitivity and its capacity to reset, are central both to normal physiology and to disease. Baroreflex sensitivity refers to how vigorously the reflex responds to a given change in pressure, usually quantified as the change in heart rate interval produced per unit change in systolic pressure. A sensitive reflex produces a large, prompt correction; a blunted one responds weakly. Sensitivity can be measured clinically by observing how the heart rate responds to spontaneous fluctuations of pressure or to drugs that raise or lower it, and it is a useful index of autonomic health.

Baroreflex sensitivity declines with age, as the arteries stiffen and transmit less stretch to the receptors, and it is reduced in heart failure, diabetes, and after heart attacks. This matters because a well-functioning baroreflex protects against the electrical instability of the heart, and a markedly depressed baroreflex sensitivity after a heart attack is associated with a higher risk of dangerous arrhythmias and sudden death, making it a marker of prognosis. Conversely, physical fitness and regular exercise tend to preserve or enhance baroreflex sensitivity.

Resetting is the more conceptually important property, and it explains the reflex's role, or rather its lack of a role, in setting long-term pressure. If arterial pressure is held at a new level for more than a day or so, the baroreceptors and the central pathways gradually adjust so that the reflex begins to defend the new pressure as if it were normal. The whole stimulus-response curve shifts along the pressure axis toward the prevailing level. This is why the baroreflex cannot cause or cure chronic hypertension: faced with a persistently raised pressure, the reflex does not keep fighting to lower it but instead resets and comes to treat the high pressure as the value to be protected. Acute resetting begins within minutes and a slower chronic resetting develops over days, involving changes in the receptors themselves and in the central processing.

The distinction between sensitivity and set point is worth holding firmly. Resetting changes the pressure the reflex defends, the set point, while sensitivity changes the gain of its response around that point. In established hypertension the reflex is typically reset to defend the elevated pressure and is often also blunted, so it buffers day-to-day variability around a high average without opposing the high average itself. This is a humbling illustration of a general principle in physiology: a negative feedback system stabilises a variable around whatever set point it is given, and it does not determine that set point, which for arterial pressure is fixed over the long term by the hormonal and renal systems rather than by the neural reflex that so effectively smooths the short term.

sections.heading: Chemoreceptors and Other Rapid Reflexes
sections.body:
The baroreflex is the principal rapid regulator of pressure, but it works alongside several other fast reflexes that share the same efferent machinery and can reinforce or override it. Most important are the chemoreceptors, sensors that monitor the chemical state of the blood rather than its pressure. The peripheral chemoreceptors, clustered in the carotid bodies near the carotid sinus and in aortic bodies near the arch, respond to a fall in the oxygen content of arterial blood and to rises in carbon dioxide and acidity. Their primary job is to drive breathing, but when oxygen falls sharply or pressure drops so low that even the chemoreceptors become underperfused, they also strongly stimulate the sympathetic system, raising pressure. This chemoreceptor contribution becomes significant chiefly at low pressures, below the range where the baroreflex operates best, so the two systems are complementary, the baroreflex guarding the normal range and the chemoreflex adding emergency support when pressure falls dangerously.

The central nervous system ischaemic response is the most powerful pressure-raising reflex of all, a last-ditch reaction triggered when blood flow to the brainstem itself becomes inadequate, as in severe shock or greatly raised intracranial pressure. The resulting rise in carbon dioxide and fall in oxygen within the medulla directly and massively activate the sympathetic outflow, producing an intense vasoconstriction that can drive arterial pressure to very high levels in an effort to force blood through the compromised brain. When raised intracranial pressure triggers it, the response, together with the reflex slowing of the heart that the resulting high pressure provokes through the baroreflex, produces the ominous clinical triad of rising blood pressure, slow heart rate, and irregular breathing known as the Cushing reflex, a warning of critical brain compression.

Several lower-pressure and mechanical reflexes fine-tune the system. Stretch receptors in the atria and great veins sense the filling of the venous side, and their signals adjust heart rate and fluid handling; the Bainbridge reflex, by which a rise in venous return and atrial stretch speeds the heart, helps the heart keep pace with incoming blood and prevents blood from damming up on the venous side. Respiration continuously modulates pressure and heart rate, producing the beat-to-beat variability that is itself a sign of a healthy autonomic system. Together these reflexes form a layered, redundant defence, and their coordinated action, rather than the baroreflex alone, keeps the short-term circulation stable across the enormous range of demands, from sleep to sprinting, that daily life imposes. Because these reflexes overlap and reinforce one another, the blunting or failure of any single one is usually masked by the others, which is part of why physiologists found their individual contributions so difficult to disentangle experimentally.

sections.heading: Medium-Term Control: Hormones and Fluid
sections.body:
When a fall in pressure persists beyond the few minutes that the neural reflexes can comfortably sustain, a slower and more durable tier of control takes over, dominated by hormones that adjust both vessel tone and the volume of fluid in the circulation. The central player is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Specialised cells in the kidney, the juxtaglomerular cells, sense a fall in the pressure or flow reaching the kidney, as well as sympathetic stimulation and a fall in the salt delivered to a part of the tubule, and respond by releasing the enzyme renin into the blood. Renin acts on a circulating protein from the liver, angiotensinogen, cleaving it to angiotensin I, which is then converted, chiefly in the lungs by angiotensin-converting enzyme, to the active hormone angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II raises pressure by several routes at once. It is a powerful direct constrictor of arterioles, raising peripheral resistance within minutes. It stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, a hormone that acts on the kidney over hours to promote the reabsorption of sodium and, with it, water, thereby expanding blood volume. It enhances sympathetic activity and stimulates thirst and the release of antidiuretic hormone, all of which support pressure. This cascade is why drugs that block it, the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and the angiotensin receptor blockers, are among the most widely used treatments for hypertension and heart failure.

Antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, is released from the posterior pituitary in response to rising blood concentration and, when the fall is large, to reduced pressure and volume sensed by the atrial and arterial receptors. Its main action is to conserve water by concentrating the urine, which defends volume, and at higher concentrations it also constricts vessels, which defends pressure directly, the property that gives it its alternative name. Because it responds strongly only to substantial falls in volume or pressure, it is more an emergency and fine-tuning hormone for pressure than a routine one.

Opposing these pressure-raising and volume-conserving hormones are the natriuretic peptides, chiefly atrial natriuretic peptide, released from the heart's atria when they are stretched by a high blood volume. These peptides promote the excretion of sodium and water and relax vessels, lowering volume and pressure, and they represent the body's counter-regulatory brake against overfilling. The balance between the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and the natriuretic peptides, played out over minutes to hours through changes in vessel tone and in the kidney's handling of salt and water, sets pressure in the intermediate term and forms the bridge between the instantaneous neural reflexes and the slow, decisive control exercised by the kidney over days.

sections.heading: Long-Term Control: The Kidney and Pressure Natriuresis
sections.body:
Over days and weeks the ultimate control of arterial pressure rests with the kidney, through its command over the total volume of fluid in the body. The logic, developed most fully by Arthur Guyton and colleagues in the mid-twentieth century, rests on a single powerful mechanism called pressure natriuresis and diuresis: as arterial pressure rises, the kidney excretes more sodium and water, and as pressure falls, it excretes less. Because the amount of fluid in the body, and hence blood volume, depends on the balance between intake and excretion, this creates a feedback loop that adjusts volume until pressure returns to the level at which intake and output are balanced.

The strength of this mechanism lies in a property Guyton called infinite gain. A neural reflex has a finite gain and settles at a compromise that leaves some of the original error uncorrected, but the renal mechanism, in principle, does not stop adjusting fluid volume until pressure is returned exactly to its set point, because only at that precise pressure is the excretion of salt and water equal to the intake. As long as any error remains, excretion does not match intake, volume keeps changing, and pressure keeps moving toward the point of balance. In this analysis the long-term set point of arterial pressure is determined by where the kidney's pressure-natriuresis curve sits and by the level of salt and water intake, not by the fast neural reflexes, which can be entirely reset without changing the long-term average.

This framework has a striking clinical implication: for arterial pressure to remain chronically elevated, the kidney's pressure-natriuresis relationship must be shifted so that a normal excretion of salt and water occurs only at a higher pressure. Sustained hypertension, in this view, always involves the kidney, whether through intrinsic renal disease, through excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that resets the curve, through high salt intake in salt-sensitive individuals, or through other influences on renal sodium handling. The success of diuretic drugs, which promote sodium and water loss, and of salt restriction in lowering pressure is consistent with this central role of body fluid volume.

The Guytonian view has been debated and refined, and some physiologists argue that the nervous system and the vasculature contribute more to long-term regulation than the pure renal model allows, so the exact balance of long-term control remains a genuine and active scientific question. What is not disputed is that the kidney's handling of salt and water is a dominant determinant of chronic pressure, and that this slow, high-authority mechanism, rather than the elegant but resettable baroreflex, is what fixes the pressure a person's circulation defends over the course of a life.

sections.heading: Clinical Failures: Hypertension, Fainting, and Baroreflex Failure
sections.body:
The regulatory systems described here are best understood through the disorders that appear when they fail, and blood-pressure disease is among the commonest of all medical problems. Chronic hypertension, sustained high arterial pressure, is the most prevalent and consequential. In the great majority of cases no single cause is found and it is called essential or primary hypertension, reflecting the resetting of the kidney's pressure-natriuresis relationship and often an overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone or sympathetic system, frequently against a background of ageing arteries, excess weight, and high salt intake. A minority of cases are secondary to a specific cause such as kidney disease, an aldosterone-producing tumour, or narrowing of a renal artery. Because the baroreflex resets, high pressure usually causes no symptoms, which is why hypertension is called the silent killer and why it is diagnosed by measurement rather than by feeling; left untreated it damages the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes over years by the relentless mechanical stress of the raised pressure.

At the opposite extreme, orthostatic hypotension is a failure of the rapid baroreflex to defend pressure on standing, so that pressure falls, the brain is briefly underperfused, and the person feels dizzy or faints. It becomes commoner with age and is a frequent side effect of blood-pressure drugs, of dehydration, and of conditions that damage the autonomic nerves, such as diabetes and Parkinson's disease. A related event is the common faint, or vasovagal syncope, in which an inappropriate reflex, often triggered by pain, fright, or prolonged standing, suddenly withdraws sympathetic tone and increases vagal drive, dropping heart rate and pressure together so that the person loses consciousness and falls, which conveniently restores brain perfusion by removing the effect of gravity.

Baroreflex failure itself, a rare but instructive condition, follows damage to the baroreceptors or their nerves, for example after neck surgery, radiation, or certain brainstem lesions. Deprived of the buffering reflex, patients suffer violent swings of pressure, with severe surges during stress and sometimes profound falls, because the smoothing loop that normally holds pressure steady is gone. Autonomic failure from widespread nerve degeneration produces a similar loss of moment-to-moment control, classically with severe orthostatic hypotension.

The treatment of these disorders maps directly onto the physiology. Hypertension is lowered with diuretics that reduce volume, with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers that interrupt the renin-angiotensin system, with calcium-channel blockers and other vasodilators that reduce resistance, and with beta-blockers that reduce cardiac output, alone or in combination. Orthostatic hypotension is managed by raising volume, by physical measures such as compression garments and slow rising, and sometimes by drugs that constrict vessels. In every case the rational choice of therapy follows from understanding which lever of pressure, volume, resistance, or cardiac output, and which control system, neural, hormonal, or renal, is disordered.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and Connections Onward
sections.body:
Several misunderstandings about blood pressure are worth correcting explicitly, because they lead people astray in interpreting their own readings and in reasoning about the physiology. A common belief is that a person can feel when their blood pressure is high; in reality chronic hypertension is almost always symptomless, precisely because the baroreflex has reset to accept it, and headaches or flushing are unreliable guides.
