Modern interventions, from pacemakers and stents to valve replacements, catheter procedures and transplantation, all rest on the anatomy and physiology set out in this guide. Ongoing research into repairing or regenerating damaged heart muscle, into the genetics of cardiomyopathies, and into preventing atherosclerosis represents some of the most active frontiers in medicine, precisely because heart disease remains so common. A reader who grasps the chambers, valves, blood supply, wiring and cycle holds the framework on which all of that builds.

guides.title: First Aid
guides.summary: Bleeding, CPR, shock, how to treat a burn or scald, fractures and choking.

sections.heading: Priorities (DR ABC)
sections.body: The sequence exists because the fastest killers must be found and fixed first: an unnoticed hazard can create a second casualty, a blocked airway kills in minutes, and absent breathing or catastrophic bleeding kill soon after. Work the letters in order and resist the urge to jump to the obvious injury. DANGER: stop and scan before you touch anyone — traffic, fire, fuel, live wires, unstable structures, aggressive people, fast water. A second casualty helps nobody; if the scene cannot be made safe, keep your distance, call for help, and talk to the casualty from cover. RESPONSE: speak loudly and clearly ('Can you hear me? Open your eyes'), then squeeze the shoulders firmly. Someone who answers has an open airway and is breathing — that alone is valuable information. No response means you treat them as unconscious and move on immediately. AIRWAY: in an unconscious person the most common obstruction is their own tongue, which loses muscle tone and sags against the back of the throat. Place one hand on the forehead, two fingers under the bony point of the chin, and tilt the head back while lifting the chin; this pulls the tongue forward off the airway. If you suspect a neck injury (fall from height, diving, vehicle crash), try lifting the jaw forward without tilting first — but an open airway always takes priority over a perfectly still neck, because a blocked airway is invariably fatal. BREATHING: put your cheek over their mouth and watch the chest for up to 10 seconds — look for movement, listen for airflow, feel for breath. Occasional slow, snoring, gasping efforts ('agonal gasps') are not normal breathing; they occur in early cardiac arrest and mean start CPR now. CIRCULATION: sweep your eyes quickly over the body for major bleeding and control it with firm direct pressure — a torn large vessel can be fatal in minutes and outranks almost every other injury. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES as early as possible — in most protocols, the moment you find someone unresponsive. Put the phone on speaker so your hands stay free, give the location first (if the call drops, help can still come), and let the dispatcher guide you; they can talk you through CPR step by step. Worked example: you find a cyclist beside a country road. Scan: no traffic coming, the bike is clear of the lane. He does not answer or respond to a firm shoulder squeeze. Head tilt, chin lift; ten seconds watching gives one ragged gasp and nothing more. That is cardiac arrest: you call emergency services on speaker, start compressions, and only later worry about his grazed, bleeding arm. The whole drill took under a minute and put the priorities in the right order.

sections.heading: Severe bleeding
sections.body: Blood loss kills by starving the brain and heart of oxygen, and an adult can lose a fatal volume from one large torn vessel within minutes, so speed matters more than perfect technique. Direct pressure works because clotting needs a still, compressed surface: platelets and fibrin can only build a stable plug if the vessel is pinched shut and the forming clot is not washed away. Press hard on the exact bleeding point with a folded cloth, dressing or even a bare hand, and keep pressing without peeking — every look-and-lift tears the half-formed clot loose and restarts the bleed. If blood soaks through, add fresh layers on top; removing the soaked ones rips the clot out with them. Once bleeding slows, bind the dressing firmly in place so pressure continues while your hands do other things. Raise the limb above heart level if there is no fracture — gravity modestly lowers the pressure driving the leak. For deep wounds at the groin, armpit or neck, where a tourniquet cannot fit, pack the cavity: push cloth or gauze deep into the wound directly onto the bleeding point and hold hard pressure on top for at least ten unbroken minutes. TOURNIQUET: if life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg will not stop with firm pressure, apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound — never over a joint — and tighten until the bleeding actually stops, not merely slows. Applied properly it hurts; that is expected, and you must not loosen it out of sympathy. A commercial windlass tourniquet is best, but an improvised band works: folded cloth at least 4-5 cm wide (never cord or wire, which cut through tissue), tied around the limb, with a rigid stick through the knot twisted until flow stops and then secured. Note the time of application in writing — on the casualty's skin if necessary — because hospital staff need it, and leave the tourniquet visible and untouched until professionals take over. A correctly applied tourniquet is generally safe for the time it usually takes to reach care, and limbs are saved far more often than lives are without one. Watch for shock while you work: pale, cold, clammy skin and a fast weak pulse mean lay them flat and keep them warm while maintaining pressure. Worked example: a chainsaw kick-back opens a forearm and bright red blood pulses out in spurts. You clamp a folded shirt over it and lean your body weight on; it soaks through in a minute, so you add a second layer and keep pressing. Still pulsing after several minutes of genuine hard pressure: cloth band 5-7 cm above the wound, stick through the knot, twist until the spurting stops, secure the stick, write the time on his arm, and call for evacuation.

sections.heading: CPR (adult)
sections.body: When the heart stops, breathing stops seconds later, but the blood still holds a few minutes' worth of oxygen — chest compressions exist to push that reserve through the brain and heart muscle until a defibrillator can restart an organised rhythm. Brain damage begins within a few minutes without circulation, which is why the bystander, not the ambulance, decides most outcomes. Confirm the situation first: the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally — occasional snoring gasps (agonal breathing) count as not breathing. Send someone to call emergency services and fetch an AED, or call on speakerphone yourself. Kneel beside the chest, place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest — the lower half of the breastbone — your other hand on top with fingers interlocked, arms straight, shoulders directly above your hands so your body weight does the work. Push hard and fast: 5-6 cm deep at 100-120 compressions per minute, the tempo of the song 'Stayin' Alive'. Let the chest come all the way back up between pushes — full recoil is what lets the heart refill — while keeping your hands in contact with the chest. If trained and willing, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths: head tilt, chin lift, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow steadily for about one second until the chest just rises; harder blowing only forces air into the stomach. If untrained, or unwilling to give breaths, continuous compressions alone are effective and are what emergency dispatchers coach over the phone. Interruptions are the enemy: every pause collapses the blood pressure you have built, so keep any break under ten seconds. Good CPR is exhausting and quality drops within a couple of minutes, so when another rescuer is available, swap every 2 minutes with minimal pause. Ribs often crack under correct compressions, especially in older people; it feels dreadful but is survivable — stopping is not, so carry on. AED: attach it the moment it arrives. Bare the chest, place the pads exactly as the printed pictures show (below the right collarbone, and on the lower left side of the chest), and follow the voice prompts, making sure nobody touches the casualty while it analyses or shocks. Every minute of delay to defibrillation substantially cuts the chance of survival — commonly estimated at around ten percent per minute when no CPR is given — which is why the AED is sent for at the very start. Do not stop unless the person clearly wakes, moves and breathes normally; professionals take over; or you are physically unable to continue. If they recover, put them in the recovery position and keep watching the breathing — cardiac arrest can recur within minutes.

sections.heading: Choking
sections.body: Choking is a foreign object blocking the airway at the throat — most often food — and your response depends entirely on whether air is still moving. The universal sign is hands clutched to the throat; ask plainly, 'Are you choking?'. MILD obstruction: they can speak, cry or cough forcefully. A strong cough generates far more expelling pressure than anything you can do from outside, so encourage them to keep coughing and do nothing else except stay close and watch — back-slapping someone who is coughing effectively can drive the object deeper. SEVERE obstruction: they cannot speak or cough, breathing is silent or high-pitched, and they grip their throat, turn grey-blue and panic. Act immediately. Give up to 5 back blows: lean them well forward (so a freed object falls out of the mouth rather than back down the throat), support the chest with one hand, and strike hard between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, checking after each blow whether the obstruction has cleared. If five back blows fail, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts — the Heimlich manoeuvre: stand behind them, wrap your arms around the waist, place a fist thumb-side-in just above the navel and well below the tip of the breastbone, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply inwards and upwards. The abrupt pressure rise beneath the diaphragm acts as an artificial cough. Alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears or the person goes unconscious. If they go unconscious: lower them carefully to the ground, call emergency services, and start CPR beginning with chest compressions — compressions themselves raise airway pressure and can dislodge the object. Look in the mouth before giving any breaths and remove only what you can actually see; never sweep a finger blindly, which can wedge the object tighter. Special cases: for someone heavily pregnant, or too large for your arms to encircle, use chest thrusts instead — fist on the centre of the breastbone, sharp backward pulls. For an infant under one year, never use abdominal thrusts: lay the baby face-down along your forearm with the head low, give 5 measured back blows, then turn the baby face-up and give 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone, alternating until clear. Alone and choking yourself: call emergency services (an open line summons help even if you cannot speak) and drive your own upper abdomen sharply against a chair back. Afterwards, anyone who received abdominal thrusts should see a doctor even if they feel fine — the manoeuvre can bruise or tear internal organs — and lingering cough, wheeze or a something-still-stuck feeling needs assessment for a retained fragment.

sections.heading: Shock
sections.body: In first aid, shock means the circulation is failing to deliver enough oxygenated blood to the organs — not emotional fright. Common causes are heavy bleeding (external, or hidden inside the chest, abdomen or pelvis), severe fluid loss from burns, vomiting or diarrhoea, heart problems, overwhelming infection, and severe allergic reaction. The signs are the body's own compensations, which is why spotting them early matters: the skin turns pale, cold and clammy because skin vessels clamp down to redirect blood to the brain and heart; the pulse becomes rapid and weak as the heart races to circulate a shrinking volume; breathing goes fast and shallow; the casualty may be thirsty, restless, anxious or unusually quiet, and later confused, drowsy or nauseated. Fading consciousness is a late and grave sign — it means the compensations are failing. Your management is simple and buys time, but only hospital care fixes the cause, so call emergency services early and say the person is 'showing signs of shock'. First treat what you can treat: control external bleeding with direct pressure, cool extensive burns, and help with an adrenaline auto-injector if this is anaphylaxis and they carry one. Lay the person flat on their back on an insulating layer — the bare ground drains body heat quickly. If there is no suspected spinal injury, leg fracture or breathing difficulty, raise the legs about 15-30 cm; gravity returns a useful volume of pooled blood from the legs to the core circulation. Keep them WARM with coats or blankets under as well as over the body: a cooling casualty clots poorly and deteriorates faster, so warmth is treatment, not merely comfort. Reassure calmly and honestly — fear drives adrenaline and raises the oxygen demand a failing circulation cannot meet. Give NOTHING to eat or drink, however thirsty they say they are: shock causes vomiting, an anaesthetic may be needed soon, and vomit in a semi-conscious person can be inhaled into the lungs; on a long wait, moisten the lips only. Loosen tight clothing at neck and waist. Re-check breathing, pulse and alertness every few minutes, and be ready to start CPR or to turn them into the recovery position if they vomit or lose consciousness. Worked example: a man who fell from a ladder insists he is fine, but ten minutes later he is grey, sweating and yawning, his pulse racing, with no visible wound — treat that as internal bleeding until proven otherwise. You lie him down, raise his legs on a rucksack, cover him with two coats, keep him talking, refuse his request for water, and tell the ambulance he is deteriorating. Nothing complicated — but every step slowed the spiral while help travelled.

sections.heading: Recovery position
sections.body: Someone unconscious but breathing goes on their SIDE, because a person left on their back is in quiet danger even while breathing well: every muscle is slack, so the tongue sags against the back of the throat, and the reflexes that normally trigger coughing and swallowing are switched off. If they vomit — common after injury, seizures, intoxication or near-drowning — stomach contents pool at the back of the throat and run into the lungs. Turning them on their side uses gravity to solve both problems at once: the tongue falls forward instead of backward, and fluid drains out of the mouth instead of down the airway. Use it for anyone unconscious and breathing normally, including someone who has started breathing again after CPR. Technique: kneel at their side. Place the near arm out at a right angle to the body, palm up. Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek. With your other hand, pull the far knee up until the foot is flat on the ground, then pull that bent knee toward you to roll the whole body smoothly onto its side against your knees. Tilt the head back to open the airway and settle the top hand under the cheek so the head stays tilted; adjust the top leg so hip and knee rest at right angles, propping the body stably. The mouth should point slightly downhill. Then keep checking breathing every minute or two — chest movement, air on your cheek — because breathing at the moment you rolled them is no guarantee for later. If they stay down a long time, roll them onto the other side after about 30 minutes to protect the lower arm's circulation and nerves. Two cautions. Suspected spinal injury (fall from height, diving accident, vehicle crash): leave them as found and steady the head, opening the airway by lifting the jaw if needed — but if they vomit, or you must leave to get help, or breathing is threatened, roll them anyway, keeping head, shoulders and hips moving as one unit; a blocked airway kills faster and more certainly than careful movement worsens most spinal injuries. Visibly pregnant women go on their LEFT side: on the back or right side the weight of the womb can compress the large vein returning blood to the heart and drop the blood pressure. A worked check: a friend collapses at a party, smells of alcohol, and snores loudly on his back — that snoring is the tongue half-blocking his airway. Rolled into the recovery position, the snoring stops; when he later vomits, it runs onto the floor, not into his lungs. Stay with him and keep checking breathing until help arrives. (Diagram: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

sections.heading: Burns and scalds — how to treat a burn
sections.body: Burned tissue keeps cooking after the source is gone: heat stored in the skin continues to deepen the injury for minutes, which is why immediate, prolonged cooling is the single most useful treatment. Hold the burn under cool (not iced) running water for a full 20 minutes — far longer than instinct suggests, and still worth doing up to about three hours after the injury. Cooling halts the spreading heat damage, relieves pain, and limits swelling. Never apply ice or iced water: the intense cold constricts blood vessels and can deepen the injury. While the water runs, remove rings, watches, bracelets and loose clothing near the area before swelling makes it impossible — a ring left on a burned finger can strangle it like a tourniquet. Do not pull away clothing stuck to the skin; cut around it. Cool the burn but warm the patient: cooling a large area can tip a casualty, especially a child, into hypothermia, so cover the rest of the body while you cool the part. Afterwards, cover the burn loosely with cling film laid lengthwise along the limb (discard the first few turns off the roll; the inner surface is effectively clean), a clean plastic bag for a hand or foot, or a clean non-fluffy cloth. This shields the exposed nerve endings from moving air — much of the pain — and keeps contamination out while still letting a professional assess it. Never apply butter, oils, toothpaste or creams: they trap heat, add bacteria, and have to be scrubbed off later. Do not burst blisters; intact blister skin is a sterile natural dressing. Judging severity: superficial burns are red and painful like sunburn; partial-thickness burns blister and weep; full-thickness burns look white, waxy, leathery or charred and may be painless because the nerve endings are destroyed — pale, painless areas are the most serious, not the least. Estimate size using the casualty's own palm with fingers as roughly one percent of their body surface. Get professional care for any full-thickness burn; anything larger than their palm; burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals or across joints; any burn circling a limb, neck or chest; electrical and chemical burns; any smoke or hot-gas inhalation (singed nostrils, sooty spit, hoarseness — the airway can swell shut hours later); and significant burns in young children or the elderly. For chemical burns, brush off dry powder first, then irrigate with copious running water for at least 20 minutes, keeping run-off away from unburned skin and your own hands. Worked example: boiling water over a wrist — straight to the sink, watch and rings off in the first minute, twenty minutes of cool running water by the clock, a blanket round her shoulders meanwhile, then loose cling film and a doctor, because the blistered patch is bigger than her palm.

sections.heading: Cleaning a wound
sections.body: Infection is the real danger once bleeding is controlled, and everything about wound care follows one principle: bacteria and dead tissue left in a wound multiply, while a clean, draining wound heals. The most effective tool is not antiseptic but water in volume. IRRIGATE: flushing dilutes bacteria and physically carries out the dirt and debris they ride on. Use the cleanest water available — sterile saline is ideal, but drinkable water, bottled or boiled-then-cooled, is a well-established substitute. Pressure matters as much as volume: poured water rinses only the surface, while a jet dislodges embedded grime, so punch a pinhole in a water bottle or bag and squeeze hard, playing the jet across the whole wound. Use litres, not splashes, and keep going until you see clean tissue and no foreign matter. Pick out remaining grit or splinters with clean tweezers (boiled or flamed, then cooled). Do not scrub deep tissue raw, and keep strong antiseptics such as undiluted iodine or hydrogen peroxide out of the open wound bed — they damage the living cells that do the healing; if used at all, use them diluted on the intact skin around the wound. If nothing sterile is available, clean water remains the priority; honey or clean sugar packed into a wound is a traditional antibacterial dressing in extremis — the concentrated sugar dehydrates bacteria — but it is a stopgap on the way to care, not a substitute for it. Cover with the cleanest dry cloth you have and change it daily, or sooner if soaked through, inspecting the wound each time. Resist taping or stitching a dirty wound tightly closed in the field: a deep puncture, an animal bite, or any wound you could not fully clean is safer left loosely covered and draining, because sealing bacteria into a warm moist pocket invites an abscess. Deep or dirty wounds also raise tetanus: if the casualty's last vaccination was years ago, they need a booster once they reach care. WATCH FOR INFECTION over the following days — trouble usually declares itself within 24-72 hours: spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, throbbing pain that worsens instead of settling, or fever. Drawing a pen line around the red margin at each dressing change makes any spread obvious. A red streak running UP the limb from the wound plus fever is a life-threatening emergency — the infection is travelling along the lymph channels toward the bloodstream — get to medical care fast. Worked example: a fall on a gravel trail leaves a deep, filthy knee laceration. Ten minutes of hard bottle-jet irrigation with two litres of drinking water, tweezers for three stubborn stones, a loose clean dressing, and a pen line around the pink margin that evening to compare against tomorrow.

sections.heading: Splinting a fracture
sections.body: A broken bone itself rarely kills, but its sharp ends can do real harm: every movement lets them saw at the muscle, vessels and nerves around them, worsening pain, bleeding and tissue damage — a broken thigh bone can spill more than a litre of blood into the leg. A splint's entire job is to stop that movement. Do not try to straighten a badly deformed limb; forcing it can tear the very structures you are trying to protect. Splint it in the position found, padding generously to fill the gaps. The mechanical rule: immobilise the joints ABOVE and BELOW the break, because bone ends cannot move if neither neighbouring joint can. A broken forearm needs the wrist and elbow fixed; a broken lower leg needs the ankle and knee. Use rigid supports — straight sticks, a trekking pole, a rolled sleeping mat, even a folded newspaper — and pad them with cloth wherever they touch skin, because bare rigid edges pressed on skin cause damage within hours. Tie the supports on either side of the break, not directly over it, using bandage, cloth strips or belts: snug enough that nothing shifts, never so tight it cuts off circulation. Then check the circulation beyond the splint immediately, and again every 15 minutes or so: the fingers or toes past it should stay WARM and PINK, feeling should be normal, and a pressed nail bed should flush pink again within a couple of seconds. If they turn cold, blue or numb, loosen the ties and re-tie — a splint that strangles the limb is worse than no splint. Swelling continues for hours after an injury, so ties that were fine at first can become too tight later; keep re-checking. For an arm, add a sling to carry the weight and then bind the slung arm gently to the chest so it cannot swing. Splint before moving the person if at all possible — moving someone with an unsplinted fracture converts a simple break into a mangled one. An open fracture — bone through the skin, or a wound over the break — gets a clean dressing over the wound first; control bleeding with pressure around, never on, protruding bone, and never push anything back in. Worked example: a hiker snaps her forearm in a fall. You leave the arm bent as she guards it, lay a padded stick along each side from palm to elbow, tie above and below the painful point, sling the arm with a folded shirt, bind the sling to her body, and press a fingernail — pink return within a second. Fifteen minutes into the walk out you check again, find her fingers cooling and dusky, and loosen the lower tie a turn until colour returns.

sections.heading: Sprains — RICE
sections.body: A sprain is an overstretched or partly torn ligament — one of the fibrous straps holding a joint together — and the pain, ballooning swelling and bruising come from bleeding and inflammatory fluid leaking into the tissues around it. For a twisted ankle, knee or wrist with no obvious fracture, RICE aims to limit that leak in the first 24-48 hours, because a joint that swells less recovers function sooner. REST: stop using the joint now — hobbling on a fresh sprain tears more fibres and restarts the bleeding. Rest is relative, though: after the first day or two, gentle pain-free movement speeds recovery by keeping the joint mobile and the muscles working, so rest means protect, not immobilise for a week. ICE: cold narrows the local blood vessels, slowing the leak and dulling pain. Apply ice, a cold pack or a bag of frozen vegetables for 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off, repeating while awake through the first 24-48 hours. Never ice bare skin — wrap the pack in cloth — and never fall asleep on one; both cause cold injury. COMPRESS: wrap the joint with an elastic bandage, starting below the injury and working up toward the heart, each turn overlapping half the previous one. It should feel firmly supportive; if the toes or fingers beyond it go numb, tingle, throb or turn dusky, it is too tight — unwrap and redo it looser. Loosen or remove it at night. ELEVATE: prop the limb above heart level whenever sitting or lying — ankle on stacked cushions, wrist on a folded coat across the chest — so gravity drains fluid away instead of letting it pool. Equally important is what NOT to do in the first couple of days, remembered as HARM: no Heat (hot baths or heat packs widen vessels and worsen swelling), no Alcohol (the same effect, plus masked pain and poor judgement), no Running or forcing the joint, and no vigorous Massage of the fresh injury. Judging severity: a mild sprain hurts but bears weight and settles over days; a severe one may have come with a popping sensation, swells at once, and will not take weight at all. If the person cannot bear weight for even four steps, if pressing on the bone itself is markedly tender (the ankle knobs or midfoot, rather than the soft tissue between), if the joint looks grossly deformed, or if anything beyond it is numb, treat it as a possible fracture: splint it as one and get it examined, since an X-ray is the only sure way to tell, and fractures strapped up as sprains heal badly. Worked example: an ankle rolled stepping off a kerb — no bone tenderness, weight-bearing with a limp — gets RICE at home, a wrap and elevation through the evening, gentle ankle circles from day two, and is near normal in a fortnight.

guides.title: Health & Hygiene
guides.summary: Staying clean, healthy and rested in the field.

sections.heading: Hands & waste
sections.body:
Almost every disabling field illness that comes from the environment travels the same route: a pathogen shed in stool reaches a hand, the hand reaches the mouth or the food, and you swallow it. Hands are the vector, which is why they are the single highest-yield thing you can clean. Soap does not need to kill anything to work; it is a surfactant, meaning its molecules surround the oils and grime that microbes cling to and lift them off the skin so running water can carry them away. That is why the mechanical scrub matters more than the soap itself. Work up friction on all surfaces for at least 20 seconds — palms, backs of hands, between the fingers, the thumbs, and especially under and around the fingernails, where debris and organisms lodge and survive casual rinsing. Keep nails trimmed short for exactly that reason. Rinse under poured or running water rather than a still bowl everyone dips into, then dry your hands, because wet hands both pick up and pass on far more bacteria than dry ones — a clean cloth or air-drying finishes the job the scrub started.

When no soap is available, do not skip the wash — vigorous rubbing under water alone removes a large fraction of surface organisms, and a pinch of wood ash or clean sand adds abrasion that helps. Reserve alcohol-based sanitizer for when water is truly gone, remembering it fails on visibly dirty hands because organic matter shields the germs from the alcohol. Fix the two moments that break the chain: after relieving yourself, and before touching any food or water.

Waste disposal is the other half of the same problem. Dig a cat-hole at least 60 m (200 ft) — roughly 70 adult paces — from any water source, camp, and trail, siting it downhill so runoff cannot carry contamination back toward water you drink. That 60 m buffer is not arbitrary — it gives soil the distance it needs to filter and let resilient pathogens like Giardia and Cryptosporidium die off before they can reach a stream or spring. Make the hole 15-20 cm (6-8 in) deep, into the dark, biologically active topsoil where microbes break waste down fastest, but above the water table. Cover and disguise it fully when done; a buried cat-hole keeps flies off the waste, and flies that walk on feces and then land on food are a documented transmission path in camps. For a group staying put, dig a single sited latrine downwind and well away from the kitchen, and put a hand-wash station right beside it so the wash actually happens at the moment it counts.

sections.heading: Feet
sections.body:
Your feet carry the entire expedition, and the two injuries that most often end a journey — trench foot and blisters — are both driven by the same enemy: persistent moisture. Skin that stays wet for hours macerates, turning pale, soft, and wrinkled; a macerated barrier tears under a fraction of the friction that intact skin shrugs off, and the warm damp space between the toes is exactly what the fungus behind athlete's foot (tinea pedis) needs to take hold. So the governing rule is simple and relentless: keep feet clean and, above all, dry, and air them at every rest stop for ten to fifteen minutes, elevated if you can to drain swelling.

Trench foot, or non-freezing cold injury, comes from prolonged exposure to cold and wet above freezing — often below about 15C (59F) for many hours, not from ice. The chronic dampness and cold clamp down the small blood vessels, starving the tissue of oxygen and injuring nerve and soft tissue; the foot goes numb and pale, then turns red, swollen, and painful as it rewarms. Treat it by getting the foot warm, dry, and elevated; rewarm gently and do not rub it or apply direct high heat, which damages the fragile tissue. Prevention beats treatment overwhelmingly: change into dry socks daily — and mid-day if they soak through — rotating at least two pairs so one always dries against your body or in the sun while the other is worn.

Blisters begin as a hot spot: a patch of skin that feels warm, tender, or red because repeated shear is separating the epidermal layers before fluid has yet filled the gap. That warning is your window. Stop the moment you feel it and cover the spot with tape, moleskin, or a slick blister patch to take the friction off the skin — acting at the hot-spot stage prevents almost every blister, whereas an already-formed blister is a raw wound waiting to be infected. Trim toenails straight across to avoid ingrown edges, and a dusting of foot powder or plain cornstarch cuts moisture and friction. As a worked example: on a multi-day wet hike, a walker who swaps to a dry pair at lunch, airs the wet pair on their pack in the sun, and tapes the first hot spot arrives with sound feet, while the one who marches through wet socks is limping on blisters and early trench foot by day three.

sections.heading: Small problems, big risks
sections.body:
In ordinary life a minor cut, a chafed heel, or a sore in the mouth is an annoyance you forget about. In the field the same trivial problems are how people become genuinely, sometimes dangerously, ill — because the body's defenses are stretched thin by fatigue, cold, and under-eating, and the environment is full of bacteria looking for a way in. Intact skin is a barrier; the instant it breaks, organisms like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus can colonize the wound and spread into the tissue. Clean every small cut, scrape, or popped blister promptly by irrigating it with clean or disinfected water (a firm stream lifts debris and bacteria out), then cover it to keep dirt off, and re-clean it daily. Watch for the signs that a local infection is becoming a systemic threat: redness that spreads outward, increasing warmth, swelling, pus, and — the urgent one — a red streak running up the limb from the wound (lymphangitis) or a fever. Red streaking or fever means the infection is moving through the body and needs real medical care; the field cannot cure sepsis.

A concrete example: a blister on a sweaty foot pops, goes uncovered inside a damp sock, and within two days the surrounding skin is hot, red, and tender — a cellulitis that could have been prevented by a strip of tape and a clean rinse. The same logic applies to a neglected toothache, which can swell the face and become an emergency, so do not ignore mouth pain; keep the teeth clean even with a frayed twig.

Two smaller hazards deserve naming because they surprise people. Cracked, chapped skin on lips, fingertips, and knuckles is a broken barrier just like a cut — fissures let infection in — so protect them with balm or grease and keep them from drying out. And your eyes take real damage from ultraviolet light: hours of sun on snow, water, sand, or at altitude can burn the cornea, producing photokeratitis (snow blindness) — gritty, intensely painful, light-sensitive eyes that typically appear 6 to 12 hours after exposure and are temporarily disabling. Prevent it with sunglasses, or improvise slit goggles from a strip of bark, cardboard, or cloth with a narrow horizontal cut, and rest the eyes in darkness if it strikes. None of these problems is impressive on its own; each is worth a minute of attention because the field magnifies small things.

sections.heading: Rest
sections.body:
Rest is not a luxury you earn after the work is done — it is the survival skill that determines whether you make the work harder. Sleep loss degrades exactly the faculties survival depends on: attention, reaction time, and judgment. The effect is measurable and steep. Well-documented laboratory work has shown that being awake for roughly 17 to 19 hours impairs performance comparably to a blood-alcohol concentration around 0.05%, and staying awake about 24 hours reaches the neighborhood of 0.10% — legally drunk in most places. You do not feel this happening; the hallmark of sleep deprivation is that it quietly steals your ability to notice you are impaired, so you keep making confident decisions that are quietly wrong. That is how a navigation error, a bad river-crossing call, or a careless step becomes the event that turns a hard day into a disaster.

Sleep is also physical repair. Deprivation suppresses the immune system, slows wound healing, and impairs the body's ability to regulate its own temperature — a serious compounding problem in cold. The good news is that recovery is front-loaded: the first four to five hours of sleep capture most of the deep, slow-wave sleep that does the heaviest restorative work, and even a short nap of 20 to 30 minutes restores a large slice of alertness. Keep naps under about 30 minutes, though, or you wake groggy from sleep inertia.

To actually sleep well in the field, insulate yourself from the ground first: the earth pulls heat out of you by direct conduction far faster than cold air does, so a sleeping pad's insulation often matters more for warmth than the bag's rating. Shelter from wind, stay dry, and eat before sleeping — your body burns fuel to stay warm overnight, and going to bed fed and warm is what lets you sleep through rather than shiver awake. Treat morale the same way you treat water and food: it is a finite resource to be managed. When a problem feels overwhelming, apply the old field discipline of STOP — Stop, Think, Observe, Plan — and, wherever safety allows, eat, warm up, and sleep before you tackle the hardest decision. Caffeine can mask fatigue for an hour but it does not repay sleep debt; the debt keeps accruing until you pay it with actual sleep. As a rule of thumb, if a task is not urgent and the light is bad, the strong move is almost always to rest and do it at first light with a clear head.

sections.heading: Oral care with limited supplies
sections.body:
Plaque is a living biofilm — a few hundred bacterial species glued to the tooth surface in a self-secreted polysaccharide matrix — that begins reforming within minutes of a clean brushing. Left undisturbed 24-48 hours it mineralizes into calculus (tartar), which no toothbrush can remove; left undisturbed for weeks, bacterial acid byproducts (mainly lactic acid from Streptococcus mutans fermenting sugars) demineralize enamel below pH 5.5, starting a cavity, while a different bacterial mix along the gumline triggers gingivitis — inflammation that, untreated for years, can progress to periodontitis and real bone loss around the tooth roots. Mechanical disruption of that biofilm, not toothpaste flavor or foam, is what matters: a brush working at a 45-degree angle to the gumline in short vibrating strokes for two minutes covers the flat tooth surfaces, while floss or an interdental brush covers the tight contact points between teeth, where a disproportionate share of cavities start.

Timing and diet matter as much as technique. Every time you eat fermentable carbohydrate, mouth bacteria produce acid that drops the pH into the demineralizing range for roughly 20 to 30 minutes before saliva buffers it back — the Stephan curve. This means frequency, not total quantity, is the enemy: constant grazing or sipping sugary drinks keeps the enamel under near-continuous acid attack, whereas the same sugar eaten at one sitting gives the mouth long recovery windows. When you cannot brush after eating, simply swishing plain water helps clear food and dilute acid. One counterintuitive caution: do not brush in the half hour right after acidic food, drink, or vomiting, because the enamel is temporarily softened and brushing abrades it — rinse with water first and wait about 30 minutes.

Without a purpose-built brush, a frayed-end twig (the 'chew stick' used across cultures for millennia, classically from an antimicrobial wood like neem or walnut) or a clean cloth wrapped over a finger and rubbed firmly against each tooth surface does real, measurable plaque removal — not as good as bristles reaching interproximally, but far better than nothing. A pinch of salt dissolved in water makes a serviceable antiseptic rinse that raises local pH and discourages acid-producing bacteria; baking soda brushed on damp is a mild abrasive that also buffers acid. What has no good substitute is fluoride — it substitutes into the enamel crystal lattice as fluorapatite, which resists acid dissolution far better than the original hydroxyapatite — so when a real fluoride toothpaste is available, even a smear used with an improvised brush outperforms full technique without it.

Take a neglected mouth seriously, because a dental problem in the field can become a medical emergency. A deep cavity that reaches the pulp can abscess, swelling the face and, in the worst case, spreading infection into the tissues of the neck and floor of the mouth (Ludwig's angina) where it can threaten the airway — a genuine reason to seek care. For pain relief while you get help, warm salt-water rinses ease gum infection, and a drop of clove oil (its active compound, eugenol, is a traditional topical anesthetic) dabbed on an aching tooth gives temporary relief. These buy time; they do not cure the underlying infection.

sections.heading: Skin, bathing, and washing when water is scarce
sections.body:
Skin hosts its own microbiome, and healthy skin depends on an intact acid mantle (surface pH around 4.5-5.5, maintained by sebum and sweat) that suppresses pathogenic bacteria and fungi. Both directions of imbalance cause real problems: over-washing with harsh soap and hot water strips sebum, raises skin pH, and paradoxically increases infection risk and cracking, while under-washing lets sweat, dead skin, and oils accumulate in body folds, feeding the yeast Malassezia and bacteria that cause intertrigo (a raw, often foul-smelling rash in skin-on-skin folds — groin, underarms, under overlapping abdominal folds) and folliculitis (infected hair follicles, seen as small red or pus-filled bumps, often from friction combined with sweat).

When water for a full bath isn't available, a focused sponge bath targeting the axillae, groin, and any skin folds captures most of the hygienic benefit for a fraction of the water: apocrine sweat glands (which produce the compounds bacteria break down into body odor) concentrate almost entirely in the armpits and groin, so cleaning those two areas thoroughly does more than a lukewarm rinse of everywhere else. A liter of water, a cloth, and a small amount of soap (or none — mechanical friction alone removes a large fraction of surface bacteria) covers a serviceable daily wipe-down; alcohol-based hand sanitizer or unscented wipes are a reasonable stopgap for the same target areas, though they don't replace it for more than a few days before folliculitis and odor build up. Remember that sanitizer and wipes fail on visibly soiled skin, because dirt and organic matter inactivate the alcohol — when you are actually grimy, soap and water win.

The other everyday skin failures in the field are chafing and heat rash, and both are preventable. Chafing is friction damage where skin rubs skin or wet fabric — inner thighs, under a pack strap, along a waistband — and once the barrier is raw it burns and can get infected; head it off by keeping those areas dry, reducing friction with a thin film of petroleum jelly or an anti-chafe balm, and choosing non-cotton next-to-skin layers. Heat rash (miliaria) is different: in hot, humid conditions the sweat ducts block and inflame, producing a prickly field of tiny bumps; the cure is to get cool and dry and wear loose clothing so sweat can evaporate. Whatever you wash with, keep it personal — never share a towel, since ringworm (another tinea fungus) and Staph pass readily on damp shared cloth. As a practical picture: in a hot camp with two liters to spare for washing, spend it on a thorough armpit-groin-feet wipe and then dry those areas completely, rather than a token splash over your whole body that leaves the high-risk folds warm and damp.

sections.heading: Menstrual hygiene in the field
sections.body:
Menstrual blood is not more infectious to handle than other blood, but managing a period with reduced supplies raises two real risks: skin breakdown from a product left in place too long, and, for tampon users, toxic shock syndrome (TSS) — a rare but life-threatening illness from a toxin (TSST-1) produced by Staphylococcus aureus that can colonize a tampon left in too long, especially a high-absorbency one. The rule that matters is time-based, not blood-volume-based: change a tampon at least every 4-8 hours regardless of how full it looks, never past 8 hours including overnight. Sudden high fever, a sunburn-like rash, vomiting, or dizziness during tampon use is a genuine emergency: remove it immediately and seek care, since untreated TSS can progress to organ failure within a day.

When commercial products run out, a clean folded cotton cloth held by underwear or a wrap, changed as often as practical and rinsed in cold water (hot water sets blood protein and worsens staining) and sun-dried when possible, reduces harm meaningfully compared to nothing. The sun-drying is not just for staining — full ultraviolet exposure helps disinfect the cloth — and the cloth must be completely dry before it is worn again, because damp fabric against the vulva breeds odor, fungal growth, and skin breakdown. A menstrual cup, if available, holds up to 30mL versus roughly 5mL for a regular tampon and can be safely worn up to 12 hours, making it the most supply-efficient option for extended field conditions. It also generates almost no waste and can be reused for years, but it demands clean hands and clean water to empty and rinse during use, and it should be boiled in water for a few minutes between cycles to sterilize it — so it is most useful where you have at least some reliably clean water. Whatever the method, hand-washing before and after changing is the single highest-yield habit.

Two practical points close the loop. Dispose of used disposable products by packing them out or burning them and deep-burying the remains — do not leave them where animals will dig them up. And do not be alarmed if your cycle becomes irregular or stops during hard field conditions: the physical stress, weight loss, and calorie deficit of an expedition commonly suppress the hormonal signals from the hypothalamus that drive menstruation, and this is a normal, reversible response rather than a sign of illness. Plan supply around your own typical cycle length plus a margin, carry one reusable backup (a cup or cloth) against the day disposables run out, and keep a dark-colored cloth for discreet drying.

sections.heading: Clothing, bedding, and fabric hygiene
sections.body:
Damp fabric against skin dramatically increases the mechanical friction that breaks down the skin's protective barrier, opening the door to fungal infection (tinea, the family that includes athlete's foot and jock itch, which specifically thrives in warm, moist, occluded skin) and bacterial folliculitis. It's also a thermal problem — wet clothing conducts heat away roughly 25 times faster than dry air at the same temperature, which is why 'cotton kills' is real field wisdom: cotton absorbs many times its weight in water and holds it against skin, while wool and most synthetics wick moisture away and retain some insulating value even damp.

This is the logic behind the layering system: a thin base layer of wool or synthetic worn against the skin to move sweat away, a middle layer that traps still air for insulation, and an outer shell to block wind and rain. Keeping the skin-contact base layer dry is what keeps the whole system working, so those are the garments to prioritize for washing and drying. Your bedding follows the same rule: a sleeping bag quietly absorbs the moisture your body gives off all night, and a damp bag loses loft and warmth, so air it and, whenever the sun is out, drape it to dry each day.

Laundering without a machine still accomplishes most of what matters: agitation in even cold water physically dislodges most surface bacteria and loose soil, and a few drops of any soap lift oils that water alone leaves behind; full sun-drying afterward adds real disinfection, since UV-B radiation damages microbial DNA — the same mechanism the WHO-endorsed SODIS method uses for drinking water. Rotating at least two sets of socks and underwear, fully drying each between wears, breaks the persistent-dampness cycle even without a proper wash. Lice and scabies mites, the other major fabric-borne risk in prolonged close-quarters wear, are both killed by heat above roughly 50C/122F — cold-water washing alone won't eliminate an active infestation. Body lice live and lay their eggs in clothing seams rather than on the body, so the practical treatments are heat (a hot wash, high-heat drying, or leaving garments in a sealed black bag in full sun until they cook) or, failing heat, sealing infested items away for about two weeks so the lice and any hatching eggs starve. As a worked example, a traveler in a wet climate who cannot truly dry anything should still prioritize the two things that prevent injury: keep a dedicated dry pair of socks and a dry base layer sealed for sleep, and accept that outer layers will stay damp — the goal is protecting the skin-contact fabric, not achieving clean laundry.

sections.heading: Group hygiene and disease prevention
sections.body:
Most serious illness that spreads in shared living conditions travels the fecal-oral route: a pathogen shed in one person's stool ends up, via unwashed hands, on a shared surface, food, or water source, and is ingested by someone else. This is the mechanism behind norovirus (needing as few as 10-100 viral particles to infect, making it extraordinarily contagious in group settings), most bacterial dysentery, and hepatitis A. The single highest-yield intervention is hand hygiene at defined trigger points — after using the latrine, before handling any food or water — not vague 'wash often' advice but specifically bracketing those two moments, since that's where the transmission chain actually breaks.

Design the camp so those habits are easy. Site the group latrine downhill and downwind, well away from both water sources and the kitchen, and put a hand-wash station right next to it — even a 'tippy tap,' a hanging jug tipped by a foot cord so no one touches a shared tap with dirty hands. Keep a mental map of clean and dirty zones: the water-collection point and food-prep area are clean and never handled after the latrine without washing first. Flies are a bridge between the two, walking from exposed waste to exposed food, so cover both — food kept lidded, waste buried — cuts a real transmission path.

Shared water sources deserve special discipline: never dip hands, used cups, or contaminated ladles directly into a communal container (use a designated clean scoop, or pour) — one contaminated hand can seed an entire group's supply. Communal food should be served rather than passed hand-to-hand from a shared container, cooked thoroughly, and not left sitting warm, since the 5-60C range is where food-poisoning bacteria multiply fastest. A person with vomiting or diarrhea should be rotated off food-prep and water-collection duty for the duration of symptoms and 24-48 hours afterward, since viral shedding continues after symptoms resolve — this single step, more than any disinfectant, is what contains an outbreak in a small group before it spreads to everyone. Do not neglect the respiratory route in a crowded shelter, either: colds, influenza, and worse spread in close, poorly ventilated quarters, so keep some airflow and cover coughs. The honest limit is that once an outbreak takes hold in a group there is no field cure — your tools are isolating the sick from communal food and water, aggressive hand hygiene, and keeping everyone hydrated while it runs its course, which is exactly why prevention earns so much effort.

sections.heading: Building a Field Hygiene Kit
sections.body:
A small, deliberately chosen kit covers the highest-yield hygiene needs in far less space and weight than a full toiletry bag. The organizing principle is to spend weight only where it buys real protection: the items that prevent the specific failures this guide keeps returning to — fecal-oral illness, foot injury, skin infection in the folds, dental decay, and menstrual complications. Everything below earns its place against one of those, and anything that does not is cosmetic and stays home. Pack the whole kit inside a waterproof zip bag, because in the field the difference between working and useless soap, tape, or toothpaste is usually whether it stayed dry.

Scale the kit to the trip. For a weekend you need little more than soap, a toothbrush and fluoride paste, a small sanitizer, some tape, and a few wipes; for a multi-week journey add the laundry soap, a faster-drying towel, spare socks in the rotation, and enough menstrual supply plus one reusable backup to outlast the disposables. Maintain the kit as you go: refill the sanitizer, and replace a toothbrush once its bristles splay (roughly every three months, or immediately if it is dropped somewhere filthy or used during an illness), since a frayed or contaminated brush does less and can reintroduce germs. Keep a little redundancy in the truly critical items — a second way to clean hands, a spare for foot care — because those are the ones whose loss actually stops a journey. Finally, know the improvisations for every line, so a lost item is an inconvenience rather than a crisis: a frayed twig or a finger-wrapped cloth for the brush, wood ash or sand for scouring soap, a bandana for the towel, and any clean folded cotton for a menstrual pad.
ingredients: A travel-size bar of soap or a small bottle of biodegradable liquid soap (biodegradable matters if you'll wash near a natural water source)
A soft-bristle travel toothbrush and a small tube of fluoride toothpaste (or fluoride tablets/drops as an ultralight substitute)
20–30 feet of unwaxed dental floss (doubles as sewing thread and light cordage)
A microfiber camp towel from any outdoor or hardware store — dries far faster than cotton and packs small
A bottle of alcohol-based hand sanitizer (60%+ alcohol) for moments water isn't available
A small pack of unscented baby wipes or individually wrapped antiseptic wipes, from any pharmacy or general store
A few feet of moleskin or blister tape and a small nail clipper, for foot and nail care
A menstrual cup or a resealable bag of pads/tampons sized to trip length, plus a spare cloth for backup, if applicable
A zip-top bag of powdered laundry detergent or a small bar of laundry soap, from any grocery or general store
A wide-mouth water bottle or collapsible basin usable as a wash basin
A distinct color of tape or a marked bandana to label personal items so shared-space gear isn't mixed up between people

sections.heading: Step-by-step: a daily austere-hygiene routine
sections.body: The routine below covers the highest-risk areas first when time or water is limited, so a rushed day still gets the protection that matters most. The order is deliberate triage: it front-loads the actions whose neglect does the most damage — clean hands that break the fecal-oral chain, teeth that a day of acid attack will not wait on, and the warm damp zones (feet, groin, skin folds) where field infections actually start — before spending any remaining water and time on lower-consequence washing. Think of it as roughly ten to fifteen minutes, bracketed morning and night, that you protect the way you protect a meal. When water is desperately short, do not abandon the routine; compress it, keeping the hand-washing and the targeted fold-and-feet wipe and letting the general body rinse be the thing that waits. Consistency beats perfection here: a modest wipe-down done every day prevents far more illness than an occasional thorough scrub separated by days of neglect, because the failures this routine heads off — maceration, folliculitis, the first hot spot, plaque acid — all build up over exactly those neglected days. Adapt the emphasis to conditions, spending more of your effort drying skin in the wet and more on sun-exposure and eyes in bright, open terrain, but keep the sequence intact.
steps: On waking, before touching food or water: wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, or use hand sanitizer if water is unavailable.
Brush teeth for a full two minutes using a fluoride toothpaste (or a smear if supply is limited), angling the bristles 45 degrees into the gumline; floss once daily, ideally at night.
Using a liter or less of water and a cloth, wipe down the axillae, groin, and any skin folds first, then the feet, then the rest of the body as water allows.
Dry all washed skin fully, especially between the toes and in skin folds, before dressing; damp skin under clothing is the single biggest driver of field skin infections.
Inspect feet for hot spots, blisters, or maceration, and inspect skin folds and the groin for early redness or rash while you're already there.
Rotate to a dry pair of socks and underwear if the previous pair is even slightly damp; hang the worn pair in direct sun to air out and partially disinfect.
If menstruating, change your product on schedule (every 4–8 hours for tampons, never past 8 hours) regardless of how full it appears, and wash hands before and after.
Before sleeping, wash hands again and brush teeth; treat post-latrine hand-washing as non-negotiable, even if it uses your last bit of sanitizer.

Once every few days, or when fully dry conditions allow, launder one set of clothing in soap and water and lay it in direct sunlight to dry, rotating through your kit so nothing stays worn-and-unwashed for more than about three days.

guides.title: Human Anatomy by System
guides.summary: A systems-level tour of the human body — skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, digestive, urinary, endocrine, lymphatic/immune, integumentary and reproductive — with exact structures, functions, key numbers and the anatomical terminology used to describe them.

sections.heading: First principles: levels of organization
sections.body:
Anatomy is the study of the body's structures; physiology is the study of what those structures do. The two are inseparable, because structure predicts function at every scale — a tube is shaped for flow, a sheet for covering, a fiber for pulling. The whole subject is conventionally organized as a ladder of six levels, each assembled from the one below it, and understanding that ladder is what makes the rest of anatomy learnable rather than a list to memorize.

At the chemical level, about 99 percent of body mass is only four elements — oxygen (~65 percent by mass), carbon (~18 percent), hydrogen (~10 percent) and nitrogen (~3 percent) — with calcium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, chlorine, magnesium and sulfur making up nearly all the rest. These combine into four families of biological molecules: water, which is roughly 60 percent of adult body weight and the solvent every reaction runs in; proteins, which serve as enzymes, contractile filaments and structural collagen; lipids, which build membranes, insulate, and store fuel at about 9 kilocalories per gram; carbohydrates, the fast fuel at about 4 kilocalories per gram; and nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, which hold and transmit the instructions.

The cellular level is the smallest genuinely living unit. Current estimates put an adult at roughly 30 to 37 trillion cells of about 200 specialized types, spanning a size range that is easy to underestimate: a red blood cell is about 7 micrometers across, while a single motor neuron's axon can run more than a meter from the lower spinal cord to a muscle in the foot.

A tissue is a population of similar cells doing a shared job, and there are exactly four primary types. Epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces — the outer skin layer, the gut lining, the inside of every blood vessel — and is always anchored to a basement membrane with a free surface facing a space. Connective tissue supports and binds, and is defined by cells scattered in a nonliving matrix they secrete; that single definition covers bone, cartilage, tendon, fat and even blood. Muscle tissue shortens to produce force. Nervous tissue conducts electrical signals.

An organ is two or more tissues working as a functional unit; the heart, for instance, contains all four types at once. An organ system is a set of organs cooperating toward a broad purpose, and the human body is conventionally divided into eleven. The organism is all of them integrated.

Holding the whole arrangement together is homeostasis: the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external change. Core temperature is held near 37 degrees Celsius, arterial blood pH within 7.35 to 7.45, and fasting blood glucose near 70 to 110 milligrams per deciliter. The mechanism is almost always negative feedback — a sensor detects a deviation, an integrating center compares it against a set point, and an effector produces a response that pushes the variable back. Positive feedback, which amplifies rather than corrects, is rare and reserved for events meant to run to completion, such as blood clotting and labor contractions.

sections.heading: Skeletal and muscular systems (support and movement)
sections.body:
The adult skeleton is 206 bones. A newborn has closer to 270; the count falls with growth because separate ossification centers fuse, most obviously in the skull, the sacrum and the coccyx. The skeleton does five distinct jobs at once. It supports the body's weight, protects soft organs (the skull encases the brain, the rib cage shields heart and lungs, the vertebral column sheathes the spinal cord), provides rigid levers that muscles pull on, stores minerals — about 99 percent of body calcium plus most of its phosphorus, buffered in and out of blood on demand — and manufactures blood cells, since red marrow produces on the order of two million red blood cells every second.

Anatomically the skeleton splits in two. The axial skeleton is 80 bones along the midline: the skull, the vertebral column of 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused coccygeal), and the thoracic cage of 12 rib pairs plus the sternum. The appendicular skeleton is 126 bones: the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles that hang them off the axis. Bone itself is living connective tissue, roughly one-third collagen for tensile toughness and two-thirds mineral (hydroxyapatite) for compressive stiffness, and it is continuously remodeled by osteoblasts that lay bone down and osteoclasts that resorb it — which is why bone thickens along habitual lines of loading and thins when loading stops.

Joints, or articulations, are classified by how much movement they permit. Fibrous joints are essentially immovable, such as the sutures between skull plates. Cartilaginous joints allow slight movement, such as the intervertebral discs, whose gel-like nucleus pulposus lets adjacent vertebrae rock a few degrees each while summing to substantial spinal motion. Synovial joints move freely: two cartilage-capped bone ends sit inside a fluid-filled capsule, the synovial fluid lubricating contact to a coefficient of friction lower than ice on ice.

The muscular system comprises roughly 600 skeletal muscles and accounts for about 40 percent of body weight in an average adult. There are three tissue types. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, attached to bone by tendons — dense, nearly inelastic collagen cords that transmit force efficiently. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, found only in the heart, and its cells are electrically coupled so the whole chamber contracts as one. Smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary, forming the walls of vessels, gut, airways and bladder.

Force is produced by the sliding-filament mechanism: thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments interdigitate, and myosin heads repeatedly bind actin, swivel, release and re-cock, ratcheting the filaments past one another. Each cycle costs one molecule of ATP, and the whole process is switched on by calcium released from internal stores when the muscle fiber is electrically excited. A crucial consequence of this arrangement is that muscles can only pull, never push, so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs — the biceps flexes the elbow, the triceps extends it — and any joint that moves in two directions needs at least two opposing muscle groups.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular system (transport)
sections.body:
The cardiovascular system is a closed loop that delivers oxygen and nutrients to every cell and carries away carbon dioxide and waste. Its pump is the heart: a four-chambered muscular organ roughly the size of the owner's clenched fist, about 250 to 350 grams, sitting mid-chest with two-thirds of its mass left of the midline.

Blood traces a fixed circuit. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae into the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, is pushed through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries — the only arteries in the body carrying deoxygenated blood — and reaches the lungs, where it takes on oxygen and unloads carbon dioxide. It returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle, and is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body. The right side therefore drives the short, low-pressure pulmonary circuit and the left side the far longer, high-resistance systemic circuit, which is exactly why the left ventricular wall is roughly three times thicker than the right. The four valves are passive flaps opened and closed by pressure differences alone; their snapping shut produces the two heart sounds, the first as the tricuspid and mitral valves close at the start of contraction and the second as the pulmonary and aortic valves close at its end.

Output is arithmetic: cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. At rest, roughly 70 beats per minute times roughly 70 milliliters per beat gives about 5 liters per minute — meaning the entire circulating blood volume passes through the heart about once every minute, and during hard exercise that figure can rise four- or fivefold. The contraction itself is triggered by the heart's own pacemaker, the sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall, which fires spontaneously and does not need a nerve signal to beat; autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down.

The vessels are specialized by pressure. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure and have thick walls with substantial elastic tissue, so they stretch during ejection and recoil between beats — the recoil is what keeps flow continuous rather than pulsatile by the time blood reaches the tissues. Capillaries are the exchange vessels, walls a single endothelial cell thick and lumens sometimes narrower than a red blood cell, forcing cells to deform single-file and maximizing contact time for diffusion. Veins return blood at low pressure with thinner, more compliant walls and, in the limbs, one-way valves; because venous pressure alone cannot lift blood from the feet to the heart, the surrounding skeletal muscles act as a pump, squeezing veins with every step so the valves ratchet blood upward. This is why standing rigidly still for long periods can cause fainting while walking does not.

Blood itself is about 5 liters in an adult, roughly 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements: erythrocytes carrying oxygen bound to hemoglobin, leukocytes performing immune defense, and platelets initiating clotting.

sections.heading: Respiratory system (gas exchange)
sections.body:
The respiratory system exists to move oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of it, and its architecture is a compromise between two demands: a surface thin and vast enough for gases to cross by simple diffusion, and a barrier robust enough to keep the outside world out.

Air enters through the nose or mouth, where it is warmed, humidified, and filtered by hairs and mucus. It passes the pharynx, then the larynx, whose vocal folds produce speech and whose epiglottis folds down during swallowing to seal the airway. Below that is the trachea, held open by 15 to 20 C-shaped cartilage rings — open at the back so a swallowed bolus can bulge the esophagus forward. The trachea forks into two bronchi, which branch about 23 generations down through bronchioles to roughly 480 million alveoli, the sacs where exchange happens.

Each alveolus, about 200 to 300 micrometers across, is wrapped in a capillary net. The barrier between air and blood — alveolar cell, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelial cell — is only about 0.5 micrometers thick. Total alveolar surface area is roughly 70 square meters, the footprint of a singles tennis court, folded into a few liters of chest. Gases cross passively, from higher to lower partial pressure with no pumping required: oxygen at roughly 100 millimeters of mercury in alveolar air moves into venous blood at about 40, and carbon dioxide runs the other way down a much smaller but sufficient gradient because it is roughly 20 times more soluble.

Alveoli would collapse under their own surface tension were it not for surfactant, a phospholipid film from type II alveolar cells that lowers surface tension most in the smallest alveoli. Premature infants not yet producing surfactant develop infant respiratory distress syndrome for exactly this reason.

Breathing is mechanical. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle beneath the lungs, contracts and flattens while the external intercostals swing the ribs up and out. Thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure falls just below atmospheric — one or two millimeters of mercury — and air flows in. Quiet exhalation needs no muscular work at all: the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic recoil of lung tissue and chest wall pushes air back out. Forced exhalation recruits the abdominal wall and internal intercostals.

A resting adult breathes 12 to 20 times per minute, moving about 500 milliliters per breath, of which roughly 150 milliliters never reaches an alveolus because it sits in the conducting airways — the anatomical dead space. The most counterintuitive fact about respiratory control is that the drive to breathe is set mainly by carbon dioxide, not oxygen: rising carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, lowering blood and cerebrospinal fluid pH, which chemoreceptors in the medulla answer by increasing rate and depth. Low oxygen is only a weak backup stimulus, not urgent until arterial oxygen falls below about 60 millimeters of mercury. This is precisely why hyperventilating before a breath-hold dive is dangerous — it blows off carbon dioxide and removes the urge to breathe without adding meaningful oxygen, so a diver can lose consciousness underwater before ever feeling short of breath.

sections.heading: Nervous system (control and communication)
sections.body:
The nervous system is the body's fast control network. Where hormones act over minutes to hours, nerve signals act in milliseconds, and that speed difference is the whole reason both systems exist. Anatomically it divides into the central nervous system — brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system, which is everything else: the cranial and spinal nerves and their ganglia.

The signaling cell is the neuron. Dendrites collect incoming signals, the cell body integrates them, and if the summed input at the axon hillock crosses roughly negative 55 millivolts from a resting membrane potential of about negative 70 millivolts, the neuron fires an action potential — a self-propagating wave of sodium influx followed by potassium efflux that travels down the axon without losing amplitude. Conduction speed depends on axon diameter and on myelin, a fatty insulating sheath wrapped by glial cells with small gaps (nodes of Ranvier) about a millimeter apart; the impulse jumps node to node, raising speed from around 1 meter per second in unmyelinated fibers to 100 meters per second or more in the fastest myelinated ones. At the axon terminal the electrical signal becomes chemical: neurotransmitter is released across a synaptic cleft roughly 20 nanometers wide onto the next cell.

The brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms, contains on the order of 86 billion neurons, and consumes roughly 20 percent of resting oxygen and glucose while making up about 2 percent of body mass. The cerebrum handles thought, voluntary movement, sensation and language; its surface, the cortex, is folded into gyri and sulci so that roughly 2,000 square centimeters of sheet fits inside the skull. The cerebellum, tucked beneath the back of the cerebrum, holds more neurons than the rest of the brain combined and governs balance, coordination and the fine timing of movement. The brainstem runs the non-negotiable functions — breathing rhythm, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing — which is why brainstem injury is so much more immediately lethal than equivalent cortical injury.

The spinal cord relays traffic in both directions and also closes some circuits on its own. In a withdrawal reflex, a pain signal enters the cord, synapses onto a motor neuron through as little as one interneuron, and drives the hand off a hot surface before the signal has even reached conscious awareness. Reflexes are diagnostic precisely because their circuits are short and predictable, so an abnormal reflex localizes damage to a specific cord segment.

Functionally the peripheral system has two divisions. The somatic division carries conscious sensation inward and voluntary commands out to skeletal muscle. The autonomic division controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands automatically, and splits again into two branches with opposing effects: the sympathetic branch produces the fight-or-flight pattern (heart rate and force up, pupils dilated, airways widened, blood shunted from gut to skeletal muscle, glucose mobilized) while the parasympathetic branch produces rest-and-digest (heart slowed via the vagus nerve, digestive secretion and motility increased, pupils constricted). These branches are not on-off switches; both are active continuously, and moment-to-moment physiology is set by the balance between them.

sections.heading: Digestive and urinary systems (fuel and filtration)
sections.body:
The digestive system converts food into molecules small enough to cross a cell membrane. Its core is the alimentary canal, a continuous muscular tube roughly 9 meters long, assisted by accessory organs — salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas — that empty secretions into it without food passing through them.

Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing multiplies surface area and salivary amylase starts cleaving starch. The esophagus moves the bolus down not by gravity but by peristalsis, a ring of circular muscle contraction traveling ahead of the food, which is why swallowing works upside down. The stomach holds about 1 liter comfortably, secretes hydrochloric acid to a pH of roughly 1.5 to 3.5, and uses the enzyme pepsin — which only works at that acidity — to begin protein breakdown. It does not digest itself because a bicarbonate-rich mucus layer coats the lining and its epithelium is replaced every three to five days.

The small intestine, about 6 meters long and divided into duodenum, jejunum and ileum, is where roughly 90 percent of absorption occurs. Its surface is amplified about 600-fold by three nested levels of folding — circular folds in the wall, finger-like villi about a millimeter tall, and microvilli forming a brush border on each cell — bringing total absorptive area to roughly 250 square meters. Into the duodenum the pancreas delivers enzymes for all three macronutrient classes plus bicarbonate that neutralizes gastric acid so those enzymes can work, and the liver delivers bile, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, which contains no enzymes at all but emulsifies fat into droplets small enough for lipase to attack. The large intestine, about 1.5 meters, reclaims water and electrolytes and compacts residue into stool; its resident bacteria ferment indigestible fiber and synthesize vitamin K and several B vitamins.

The urinary system performs the complementary job of clearing the blood. Each kidney, about 150 grams, contains roughly one million nephrons. Blood arrives under pressure at a glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries that acts as a sieve: water and small solutes are forced out into the tubule while cells and large proteins stay behind. The filtration numbers are startling — about 180 liters of filtrate are produced per day, more than 40 times total blood plasma volume — and roughly 99 percent of it is reabsorbed as the filtrate travels the tubule, leaving about 1.5 liters of urine. Filtering everything and then selectively taking back what is worth keeping is metabolically expensive but exquisitely adjustable, because the body can regulate reabsorption of each substance independently.

The kidneys therefore do far more than make urine. They set extracellular fluid volume and hence long-term blood pressure, balance sodium, potassium, calcium and phosphate, maintain acid-base status by excreting hydrogen ions, activate vitamin D to its usable form, and secrete erythropoietin, the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells — which is why chronic kidney disease reliably produces anemia. Urine drains through the ureters, propelled by peristalsis rather than gravity, into the bladder, which holds roughly 400 to 600 milliliters and signals fullness at around 200.

sections.heading: Endocrine, lymphatic/immune, integumentary and reproductive systems
sections.body:
The endocrine system controls the body chemically. Glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream, where they reach every tissue but affect only cells carrying the matching receptor — the reason a single molecule can produce very specific effects. Compared with nerve signals, hormonal control is slow to start and slow to stop, which suits it to processes like growth, metabolism and reproduction. The pituitary, a pea-sized gland beneath the brain, is called the master gland because its output governs several others, though it takes its own orders from the hypothalamus above it. The thyroid sets basal metabolic rate through thyroxine, which requires dietary iodine; the adrenal glands sitting atop the kidneys release adrenaline for the immediate stress response and cortisol for the sustained one; and the pancreas holds islet cells secreting insulin, which drives glucose into cells and lowers blood sugar, and glucagon, which does the reverse. Failure of that last pair is diabetes.

The lymphatic system does two jobs. Mechanically, it collects the roughly 3 liters of fluid that leaks out of capillaries daily and returns it to the bloodstream through thin vessels that, having no pump, rely on muscle movement and one-way valves. Immunologically, it filters that fluid through several hundred lymph nodes packed with white cells that inspect it for pathogens — which is why nodes swell near an active infection. The spleen filters blood rather than lymph and recycles worn red cells; the thymus, largest in childhood, is where T-lymphocytes mature and learn not to attack the body's own tissue. Immunity itself comes in two layers. Innate immunity is fast and generic: intact skin and mucous membranes, stomach acid, inflammation, fever, and phagocytes that engulf anything recognized as foreign.
