Diabetes: blood glucose under 54 mg/dL, or any severe symptoms like seizure or unconsciousness, call 911; blood glucose above 250 mg/dL with vomiting, fruity breath, or confusion, go to the ER; otherwise, treat per the Rule of 15 or your action plan and contact your provider. Hypertension: 180/120 or higher WITH symptoms (chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, difficulty speaking), call 911 immediately; 180/120 or higher WITHOUT symptoms, recheck after 5 minutes and call your provider the same day if it stays elevated. Asthma: Red Zone peak flow, no improvement 15–20 minutes after using a rescue inhaler, inability to speak in full sentences, or blue-tinged lips, call 911.

The logic running through all three is the same: escalate on the combination of a bad number AND a sign that an organ is failing now, and never let rechecking substitute for calling when those signs are present. The reason the framework separates 'with symptoms' from 'without' is that the human body tolerates a startling range of pressures and glucose levels silently, so the number alone rarely decides urgency — the symptoms do, because they mark the moment tolerance has failed and tissue is being injured. A worked example for each: a glucose of 48 mg/dL in someone still awake and able to swallow is a Rule-of-15 situation, but a glucose of 48 with a seizure or someone you cannot rouse is a glucagon-and-911 situation — the number is similar, the response is not. A blood pressure of 190/122 with no symptoms is a same-day phone call, but 190/122 with slurred speech is an ambulance. A yellow-zone peak flow that climbs back to green after a rescue inhaler is a note in the log, but a red-zone reading that does not budge, or blue lips, is a 911 call regardless of the meter. These thresholds are deliberately memorable because in the moment, you won't want to be looking them up — and remember that they are general reference points; your provider may have given you personalized action-plan numbers, and when they have, those come first. Two habits make the framework work under pressure. First, write the exact cutoffs and your emergency contacts on a card taped inside a cupboard or saved on your phone's lock screen, because panic erases memory and a shaking or breathless person should not be hunting through an app. Second, when you are genuinely unsure which side of a threshold you are on — a glucose you cannot quite read, a pressure that keeps bouncing, a breathlessness you cannot rate — treat the ambiguity as a reason to escalate, not to wait; the cost of an unnecessary call is minutes and mild embarrassment, while the cost of a missed emergency is measured in organs. Erring toward the phone is the correct bias built into every threshold above, and it is the one instinct to keep even on the day you feel you are overreacting.

sections.heading: Living With It Long Term — Why These Three Travel Together
sections.body:
Diabetes, hypertension, and obesity cluster together often enough that the pattern has a name — metabolic syndrome — rooted in shared underlying insulin resistance and low-grade systemic inflammation that drives all three simultaneously. The common thread is worth understanding because it explains why they travel as a pack rather than by coincidence: excess visceral fat (the fat packed around the abdominal organs, not the soft fat under the skin) is metabolically active, releasing free fatty acids and inflammatory signals that make the body's cells less responsive to insulin. That resistance forces the pancreas to pump out more insulin, and high circulating insulin in turn nudges the kidneys to retain sodium and the arteries to stiffen — so the same root pushes glucose up and blood pressure up at once. This is why tracking one condition frequently surfaces a problem in another: rising home blood glucose readings alongside a climbing blood pressure trend is a meaningfully different — and more urgent — picture than either alone, and a single combined logbook makes that connection visible in a way that separate scraps of paper don't.

The encouraging flip side of the shared mechanism is that the same lifestyle levers move all three together: losing even a modest amount of visceral fat, moving regularly, cutting excess sodium and refined carbohydrate, and sleeping enough improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and glucose control at the same time, which is why these measures are prescribed across all three conditions. On adherence: the habits that actually stick are the ones anchored to something you already do every day — taking a pill next to your toothbrush, checking blood pressure while the coffee brews — a technique of attaching a new behavior to an established cue, which is far more reliable than willpower or memory. And remember that silent control is still working control; the absence of a dramatic symptom on a well-managed day is the system doing exactly what it's supposed to do, not a sign the medication isn't needed. The long game here is measured in decades of protected kidneys, arteries, and eyes, none of which announce their gratitude day to day — the logbook and the routine are how you make an invisible benefit real enough to keep doing. It helps to reframe the daily readings not as a test you can pass or fail but as feedback in a system you are steering: a green week is confirmation to keep the course, a slowly drifting number is an early nudge to talk to your provider before anything becomes urgent, and a single outlier is usually just noise to be logged and watched. Because the three conditions share machinery, a small win in one often shows up in the others within weeks — a month of daily walks can lower a fasting glucose, shave points off a morning pressure, and ease exertional breathlessness at the same time, which is the most motivating thing a combined logbook can reveal. That linkage, visible only when the numbers sit side by side, is the practical payoff of understanding why these three travel together.

guides.safetyNote: Home monitoring supports but never replaces your physician's management plan. The numeric thresholds in this guide are general reference ranges, not a personalized target — your own target ranges may be adjusted by your doctor based on your health history. Any reading in the emergency ranges described here warrants an immediate call to emergency services, not a wait-and-see approach.

guides.title: Poisoning and Overdose: Recognition, Response, and When to Call Whom
guides.summary: How to recognize what kind of poisoning you're dealing with from its signs alone, what to actually do in the first minutes, and the difference between calling poison control and calling emergency services.

sections.heading: What Poisoning Actually Is
sections.body: A poison is any substance that injures the body through chemical action, and the sixteenth-century physician Paracelsus supplied the sentence that still governs the whole subject: the dose makes the poison. Nothing is intrinsically safe and nothing is intrinsically toxic — water drunk fast enough to dilute blood sodium has killed people, and botulinum toxin, the most acutely lethal substance known by weight, is injected into faces by the thousands of doses weekly. What matters is how much of a substance reaches the tissue that can be damaged, how quickly it gets there, and how big the person is. Toxicologists therefore quote doses per kilogram of body mass, and that single unit explains most childhood poisoning: a 12 kg toddler who swallows two adult iron tablets or a single strong opioid pill has taken a dose per kilogram five to seven times what the same pills deliver to an 80 kg adult. Three words are often used loosely and are worth separating. A toxin is a poison made by a living organism, such as the amatoxin in a death cap mushroom. A venom is a toxin an animal actively injects. An overdose is simply too much of a substance that is beneficial or tolerable at a lower dose — the drug is not different, only the quantity. Poison enters by five routes, and the route changes both speed and treatment. Ingestion is the most common and usually the slowest, because absorption from the gut takes 30 minutes to several hours. Inhalation is the fastest, since the lungs present roughly 70 square metres of membrane directly onto blood; carbon monoxide can render someone unconscious in a closed garage in minutes. Skin absorption is slow for most household products but rapid for organophosphate pesticides and certain solvents. Eye exposure damages locally and immediately. Injection bypasses every barrier the body has. Damage is then either local — the chemical burns what it touches, as drain cleaner burns the mouth and oesophagus — or systemic, where the substance is absorbed and injures organs far from the point of entry. The most dangerous property of poisoning, and the one that catches families out, is latency. A person can look, speak and behave entirely normally while a fatal process is already under way, because the damage is being done by a metabolite the liver has not yet finished producing. That gap between exposure and appearance of illness can be many hours, which is why the decision to seek advice is made on what was taken and how much, never on how well the person currently seems. It also helps to distinguish exposure from poisoning. An exposure is simply contact — a child who licked a dishwasher tablet, an adult who took one extra tablet. Most exposures never become poisonings, and the great majority of calls to poison centres are resolved at home with advice rather than a hospital visit. The purpose of assessing quickly is not to treat everything as catastrophic but to identify the minority of exposures carrying a hidden, time-sensitive risk — identified by substance and quantity, not by how frightening the moment feels.

sections.heading: How Poisons Actually Hurt the Body — Four Mechanisms
sections.body: Almost every poisoning encountered in ordinary life works through one of four mechanisms, and recognising which one is operating tells you what the danger actually is and how fast it will arrive. The first is direct chemical destruction. Strong acids and strong alkalis do not need to be absorbed at all; they dissolve tissue on contact. Acids coagulate protein, forming a scab that partly limits how deep the burn goes, while alkalis such as oven cleaner, drain opener and lye cause liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fat and driving steadily deeper into the wall of the oesophagus for as long as they remain in contact. This is why alkali burns are generally the more feared of the two, and why inducing vomiting after either one is so damaging: it drags the corrosive back through the same tissue a second time. The second mechanism is interference with a receptor, enzyme or transport protein the body cannot do without. Opioids bind mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem and progressively silence the reflex that tells you to breathe, so the person dies of hypoxia while the drug itself has damaged nothing structurally. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with roughly 200 to 250 times the affinity of oxygen and additionally distorts the remaining binding sites so that the oxygen still carried is released reluctantly to tissue — the blood looks full and is functionally empty. Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase, the final enzyme of cellular respiration, so cells drown in oxygen they cannot use. Organophosphate insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leaving the transmitter acetylcholine to accumulate and fire nerves continuously. The third mechanism is the toxic metabolite, and it is the one responsible for the deceptive quiet period. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is harmless until the normal conjugation pathways saturate; the surplus is then converted to NAPQI, which is neutralised by the liver's store of glutathione until that store is exhausted, after which NAPQI destroys liver cells over the following days. Methanol is metabolised to formic acid, causing blindness and acidosis; ethylene glycol antifreeze becomes glycolic and oxalic acid, crystallising in the kidneys. In each case the parent substance is comparatively benign and the poison is manufactured inside the patient. The fourth mechanism is physical or electrochemical rather than pharmacological: a swallowed button battery generates hydroxide at its negative pole and burns through the oesophageal wall within two hours; liquid hydrocarbons such as lamp oil and petrol are barely absorbed from the gut but destroy lung tissue if even a small volume is aspirated during swallowing or vomiting. Knowing which mechanism is in play predicts the shape of the emergency. Direct chemical damage announces itself immediately and the injury is done at the moment of contact. Receptor and enzyme blockade produces dramatic signs within an hour and is often reversible if the person is supported long enough for an antidote to act. Metabolite poisoning produces almost nothing at first and is treatable only inside a window that closes while the patient looks well. Physical mechanisms depend on position and time rather than dose, which is why a swallowed battery is an emergency measured on a clock.

sections.heading: Reading the Body's SOS Signals — Toxidromes
sections.body: When the substance is unknown, the body itself narrows the field. A toxidrome is a recognisable cluster of vital signs and physical findings produced by a whole class of poisons acting on the same receptor system, and clinicians use them constantly to start treatment before any laboratory result exists. Five are worth knowing by sight. The opioid toxidrome is the triad of pinpoint pupils, depressed consciousness and slow, shallow or irregular breathing — a respiratory rate under about 12 breaths a minute in an adult is a warning, under 8 is an emergency, and snoring or gurgling in someone who cannot be roused is agonal breathing, not sleep. Heart rate and blood pressure fall late; breathing fails first, which is why counting breaths for a full 30 seconds matters more than any other single observation. The sympathomimetic toxidrome, produced by cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine and high-dose decongestants, is the mirror image: wide pupils, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, agitation, tremor, and skin that is hot and visibly sweating. The anticholinergic toxidrome, caused by diphenhydramine and other older antihistamines, some sleep aids, tricyclic antidepressants and plants such as jimsonweed, is traditionally memorised as mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat and hot as a hare: confusion often with hallucinations, flushed skin, urinary retention, blurred vision from dilated pupils and fever. The single finding that separates it from the sympathomimetic picture is the skin — anticholinergic poisoning shuts sweating off, so the skin is hot and bone dry, whereas stimulant toxicity is hot and drenched. The cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate or carbamate pesticides and nerve agents is the opposite again: every secretion runs. It is remembered as SLUDGE — salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal cramping and emesis — with pinpoint pupils, muscle twitching and weakness. The finding that kills is bronchorrhoea, a flood of respiratory secretions that drowns the patient. The sedative-hypnotic toxidrome from benzodiazepines, alcohol and related drugs is depressed consciousness with comparatively preserved vital signs; benzodiazepines alone rarely kill an adult, but combined with alcohol or an opioid the respiratory depression becomes additive and lethal. Two honest caveats belong with all of this. Real overdoses are frequently mixed, and one substance can mask another's signs entirely — a stimulant taken alongside an opioid can leave pupils mid-sized and the heart rate normal while breathing still fails. And a toxidrome narrows possibilities without ever confirming a diagnosis; it guides the first few minutes, not the treatment plan. A sixth pattern, serotonin syndrome, is worth recognising because it arises from ordinary prescribed medicines rather than misuse: combining antidepressants, or adding tramadol, triptans, linezolid or the cough suppressant dextromethorphan to one, can produce agitation, fever, sweating, overactive reflexes and — the most distinctive sign — clonus, a rhythmic beating of the foot when the ankle is briskly flexed upward, typically far more marked in the legs than the arms. Finally, some of the most dangerous poisons produce no toxidrome at all in the early hours, which is precisely why an absence of findings never rules a serious ingestion out.

sections.heading: Everyday Poisoning Scenarios, By Name
sections.body: Most poisoning is not exotic. A small number of named scenarios account for the great majority of serious cases, and each has its own characteristic trap. Acetaminophen, sold as paracetamol or Tylenol and hidden inside dozens of combination cold and pain products, is the most consequential of all because the person feels well. Toxicity is generally considered possible above roughly 150 mg per kilogram taken within 24 hours — about 10 to 12 extra-strength tablets for a 70 kg adult — but nausea may be the only symptom for the first day and liver failure declares itself on days three to five. The antidote, N-acetylcysteine, is close to fully protective if started within eight hours of ingestion and loses effectiveness steadily thereafter, so the clock, not the symptoms, drives the decision. Button batteries are the paediatric equivalent: a 20 mm lithium cell lodged in a child's oesophagus can burn through the wall within two hours. Guidance from paediatric gastroenterology societies is to go directly to an emergency department and, for a child over 12 months who ingested it within the last 12 hours and can swallow, to give 10 mL of honey every 10 minutes up to six doses on the way, because honey coats the battery and slows the alkaline burn; it delays harm, it does not treat it. Carbon monoxide is odourless and colourless and mimics influenza — headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion — with two giveaways: several people and often pets in the same building become ill together, and everyone improves after time outdoors. Mixing household cleaners is a routine domestic disaster: bleach plus ammonia yields chloramine gas, bleach plus an acidic toilet or limescale cleaner yields chlorine, and both cause immediate coughing and chest tightness in an enclosed bathroom. Corrosive drain and oven cleaners burn the mouth, throat and oesophagus on contact. Liquid hydrocarbons — lamp oil, petrol, furniture polish, tiki-torch fuel — are dangerous chiefly because of their low viscosity, which lets a small amount slip into the lungs. Iron tablets and adult prescription medicines are the classic one-pill-can-kill hazards for toddlers, alongside cannabis edibles, which are dose-dense and look exactly like sweets. Alcohol in a small child causes not just sedation but dangerous hypoglycaemia. Illicitly obtained tablets and powders are now frequently adulterated with fentanyl, so potency is unknowable from appearance. And with foraged mushrooms, the deadly Amanita species characteristically produce vomiting six to twelve hours after the meal, then a false recovery, then liver failure — an interval so long that people often fail to connect the illness to the meal at all. Two further scenarios round out the domestic list. Laundry and dishwasher detergent capsules contain concentrated surfactant under a film that dissolves instantly in a wet mouth, and unlike ordinary detergent they cause vomiting, airway irritation and occasionally drowsiness in small children. And antifreeze containing ethylene glycol, along with methanol-based windscreen wash and some fuel additives, tastes sweet, produces an apparent drunkenness with no smell of alcohol, then goes quiet for hours while its metabolites damage the kidneys or the optic nerve; both have antidotes that work only if given early.

sections.heading: The First Response — What to Do, and What NOT to Do
sections.body: The first decision is not about the patient at all; it is about whether the scene is safe. With any suspected gas — carbon monoxide from a generator or heater, chlorine or chloramine from mixed cleaners, fumes in a confined space — rescuers who rush in become the second and third casualties, a pattern repeated in grain silos, cellars and bathrooms every year. Get everyone out into fresh air first, leave doors open behind you, and do not go back for possessions. With a spilled chemical, avoid contact with contaminated clothing and skin. Once the scene is safe, assess in the order that reflects how people actually die: are they responsive, are they breathing, and is the breathing adequate. Count breaths for a full 30 seconds and double it rather than guessing. An unresponsive person who is breathing should be rolled onto their side into the recovery position, because the single commonest preventable death in poisoning is aspirating vomit while lying on the back. Then make the call, and while you wait, gather evidence: the actual container, the pill bottle, the plant, a photograph of the label and ingredient list, and a written note of how much is missing and what time it happened. That note is worth more to the clinician than any description of symptoms. Route-specific first aid is straightforward. Skin exposure: remove contaminated clothing, cutting it off rather than pulling it over the head, and rinse the area with running lukewarm water for 15 to 20 minutes. Eye exposure: remove contact lenses and irrigate with lukewarm water for 15 to 20 minutes, holding the lids open, letting the water run from the inner corner outward so it does not wash into the other eye. Inhalation: fresh air, and do not re-enter. Now the prohibitions, which matter as much as the actions. Do not induce vomiting by any method — not by finger, not with salt water, and not with syrup of ipecac, which paediatric bodies withdrew from recommendation in 2003 because it delays effective treatment, causes prolonged vomiting that prevents the use of oral antidotes, and re-exposes the oesophagus to anything corrosive. Do not give activated charcoal at home; it is useless for many substances, deadly if aspirated, and time-critical in a way domestic administration cannot meet. Do not try to neutralise an acid with a base or the reverse — the reaction is itself exothermic and adds a thermal burn to a chemical one. Do not give anything to drink to someone drowsy, convulsing or unable to swallow; small sips of water or milk are sometimes advised for corrosives, but only when a poison specialist instructs it. And never leave someone to sleep it off unobserved: the quietly deteriorating patient is the one who dies, and someone should stay within sight and within reach until either the person is clearly recovering or professional help has taken over.

sections.heading: Poison Control vs. 911 — How to Decide
sections.body: Two different services exist because two different questions arise, and choosing correctly costs nothing while choosing wrongly costs minutes. Call emergency services — 911 in the United States and Canada, 999 in the United Kingdom, 112 across the European Union and much of the world, 000 in Australia — whenever the person is unconscious or cannot be roused, is not breathing or is breathing slowly, noisily or irregularly, is having a seizure, is turning blue or grey around the lips and fingertips, has swallowed something corrosive and is drooling or unable to swallow, or is showing any sign of an opioid overdose. The same applies whenever the situation is deteriorating in front of you, when there is a gas exposure affecting more than one person, and, importantly, whenever you are alone with the patient and calling for advice would mean leaving them unwatched. Nobody has ever been criticised for calling an ambulance to a poisoning that turned out to be minor. Call a poison centre — 1-800-222-1222 anywhere in the United States, and equivalents in most countries, which a pharmacy, hospital switchboard or library can supply and which is worth looking up before you need it — for the far more common situation where an exposure has happened but the person is awake, breathing normally and either well or only mildly unwell. This is the service for questions such as whether the amount swallowed is actually dangerous, whether a doubled dose of a prescription matters, what a particular plant or berry is, whether a chemical splash needs an emergency department, and what to watch for over the next several hours. The centres are staffed around the clock by pharmacists, nurses and medical toxicologists, the call is free and confidential, and they will telephone you back to check on the patient. They are not a lesser service: hospitals and ambulance crews telephone the same specialists for advice. In the United States they also offer webPOISONCONTROL, an online triage tool for people who would rather type than talk. Have ready, before you dial, the product name and its ingredient list, the amount involved as a worst-case estimate, the time of exposure, the person's age and weight, their symptoms and any regular medications, and your address. One further point deserves saying plainly: fear of legal consequences kills people in drug overdoses. Most US states and many other jurisdictions have Good Samaritan laws that give limited protection to those who summon help, and the person who calls is the reason someone survives. If in genuine doubt about which number to use, call the emergency service. A dispatcher can loop in a poison specialist, whereas a poison specialist cannot reach through the phone to open an airway, and the cost of an unnecessary ambulance is a great deal lower than the cost of a delayed one.

sections.heading: Naloxone — Reversing an Opioid Overdose
sections.body: Naloxone is one of the few genuine antidotes an untrained member of the public can safely use. It is a competitive antagonist at the mu-opioid receptor, meaning it binds the same site as heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, morphine or methadone but with greater affinity and no activating effect of its own, so it physically displaces the opioid and the suppressed drive to breathe returns. The commonest form is a single-use 4 mg intranasal spray requiring no assembly: lay the person on their back, tilt the head, insert the nozzle into one nostril until your fingers touch the nose, and press the plunger firmly once. It works on an unconscious person because absorption is across the nasal lining, not by inhalation. Intramuscular kits deliver 0.4 mg into the outer thigh, through clothing if necessary. Response usually begins within two to five minutes; if there is no improvement, give a second dose in the other nostril and continue every two to three minutes for as long as doses last. Two facts about naloxone are more important than the technique. The first is that it wears off — its effect lasts roughly 30 to 90 minutes, which is often shorter than the opioid it is displacing, and fentanyl analogues and methadone in particular outlast it comfortably. A person can wake, appear fine, and stop breathing again half an hour later. Naloxone is therefore never an alternative to calling an ambulance; it buys transport time. The second is that the immediate cause of death in opioid overdose is lack of oxygen, so rescue breathing matters as much as the drug: after giving the dose, if breathing is absent or barely present, deliver a breath every five seconds while waiting. Naloxone is remarkably safe. Given to someone whose collapse is due to alcohol, benzodiazepines, stimulants, a stroke or low blood sugar, it does essentially nothing, so uncertainty about the cause is a reason to give it rather than withhold it. In a physically dependent person it precipitates abrupt withdrawal — sweating, vomiting, cramps, agitation and sometimes anger — which is deeply unpleasant but is not itself life-threatening; place them on their side afterwards, because vomiting into an airway is the real hazard. Store kits out of freezing and extreme heat, check the expiry date, and keep them where a bystander can find them rather than locked away. Where naloxone is available over the counter, obtaining a kit before it is needed is the entire point. Two limits are worth stating plainly. Naloxone does nothing for an overdose of benzodiazepines, alcohol, stimulants or gabapentinoids, so in a mixed overdose it may restore breathing only partially or not at all — which is not a reason to withhold it, but is a reason never to treat a poor response as proof that opioids were not involved. And the very high potencies now circulating mean that two, three or more doses are sometimes required, so a single-dose kit should be thought of as a minimum rather than a complete provision.

sections.heading: Tools, Materials & Where to Get Them
sections.body: Nothing on this list is expensive, and the reasoning behind each item is worth more than the item. A telephone number is useless if it has to be searched for while someone is vomiting, so the point of storing it twice — in the phone and on paper inside a cupboard — is redundancy against the two commonest failures, a flat battery and a mind that has gone blank. Naloxone belongs in a household long before anyone believes it is needed, because the people who most often administer it are family members and bystanders, not the person at risk, and because a supply adulterated with fentanyl means an overdose can occur on a first or occasional use. A carbon monoxide detector with a digital parts-per-million readout is chosen over a bare alarm deliberately: it shows a rising low-level exposure that has not yet crossed the alarm threshold, which is exactly the pattern produced by a failing boiler or a blocked flue, and chronic low-level poisoning is routinely misdiagnosed as flu for weeks. A torch earns its place for two specific tasks that are surprisingly hard in a dim room: judging whether pupils are pinpoint or wide, and reading an ingredient list printed in four-point type on a curved bottle, which is the single piece of information a poison specialist most wants. The notepad addresses memory under stress. People reliably misremember times and quantities within minutes of an emergency, and a figure written down at the moment — thirteen tablets missing, roughly nine forty in the evening — is evidence, while the same figure recalled an hour later is a guess. A lockable box exists because child-resistant caps are a delay, not a barrier. And the insistence on original labelled containers is the most quietly important item of all: decanting bleach into a drinks bottle removes the ingredient list, the concentration and the manufacturer's emergency instructions in one action, and it converts a container the brain reads as dangerous into one it reads as safe to swallow.
ingredients: Poison Control's number (1-800-222-1222 in the US, or your country's equivalent, found through a pharmacy or library) saved in every household phone and posted somewhere visible, like inside a kitchen cabinet
A naloxone nasal-spray kit, available at most pharmacies without a prescription in many areas — check availability and any included training material with your local pharmacy
A battery-powered carbon monoxide detector with a digital readout — hardware store or general retailer
A basic first-aid reference manual or wallet card covering poisoning response — library, bookstore, or often free from a pharmacy or local Red Cross chapter
A bright flashlight, for checking pupil size and reading small print on product labels in a dimly lit cabinet
A notepad and pen, or a phone notes app, kept near where medications and chemicals are stored, for recording exactly what was taken, how much, and when
A lockable storage box or cabinet for medications and hazardous chemicals — hardware store or general retailer
The original, labeled container for every medication and chemical in the home — never a repurposed food or drink container

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Rehearse a Home Poison-Response Plan
sections.body: A plan that exists only as an intention fails at the moment it is needed, because acute stress narrows attention, degrades recall of anything not already automatic, and reliably steals ordinary information such as your own address. Everything in this procedure is designed around that fact: the aim is to move decisions out of the emergency and into a quiet afternoon beforehand. Two of the steps do more work than the rest and deserve to be understood rather than merely performed. Reading a product's own emergency instructions aloud, once, for something you already keep under the sink is startlingly informative, because manufacturers' guidance is specific to the chemistry — some corrosives say explicitly not to induce vomiting and to sip water, others say nothing by mouth at all — and this is knowledge you will not reconstruct from first principles while panicking. Role-playing the call matters for a different reason: the questions a poison specialist asks are not the ones people expect. They want the ingredient list rather than the brand, a worst-case estimate of quantity, the clock time rather than how long ago it felt, and the patient's weight. Rehearsing those answers converts a stumbling five-minute call into a ninety-second one, and in a time-critical ingestion that difference is real. Do the audit room by room and in daylight, including the garage, handbags, bedside drawers and visitors' luggage, because those last three are where the pills that poison toddlers overwhelmingly come from. Repeat the exercise annually, and after any change of household.
steps: Save the Poison Control number in your phone right now, under a name you'd recognize in a panic (e.g., 'POISON CONTROL — CALL FIRST'), and write it on a card taped inside a kitchen cabinet.
Walk through your home room by room and list every medication, cleaning product, and chemical you find, noting where each is stored and whether it's in its original, labeled container.
Relocate anything within reach of a child or a confused family member into a single locked cabinet or box, and discard anything expired.
Pick one product from your list and actually read its label's 'if swallowed' or 'if inhaled' instructions out loud — most people have never done this even once for products they use regularly.

With a family member, role-play a call to Poison Control: have them ask you the questions a real operator would (what was taken, how much, when, the person's age and weight, current symptoms) and practice answering clearly and quickly.

If you keep naloxone on hand, read through the device's full instructions before an emergency, and if your pharmacy offers a practice or trainer device with no active medication, physically rehearse the administration motion once.
Test your carbon monoxide detector's function button and check or replace its battery, and confirm you know the difference between its 'low battery' chirp and its actual alarm pattern.

Post a simple written emergency plan near your phone: the Poison Control number, your local emergency number, your home address (surprisingly easy to blank on under real stress), and the location of your naloxone kit if you have one.

sections.heading: Myths That Get People Hurt
sections.body: Poisoning attracts more confidently repeated bad advice than almost any other emergency, and several of the most popular items are actively lethal. The first is making the person vomit. Syrup of ipecac sat in medicine cabinets for decades and was withdrawn from recommendation by paediatric authorities in 2003 after evidence showed it did not improve outcomes and did cause harm: it produces prolonged vomiting that prevents the use of oral antidotes and activated charcoal in hospital, it delays departure for care, and with a corrosive or a hydrocarbon it drags the substance back across tissue it has already burned or delivers it into the lungs. Salt water as a home emetic is worse still and has killed both children and adults through acute hypernatraemia, a sodium level high enough to shrink brain cells. The second myth is that milk neutralises poisons. It does not; it dilutes at best, it delays nothing dangerous, and for some substances it speeds absorption of fat-soluble compounds. The third is chemical neutralisation — vinegar for a swallowed alkali, bicarbonate for an acid — which generates heat inside an already burned oesophagus. The fourth cluster surrounds intoxication: coffee, a cold shower, walking someone around and slapping them awake do nothing to remove alcohol or opioids, waste the only useful minutes, and in hypothermic or sedated people the cold shower itself is dangerous. Alcohol leaves the blood at a fixed rate that no intervention accelerates. The fifth is the universal antidote of folklore — burnt toast, strong tea and milk of magnesia — which has no basis whatever and is dangerous chiefly because it manufactures a feeling that something has been done. The sixth is treating activated charcoal as a home remedy; hospitals give it under conditions the home cannot meet, and aspirated charcoal causes severe pneumonitis. The seventh is judging severity by appearance, which is precisely the mistake acetaminophen and Amanita mushrooms are built to exploit. The eighth is that natural means safe, in a world containing oleander, foxglove and death cap. The ninth is that carbon monoxide can be smelled, or that a smoke alarm will detect it — it is entirely odourless and smoke detectors are blind to it. And the tenth, which costs the most lives, is that calling for help after a drug overdose will bring the police down on everyone present; in most of the United States and many other jurisdictions Good Samaritan legislation exists specifically to remove that fear. Two smaller myths round the list out. Poison centres are not only for children and not only for emergencies — a large share of their calls are ordinary medication questions from adults, and using them for exactly that is what keeps them funded and staffed. And an out-of-date conviction that something must be done immediately is itself a hazard: with most exposures the correct first action is to stop, secure the substance and its label, and make one phone call, because a wrong intervention delivered in the first five minutes is far harder to undo than five minutes of doing nothing.

sections.heading: Special-Risk Groups
sections.body: Risk is not distributed evenly, and several groups are vulnerable for reasons that are structural rather than behavioural. Children under six account for roughly half of all reported exposures in countries that collect the data, driven by exploratory mouthing, an attraction to bright liquids and sweet-looking tablets, and a body mass so small that an adult dose becomes a massive one per kilogram. A specific category is worth memorising as one-pill-can-kill: a single tablet or a small mouthful of certain adult medicines can be fatal to a toddler, including strong opioids, some blood-pressure drugs of the calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker families, sulfonylurea diabetes tablets, iron supplements, camphor and topical oil of wintergreen, which is concentrated methyl salicylate. Cannabis edibles belong here too, being dose-dense and visually identical to confectionery. Adolescents and young adults present a different pattern in which exposures are more often deliberate, larger and mixed, and where impulsivity means that restricting access to quantity genuinely changes outcomes. Older adults are at risk through polypharmacy and physiology together: a person taking eight medications faces a combinatorial number of interactions, kidney and liver clearance decline with age so standard doses accumulate, visual impairment makes similar tablets indistinguishable, and mild cognitive impairment produces the double-dose error — taking a medicine again because there is no memory of the first time. Pregnancy carries specific hazards: carbon monoxide crosses the placenta and foetal haemoglobin binds it more avidly than the mother's, so foetal levels exceed maternal ones and lag behind in clearing, which is why oxygen treatment is given for longer in pregnancy. People with liver disease, malnutrition or chronic heavy alcohol use have depleted glutathione reserves and can be harmed by acetaminophen doses that would be tolerated by others. People with opioid use disorder face a sharply elevated risk in one particular window: tolerance falls within days of abstinence, so the period following release from custody, discharge from detoxification or a hospital stay carries a documented spike in fatal overdose when a previously routine dose is resumed. Workers handling pesticides, solvents and industrial gases carry occupational exposure risk that follows them home on clothing, and changing and washing work clothes separately is a genuine protective measure for the rest of the household. People living with dementia are at particular risk of drinking a decanted chemical or repeating a dose, which is one of the strongest arguments for locked storage and blister packaging rather than open pill organisers. And pets, being smaller and undiscriminating, are frequently the first casualties in a household — a dog that collapses or a caged bird that dies is sometimes the earliest warning of a gas leak, and veterinary poison services exist for the same reasons human ones do. The common thread across every group here is that the effective interventions are environmental rather than educational: smaller quantities in the house, locked storage, unambiguous labelling, one prescriber reviewing the whole medication list, and naloxone kept where the people around the person at risk can reach it.

sections.heading: Prevention That Actually Works
sections.body: Prevention research is unusually clear about what changes outcomes and what merely feels responsible. Storage beats supervision, because supervision has gaps and storage does not. The standard formulation is up, away and out of sight: above a child's eye level, in a cupboard they cannot climb to, and behind a door, because a container that is visible is a container that becomes a goal. Child-resistant closures are a delay rather than a barrier — the regulatory test only requires that most children under five fail to open the package within five minutes, and a determined toddler with an afternoon will often succeed — so the cap buys time for an adult to notice, and a locked box provides the actual seal. Keep everything in its original labelled container, and never decant a chemical into a drink bottle or food jar; that single act removes the ingredient list a poison specialist needs, discards the manufacturer's emergency instructions, and disguises a hazard as something safe to swallow. Store household chemicals below and separate from food, never above it, so a leak cannot drip into what people eat. Handbags, coat pockets, bedside tables and visitors' luggage are the origin of a large share of paediatric medicine ingestions and should be included in any survey. Reduce quantity as well as access: dispose of expired and unneeded medicines through a pharmacy take-back scheme rather than accumulating them, and where opioids are prescribed, obtain naloxone at the same time. Never combine cleaning products, and read labels before assuming two are compatible. Fit carbon monoxide detectors on every sleeping level and outside bedrooms, test them monthly, and replace the whole unit at the manufacturer's stated end of life, typically seven to ten years, because the sensor degrades whether or not the battery is fresh. Never run a generator, charcoal grill, camping stove or petrol engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window — an attached garage with the door raised is still lethal, and generators need to be many metres from any opening. Have fuel-burning appliances, flues and chimneys serviced annually. Finally, treat the poison centre number as safety equipment: written where it can be seen, saved in every phone, and known by everyone in the house including teenagers and carers. Two further measures repay the small effort they take. Re-survey the house whenever it changes — a baby becoming mobile, an older relative moving in with a bag of medicines, a houseguest's suitcase, a course of strong painkillers after surgery — because most paediatric poisonings involve a substance that was in the home only temporarily and was set down somewhere it would not ordinarily be. And be honest about the limits of what prevention can achieve: no storage arrangement makes a house poison-proof, so the goal is to remove the easy routes to harm and to make sure that when something does happen the response is already rehearsed, the container is still labelled, and the number is already in the phone.

guides.safetyNote: Poisoning and overdose can escalate from 'looks fine' to life-threatening within hours with no warning signs in between — acetaminophen overdose and button-battery ingestion are textbook examples of this. This guide is not a substitute for calling Poison Control or emergency services; when you're unsure how serious a situation is, make the call. That uncertainty is exactly what they exist to triage, for free, and they will never fault you for calling.

guides.title: Seizures: What To Do While One Is Happening
guides.summary: How to recognise a seizure, what to do and what never to do while it is happening, how to care for someone afterwards, and exactly when a seizure becomes an emergency that needs an ambulance.
guides.safetyNote: Never put anything in the mouth of someone having a seizure and never hold them down. Both cause injuries. Call emergency services if a seizure lasts more than five minutes, if a second follows without recovery in between, if they do not wake up afterwards, if it happened in water, or if this is their first ever seizure. This is written guidance, not training and not medical advice.

sections.heading: What a seizure actually looks like
sections.body:
A seizure is a burst of disordered electrical activity in the brain, and what it looks like from outside depends entirely on which part of the brain is involved. The version most people picture — the whole body stiffening and then jerking rhythmically — is called a generalised tonic-clonic seizure, and it is the one most likely to frighten a bystander into doing something harmful.

In a tonic-clonic seizure the person usually loses consciousness without warning and falls. They may cry out as air is forced past the vocal cords; this is not pain and not a call for help. The body goes rigid for a few seconds to half a minute, then the limbs jerk in a regular rhythm that gradually slows and stops. Breathing can look alarming: it may pause during the stiff phase, become noisy and laboured during the jerking, and the lips and face may take on a bluish tinge. Saliva can froth at the mouth, sometimes tinged with blood if the tongue or cheek was bitten. Loss of bladder or bowel control is common and is worth knowing about in advance because managing it discreetly afterwards matters enormously to the person it happened to.

Most tonic-clonic seizures stop on their own within one to three minutes. That is the single most useful fact to hold onto while watching one, because the seizure will almost always end before you can do anything decisive, and the useful work is protecting the person while it runs its course.

Other seizures look nothing like this. A focal aware seizure may involve nothing more than an odd rising sensation, a strange smell or taste, twitching confined to one hand or one side of the face, while the person remains fully awake and can describe it afterwards. A focal impaired-awareness seizure looks like someone who has gone absent: staring, not responding to their name, making repetitive purposeless movements such as lip-smacking, chewing, picking at clothing or wandering. They are not ignoring you and they are not drunk or being difficult, and trying to snap them out of it does not work. An absence seizure, more common in children, can be a blank pause of a few seconds that is mistaken for daydreaming for years before anyone recognises it.

You do not need to identify the type to help. Recognising that this is a seizure rather than fainting, a stroke or intoxication is enough, and the actions in the next section are the same for all of them.

sections.heading: What to do while it is happening
sections.body:
Look at the time. This is the first thing to do and the one most often forgotten, because a seizure feels far longer than it is — a ninety-second seizure is routinely reported by witnesses as five or ten minutes. The duration determines whether this is an ordinary seizure that will stop by itself or a medical emergency, and a guess is not good enough. Note the clock, or start a timer.

Then protect them where they are. Do not try to move someone who is actively convulsing unless they are in immediate danger — at the top of stairs, in a road, next to a fire or a hot stove, or in water. Instead move the danger away from them: push back chairs and tables, clear anything hard or sharp from the space around their head and limbs. Put something soft under the head — a folded jumper, a cushion, a rolled coat, or your hands if there is nothing else. Most seizure injuries are from striking the head repeatedly against a hard floor, and cushioning it is the single most valuable physical thing you can do.

Loosen anything tight around the neck: a collar, a tie, a scarf, a lanyard. If they wear glasses, take them off.

Then stay, and let it happen. This is genuinely difficult, because every instinct says to intervene and there is nothing useful to intervene with. Talk calmly if it helps you; some people retain fragments of hearing during a seizure and a steady voice is kinder than panic. Keep other people back and ask someone to wait outside to direct an ambulance if one has been called.

Watch what happens, because you will be the only witness who can describe it. Useful details: how it started, whether the jerking involved the whole body or one side, whether the eyes turned to one side, how long each phase lasted, whether they were incontinent, and how they were afterwards. Ambulance crews and neurologists rely on bystander accounts because the person themselves remembers nothing. If you can film it safely and it is appropriate to do so, that recording is genuinely valuable to their doctors — but ask afterwards before keeping or sharing it.

When the jerking stops, move on to the recovery steps below. Do not assume it is over the instant the movement ends; recovery takes far longer than the seizure did.

sections.heading: What never to do
sections.body:
Never put anything in their mouth. Not a spoon, not a wallet, not a rolled cloth, not your fingers. This instruction survives in folk memory from a genuine misunderstanding — the belief that a person can swallow their own tongue — and it is anatomically impossible. The tongue is anchored to the floor of the mouth and cannot be swallowed. What can happen, and does, is that objects forced between clenched jaws break teeth, and the fragments are then inhaled. Fingers get bitten severely; the bite force in a tonic-clonic seizure is far beyond normal. If they are going to bite their tongue, it happens in the first seconds, before anyone could have intervened, and a bitten tongue heals. A blocked airway and broken teeth do not heal so easily.

Never hold them down or try to stop the movement. Restraint does not shorten a seizure and cannot; the electrical activity driving it is in the brain and is entirely unaffected by how firmly you hold an arm. What restraint does cause is dislocated shoulders, torn muscles and fractures, in both the person seizing and whoever is holding them. If they are thrashing near something hard, move the object, not the person.

Do not give them anything to eat or drink, and do not try to give medication by mouth, during or immediately after a seizure. Swallowing is unreliable for some time afterwards and the liquid goes into the lungs. Wait until they are fully alert and can hold a normal conversation. The exception is a prescribed rescue medication designed to be given during a seizure — these are given into the cheek or the nose, not swallowed, and only by someone trained and authorised to give them.

Do not throw water on them, slap them, or shout to try to wake them. None of it works and all of it adds distress.

Do not crowd them. A ring of onlookers is the thing people most often describe as humiliating afterwards. Ask people to step back and, if it is a public place, to move on.

And do not assume the person needs an ambulance simply because a seizure happened. Many people with epilepsy have seizures regularly, know it, and would far rather recover quietly than wake in a hospital corridor. The next section covers when that judgement changes.

sections.heading: After it stops: the recovery period
sections.body:
The minutes after a seizure are called the postictal period, and they are a real and often prolonged part of the event rather than a return to normal. Expect confusion, exhaustion, headache, aching muscles, and sometimes agitation or an emotional flood of tears. Some people are briefly unable to speak or to find words. Some sleep deeply for an hour or more. None of this is alarming by itself; it is the brain recovering.

As soon as the jerking has stopped and they are still, roll them onto their side into the recovery position: lower arm out, upper leg bent to stop them rolling forward, head tilted gently back so the airway stays open and the chin slightly down so saliva or vomit drains out rather than being inhaled. This is the single most important thing you do after a seizure, because vomiting is common and the airway is unprotected while they are not fully conscious.

Check that they are breathing. Normal breathing may take a few seconds to re-establish and may be noisy or snoring at first as the airway relaxes — repositioning the head usually clears it. If they are genuinely not breathing after the movement has stopped, that is a different emergency and you should call for help and start resuscitation.

Stay with them. Someone waking from a seizure in an unfamiliar place with strangers around is frightened and disoriented, and may try to get up and walk before they can safely stand. Speak calmly, use their name, tell them plainly what happened and where they are, and repeat it as often as needed — they may ask the same question many times and not remember the answer. Do not let them drive, operate anything, or leave alone until they are genuinely oriented, which can take twenty minutes or considerably longer.

Deal with incontinence discreetly if it happened. Cover them with a coat, clear onlookers away, and mention it to them quietly rather than in front of people. This matters more to most people than the seizure itself.

When they are able to talk, ask whether this is something that happens to them, whether they have epilepsy, and whether they have a care plan or a rescue medication. Many people carry a card, wear a medical bracelet, or have their condition on their phone's emergency information screen. If this was their first seizure, they need to be seen by a doctor even if they now feel fine, and they must not drive until they have been advised.

sections.heading: When a seizure is an emergency
sections.body:
Most seizures stop on their own and do not need an ambulance. These are the situations where they do, and the first one is the most important.

Call emergency services if the convulsing lasts more than five minutes. A seizure that does not self-terminate is called status epilepticus, and it is a genuine medical emergency: prolonged seizure activity damages neurons, and the longer it runs the harder it becomes to stop with drugs. This is precisely why you noted the time at the start. Five minutes is the threshold used by emergency services in most countries, and erring on the side of calling is correct.

Call if a second seizure begins before they have recovered consciousness from the first. Repeated seizures without recovery in between is also status epilepticus, and carries the same urgency.

Call if they do not regain consciousness within a few minutes of the movement stopping, if their breathing does not settle into a normal pattern, or if they remain blue around the lips.

Call if this is their first ever seizure, or if you have no way of knowing. A first seizure needs investigating — it can be a symptom of something else entirely, including low blood sugar, infection, head injury, stroke, poisoning or alcohol withdrawal.

Call if the seizure happened in water, at any depth. Even a brief seizure in a bath or a pool means water may have been inhaled, and the consequences can appear hours later.

Call if they were injured during it — particularly any blow to the head, or if you suspect a fracture or dislocation.

Call if they are pregnant, if they have diabetes, or if they have any serious underlying condition.

Call if the seizure is clearly different from their usual pattern. People with established epilepsy, or those close to them, usually know exactly what their seizures look like and how long they last. A seizure that departs from that pattern is worth escalating even if it stopped normally.

When you call, the dispatcher will want to know: that it was a seizure, how long it lasted, whether it has stopped, whether they are breathing, whether they are conscious, whether they have epilepsy if you know, and exactly where you are. Having the time you noted at the start turns a vague account into a useful one.

sections.heading: If seizures are part of your life, or someone's near you
sections.body:
Preparation changes the experience of a seizure more than anything a bystander can do in the moment. If you have epilepsy, or live or work with someone who does, a small amount of planning removes most of the panic from the event.

Write down a seizure plan and make sure the people around you have seen it. It should say what your seizures usually look like, how long they usually last, what helps, what does not, whether you have a rescue medication and who is authorised to give it, at what point an ambulance should be called, and who to contact. One page is enough. The purpose is that the person standing over you is not improvising.

Keep the information where a stranger will find it. A medical ID bracelet or card, and the emergency information screen on your phone, are both checked routinely by ambulance crews. Put the diagnosis, the medication and an emergency contact on both.

Keep a seizure diary. Date, time, duration, what happened, what you were doing beforehand, how much you had slept, whether you had missed a dose. Neurologists make treatment decisions on patterns, and human memory for these events is poor. Any notes app works; the value is in it being consistent rather than elaborate.

Know your triggers if you have them, without letting the list run your life. The most common by a wide margin is sleep deprivation, followed by missed medication, alcohol, illness with fever, and severe stress. Photosensitivity — seizures triggered by flashing light — is real but affects a minority of people with epilepsy, not the majority as popular culture suggests.

Make the physical environment more forgiving where it is cheap to do so. Showers rather than baths. Guards on open fires and radiators. Not locking the bathroom door. Cooking on back rings rather than front. None of this needs to turn a home into a hospital; each is a small change that removes a specific way people are seriously hurt.

Finally, talk to the people you spend time with. The most common reason a seizure goes badly handled is that nobody present knew it was a possibility, and the second most common is that somebody who had never seen one did the thing they had seen in a film. Five minutes of conversation in advance replaces both.

guides.title: Head Injury and Concussion: What To Watch For
guides.summary: How to tell an ordinary bump on the head from one that needs a hospital, the red flags that mean call an ambulance now, why the old advice about keeping someone awake was wrong, and how to recover from a concussion without making it worse.
guides.safetyNote: Call emergency services for any head injury with loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, a seizure, worsening headache, confusion that is getting worse, weakness or numbness, unequal pupils, or clear fluid from the nose or ears. Anyone taking blood-thinning medication needs assessing after any head injury, however minor it looks. This is written guidance, not training and not medical advice.

sections.heading: Recognising a concussion
sections.body:
A concussion is a brain injury caused by the brain moving inside the skull — from a direct blow, or from a jolt to the body that whips the head. You do not have to be knocked out. Most concussions involve no loss of consciousness at all, which is why so many go unrecognised, and why the question 'were you knocked out?' is a poor screening test on its own.

The most reliable early sign is that the person is not quite right and either they or the people who know them can tell. Look for confusion about what just happened, a blank or dazed look, answering slowly, repeating the same question, or being unable to recall the moments before or after the impact. Amnesia around the event is significant even when everything else looks normal.

Physical symptoms cluster: headache or pressure in the head, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision, ringing in the ears, sensitivity to light or noise, and a feeling of being 'in a fog' or slowed down. Balance is often subtly off. Some people become unusually emotional, irritable or flat, and this change in personality is frequently the thing a partner notices first while the injured person insists they are fine.

Symptoms can begin immediately or take hours to appear, which is the single most important reason not to treat 'they seem fine' as the end of the matter. A person who walks away from a fall talking normally can deteriorate over the following hours, and someone needs to be watching.

In children, look for persistent crying, refusing to feed, changes in sleep or play patterns, unsteadiness, and listlessness. In infants a bulging soft spot on the head is a red flag needing immediate assessment.

Assume a concussion in anyone who has taken a real blow to the head and behaves at all unusually. Over-calling a concussion costs a quiet afternoon. Under-calling one, and sending someone back onto a pitch or a ladder, is how a survivable injury becomes a catastrophic one — which is the subject of the section on returning to normal.

sections.heading: What to do in the first hour
sections.body:
Stop whatever they were doing, immediately and completely. No returning to the game, the ride, the climb or the shift, however well they say they feel. This one rule prevents more serious harm than everything else on this page combined, because a second impact on a brain that has not recovered is far more dangerous than the first.

If there is any possibility of a neck or spine injury — a fall from height, a road collision, a dive into shallow water, or any complaint of neck pain, numbness or tingling — keep them still and keep their head in line with their body. Do not move them unless they are in danger, and do not remove a helmet. Kneel behind the head and support it gently with both hands until trained help arrives.

If they are unconscious but breathing, and you have no reason to suspect a spinal injury, put them in the recovery position and monitor their breathing. An unprotected airway is a more immediate threat than the head injury itself.

If they are alert, sit them down somewhere quiet. Bright light and noise make everything worse and make assessment harder. Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to any swelling — twenty minutes on, twenty off — and press gently on any bleeding scalp wound, which will bleed impressively out of proportion to its seriousness because the scalp is richly supplied with blood.

Then stay with them and keep watching. Write down the time of the injury and note how they are every fifteen minutes or so for the first few hours: are they more or less alert, is the headache better or worse, have they vomited, can they still tell you where they are. That sequence is exactly what a doctor will want, and 'about the same as an hour ago' is far more useful than 'he seemed alright'.

Do not let them drive, and do not let them go home alone. Someone should be with them or checking on them for the first twenty-four hours.

sections.heading: The red flags that mean call now
sections.body:
Most head injuries are not dangerous. These signs mean this one might be, and any single one of them is enough to call emergency services rather than wait and see.

Any loss of consciousness, however brief, in anyone. Even a few seconds counts.

A headache that is getting worse rather than settling, particularly one described as the worst they have ever had.

Vomiting more than once. A single vomit soon after a blow is common; repeated vomiting suggests rising pressure inside the skull.

Increasing drowsiness, or becoming harder to rouse. This is the classic sign of a bleed developing slowly between the skull and the brain, and it can appear hours after an injury that looked trivial. Someone who is progressively less responsive needs an ambulance now, not in the morning.

Confusion that is deepening rather than clearing, agitation, or behaviour that is increasingly out of character.

A seizure of any kind after the injury.

Weakness, numbness, or clumsiness in an arm or leg, difficulty speaking or understanding, or loss of coordination.

Pupils that are unequal in size, or vision that is deteriorating.

Clear or blood-stained fluid leaking from the nose or ears, bruising appearing behind the ears or around both eyes, or a visible dent in the skull. These suggest a skull fracture.

There are also people for whom the threshold should be lower regardless of symptoms. Anyone taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication — warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel, and often aspirin — should be assessed after any head injury at all, because a bleed that would have stopped by itself may not. The same applies to anyone with a bleeding disorder, older adults, infants, anyone who has drunk enough that you cannot assess them properly, and anyone injured by a genuinely dangerous mechanism such as a car crash, a fall of more than a metre or so, or an assault with a weapon.

When you call, say what hit what and how fast, whether they were knocked out and for how long, what they are like now compared with immediately afterwards, and what medication they take.

sections.heading: Myths that get people hurt
sections.body:
You do not have to keep them awake. This is the most persistent piece of first-aid folklore about head injuries and it is wrong. Sleep does not cause a bleed and does not hide one; the concern the myth was reaching for is that a sleeping person cannot be observed, which is a real point handled by waking them periodically rather than by depriving them of sleep. Someone who has been assessed, has no red flags and wants to sleep should sleep — rest is the actual treatment. Check on them, confirm they rouse normally, and let them settle again. A person kept awake all night is exhausted, and exhaustion makes every concussion symptom worse and every assessment less reliable.

Do not 'shake it off' and do not let them talk you into carrying on. Concussed people are poor judges of their own state, because judgement is one of the things a concussion impairs. This is not stubbornness; it is a symptom. Whoever is making the decision, it should not be the person who took the blow.

Do not remove a helmet after a serious impact if there is any chance of a neck injury and help is on the way. Removing it moves the head. The exception is if the airway is obstructed and you cannot manage it any other way.

Do not give aspirin or ibuprofen in the first day if there is any suspicion of bleeding; paracetamol is the safer choice for a headache after a head injury. And do not give alcohol, which both worsens bleeding risk and makes deterioration impossible to distinguish from intoxication.

Do not assume a hard head means a safe one, or that the absence of a lump means the absence of an injury. There is no relationship between how impressive the swelling looks and how serious the brain injury is. A large scalp haematoma is usually nothing; a small mark over a slowly worsening headache is the one to worry about.

And do not let them drive that day. Reaction time and judgement are measurably impaired long after someone feels normal.

sections.heading: Recovering without making it worse
sections.body:
Recovery from concussion is usually complete, and usually takes days to a few weeks. The two things that reliably prolong it are returning to full activity too early and being hit again before healing is finished.

For the first day or two, rest genuinely: reduced screens, reduced noise, no strenuous exercise, no demanding mental work. Complete darkened-room isolation, once standard advice, is now known to slow recovery rather than speed it — the aim is to keep activity below the level that provokes symptoms, not to eliminate activity.

After that, increase gradually and use symptoms as the gauge. A useful rule: increase one step at a time, and if symptoms return, drop back a step and stay there a day longer. Light walking, then longer walks, then light exercise that does not risk contact, then sport-specific training, then full training, then competition. Reading and work follow the same pattern — short sessions first, extended as they are tolerated.

Do not return to any activity with a risk of head impact until symptoms have fully resolved and, for organised sport, until you have been cleared by someone qualified to do so. The reason is second impact syndrome: a second concussion sustained while the brain is still recovering can cause catastrophic, sometimes fatal, swelling, and it disproportionately affects children and adolescents. It is rare, and it is entirely preventable by waiting.

See a doctor if symptoms are not steadily improving after a week or two, if they return after seeming to resolve, or if mood, sleep or concentration remain disturbed. Persistent symptoms are common enough to have a name and are treatable; they are not a sign of weakness and not something to push through.

Finally, note the injury somewhere. Repeated concussions matter cumulatively, and a record of how many, how severe, and how long each took to resolve is genuinely useful information for any clinician assessing the next one.

guides.title: Electric Shock: Making It Safe Before You Help
guides.summary: Why the first move is never to touch the casualty, how to isolate the power safely, what an electrical injury does that you cannot see, and why someone who feels fine after a shock may still need a hospital.
guides.safetyNote: Never touch someone who may still be in contact with electricity. For overhead power lines stay at least ten metres away, keep others back, and wait for the utility company — voltage arcs and travels through the ground. Any shock causing unconsciousness, chest pain, palpitations, burns, or from high voltage or lightning needs emergency assessment. This is written guidance, not training and not medical advice.

sections.heading: Do not touch them
sections.body:
The instinct to grab someone being electrocuted is overwhelming and it is how rescuers become the second casualty. Current takes any path it is offered, and a hand on an arm is a path. Before anything else, establish that the person is no longer part of a live circuit.

For domestic electricity, cut the supply. Pull the plug, switch off at the socket, or trip the consumer unit — the main switch or the relevant breaker. This takes seconds and is always the right first move if the supply is reachable. If you genuinely cannot isolate it, stand on something dry and insulating and push them clear using something dry and non-conductive: a wooden broom handle, a plastic chair, a thick dry towel looped around a limb. Never use anything metal and never anything damp.

For high voltage — substations, railway lines, overhead cables, anything industrial — do none of that. High voltage arcs across air and energises the ground around a fallen conductor, so approaching at all can kill you through your feet before you touch anything. Stay at least ten metres back, keep everyone else back, and call emergency services and the utility. Only they can confirm the line is dead. If a vehicle is in contact with a line, tell the occupants to stay inside; they are safest where they are.

Water conducts, so never use it near a live source and be aware that a wet floor extends the hazard well beyond the appliance.

Only once the source is isolated or the person is clear does normal first aid begin. That sequence — isolate, then treat — is the whole of what makes electrical incidents different from every other kind, and the delay it costs is measured in seconds.

sections.heading: What the current does that you cannot see
sections.body:
Electrical injury is deceptive because the visible damage is often trivial and the dangerous damage is internal. Current entering at a hand and leaving at a foot travels through everything between, and the tissue it passes through — muscle, nerve, blood vessel, heart — takes the injury while the skin shows two small marks.

The most immediate danger is to the heart. Current across the chest can throw the heart into a disorganised rhythm that pumps no blood, which is cardiac arrest, and this can happen at domestic voltages. Alternating current is particularly effective at causing it, which is why household shocks are not automatically minor.

Alternating current also causes sustained muscle contraction, which is why people cannot let go of what is shocking them — the muscles that close the hand are stronger than those that open it, so the grip tightens. The same tetany can stop the muscles of breathing. This is why the duration of contact matters so much and why isolating the supply quickly changes outcomes.

Burns occur at the entry and exit points and along the path. Deep tissue can be cooked while the skin above it looks almost normal, and the muscle breakdown that follows can damage the kidneys over the following days. This delayed injury is the reason a hospital wants to see people who appear well.

Finally, the shock itself frequently causes a fall — off a ladder, off a roof, off a chair — so treat the mechanical injury as seriously as the electrical one, including possible spinal injury.

Lightning is a special case: it is a massive, very brief direct current that more often causes cardiac arrest and neurological injury than deep burns. Someone struck by lightning carries no charge and is completely safe to touch.

sections.heading: Treating them once it is safe
sections.body:
Check whether they are responsive and breathing normally. If they are not, this is cardiac arrest: call emergency services, start chest compressions, and use a defibrillator as soon as one is available. Electrical cardiac arrest responds well to defibrillation and resuscitation is worth continuing — outcomes after electrocution and lightning strike are notably better than for many other causes, and people have recovered fully after prolonged resuscitation.

If several people are down after a lightning strike, reverse the usual triage: attend first to those who appear dead. Those who are moving and breathing will usually keep breathing; those in arrest are the ones a few minutes of your attention can save.

If they are breathing and responsive, sit or lie them down and keep them still. Do not let them walk it off or drive.

Treat burns by cooling with clean cool running water — the same as any burn — but do not delay other care to do it, and do not immerse someone who is cold or shocked. Cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy dressing or cling film. Remember to look for the exit wound, which is often on a foot and often missed.

Immobilise and support anything that looks broken, and treat any fall as a potential spinal injury.

Keep them warm and monitor them continuously until help arrives, because rhythm disturbances can appear some time after the shock. If they deteriorate, be ready to start resuscitation.

sections.heading: When a shock needs a hospital
sections.body:
Call emergency services for any of the following, and treat 'they seem fine' as irrelevant to the decision.

Any high-voltage shock, any industrial or overhead-line contact, and any lightning strike, regardless of how well the person appears.

Any loss of consciousness, however brief, or any confusion afterwards.

Chest pain, palpitations, an irregular or racing pulse, or breathlessness at any point after the shock. These suggest the heart has been affected and warrant monitoring.

Any burn, however small, and particularly any burn where you can identify both an entry and an exit point — that pair tells you current crossed the body.

Numbness, tingling, weakness or paralysis, which suggest nerve injury.

Any shock that crossed the chest, such as hand to hand, or that involved a wet person or a wet environment, both of which increase current flow substantially.

Pregnancy, any known heart condition, or a pacemaker.

Any shock to a child, particularly a mouth injury from biting a cable, which can bleed seriously days later as the burn separates.

For a minor domestic shock in a healthy adult with no symptoms, no burn and no loss of consciousness — a brief tingle from a faulty appliance, say — a hospital visit may not be needed, but the appliance and the circuit certainly need attention before anyone uses them again. If in any doubt at all, seek advice: the assessment is quick, and the arrhythmias it looks for are not something you can rule out by feel.

sections.heading: Preventing the next one
sections.body:
Residual current devices are the single most effective protection against fatal electric shock in a home. An RCD or GFCI detects current leaking to earth — through a person, for example — and cuts the supply in tens of milliseconds, fast enough to prevent the heart rhythm disturbance that kills. Modern consumer units include them; older installations often do not, and plug-in versions are inexpensive. Test them with the test button periodically, because a device that has failed silently protects nothing.

Treat water and electricity as incompatible, without exception. No mains appliances within reach of a bath or shower, no extension leads outdoors in the wet, no handling plugs with wet hands. Outdoor and bathroom circuits should be on an RCD.

Retire damaged equipment rather than nursing it. Frayed flex, cracked plugs, scorch marks, a socket that is warm to the touch or a breaker that trips repeatedly are all faults asking for attention. A breaker that keeps tripping is doing its job and telling you something.

Do not overload sockets with stacked adaptors, and unroll extension reels fully before drawing significant current through them — a coiled reel can overheat badly.
