Know where your consumer unit is and which switch kills everything, and make sure everyone in the house knows too. In an emergency this is the difference between seconds and minutes.

Before drilling or cutting into a wall, check for buried cables with a detector, and know that cables usually run vertically or horizontally from sockets and switches.

Leave anything beyond replacing a fitting to a qualified electrician, and be particularly wary of second-hand and uncertified imported chargers and adaptors, which are a recurring source of both shocks and fires.

guides.title: Heat Stroke and Heat Illness: Cooling Comes First
guides.summary: The difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke, why confusion is the sign that changes everything, how to cool someone properly and fast, and why for heat stroke you cool first and transport second.
guides.safetyNote: Confusion, aggression, slurred speech, collapse or seizure in someone who is hot is heat stroke until proven otherwise: call emergency services and start cooling immediately. Never give fluids by mouth to anyone who is not fully alert. Paracetamol and ibuprofen do not treat heat stroke. This is written guidance, not training and not medical advice.

sections.heading: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are not the same thing
sections.body:
Heat illness is a spectrum, and knowing where someone sits on it decides everything you do next.

Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms, usually in the legs or abdomen, during or after exertion in the heat. They are unpleasant and not dangerous. Rest somewhere cool, sip fluids containing some salt, and stretch gently.

Heat exhaustion is the body struggling but still coping. The person is hot, heavily sweating, pale and clammy, with headache, nausea, dizziness, weakness, cramps and a fast weak pulse. They may feel faint on standing. Crucially, they are still mentally normal: they know where they are, they answer sensibly, they can follow what you say. Heat exhaustion responds well to rest, cooling and fluids, and most people recover within an hour.

Heat stroke is the body's temperature regulation failing outright, and it is a medical emergency with a real mortality rate. The distinguishing feature is not how hot the skin feels — it is the brain. Confusion, disorientation, slurred speech, staggering, uncharacteristic aggression, hallucination, seizure or collapse in someone who is hot means heat stroke, and it means calling for help and cooling them now.

The classic teaching that heat stroke means hot dry skin is unreliable and has cost lives. In exertional heat stroke — the kind that affects athletes, soldiers and labourers — the person is very often still pouring with sweat. Do not use sweating to rule it out. Use mental state.

The practical rule is simple. If they are hot and behaving normally, treat heat exhaustion and watch them closely, because it can progress. If they are hot and not behaving normally, treat heat stroke and call an ambulance.

sections.heading: Cooling, properly and fast
sections.body:
For heat stroke, cooling is the treatment, and how quickly the core temperature comes down is what determines the outcome. Every minute at a dangerously high temperature causes more organ damage, so cooling begins where you are, before and during transport, not on arrival at a hospital. This is the one emergency where 'cool first, transport second' is the accepted advice for exertional cases.

Get them out of the sun and out of the heat, into shade or an air-conditioned space. Remove excess and tight clothing, and any protective equipment.

The most effective method by a wide margin is cold-water immersion: a tub, a paddling pool, a stock trough, a cold bath, anything that gets the body into cold water while someone supports the head to keep the airway clear. If immersion is not possible, wet the skin continuously and fan hard — evaporation is the next best thing, and continuous dousing with cool water plus vigorous fanning works well. Ice packs or cold wet cloths at the neck, armpits and groin add to this because large blood vessels run close to the surface there, but on their own they are not enough.

Cold water does cause shivering, and shivering generates heat, but the net cooling still strongly favours immersion; do not abandon effective cooling because of it.

Keep cooling until they are clearly improving or help arrives. If a thermometer is available and someone knows how to use it, stop active cooling around 38-39C to avoid overshooting; without one, look for the mental state clearing.

For heat exhaustion the same measures apply less aggressively: shade, loosened clothing, lying down with the legs raised, cool wet cloths, and sips of fluid.

Paracetamol and ibuprofen do not lower temperature in heat stroke, because this is not fever — the thermostat has not been reset, it has been overwhelmed. Do not give them.

sections.heading: Fluids, and when not to give them
sections.body:
Someone with heat exhaustion who is fully alert should drink. Cool water is fine; drinks containing some sodium are better after heavy sweating, because sweat loses salt as well as water and replacing water alone can dilute the blood's sodium dangerously. A commercial oral rehydration solution or sports drink works, as does water taken alongside a salty snack. Sip steadily rather than gulping, which tends to cause vomiting.

Do not give anything by mouth to someone who is confused, drowsy, vomiting repeatedly, or having a seizure. They cannot protect their airway and the fluid goes into the lungs. This applies to every case of suspected heat stroke, and it is the most important restriction on this page. They need intravenous fluids, which means they need an ambulance.

Avoid alcohol, which worsens dehydration, and be cautious with very cold drinks taken quickly, which can provoke vomiting.

It is worth knowing that over-drinking plain water during prolonged exertion causes its own emergency: exercise-associated hyponatraemia, where blood sodium falls far enough to cause confusion, seizures and death. Confusingly, its early symptoms — headache, nausea, confusion — resemble heat illness. The distinguishing clue is usually the history: someone who has been drinking large volumes of plain water, has not lost weight over a long event, and may be puffy rather than obviously dehydrated. If that picture fits, do not push more water; get medical help.

For most people in most situations the practical guidance is unglamorous: drink to thirst, include salt if you are sweating hard for hours, and do not force fluids far beyond what you want.

sections.heading: Who is at risk, and the ones people forget
sections.body:
Risk is not evenly distributed, and the people most likely to die of heat are often the least likely to be exercising.

Older adults are especially vulnerable: the thirst sensation blunts with age, sweating becomes less effective, and many common medications — diuretics, beta blockers, anticholinergics, some antidepressants and antipsychotics — impair either sweating or the cardiovascular response to heat. Most heatwave deaths are older people indoors, not athletes outdoors.

Infants and young children have a high surface-area-to-mass ratio, cannot remove their own clothing, cannot get themselves a drink, and cannot tell you what is wrong.

A car in the sun is the single most lethal ordinary object in this topic. Interior temperatures rise dramatically within minutes, cracking a window makes very little difference, and children and dogs die in vehicles every summer. Never leave either in a parked car, however brief the errand and however mild the day feels.

People working or exercising in heat — construction, agriculture, kitchens, sport, military training — are at risk of exertional heat stroke even when young and fit, especially in the first days of a hot spell before acclimatisation develops, and especially in protective clothing that prevents evaporation.

Anyone with heart, lung or kidney disease, diabetes, obesity, a recent illness with fever or diarrhoea, or a previous episode of heat illness carries extra risk, as does anyone who has been drinking alcohol or using stimulants.

Humidity matters as much as temperature. Sweat cools by evaporating, and in humid air it cannot evaporate — which is why a humid thirty degrees is more dangerous than a dry thirty-five, and why the combined wet-bulb measure is the one that describes real risk.

sections.heading: Staying ahead of the heat
sections.body:
Acclimatisation is real, effective and takes about one to two weeks of progressively longer exposure. Most exertional heat illness happens in the first few days of hot weather or on the first days of a new job or trip, before adaptation has developed. Build up gradually rather than going hard on day one.

Shift the timing of anything strenuous to early morning or evening, and take deliberate breaks in shade rather than waiting until you feel you need one. In work settings, structured work-rest cycles prevent far more heat illness than any amount of individual toughness.

Dress for evaporation: loose, light-coloured, breathable clothing, and a wide brim for the head and neck. Wetting a shirt or a neck cloth is a cheap and genuinely effective cooling measure in dry heat.

Watch each other. Confusion is invisible from the inside, and the person developing heat stroke is the last to recognise it. Working in pairs with an explicit agreement to call it on each other is the most reliable safeguard there is.

At home during a heatwave, close curtains and windows during the hottest part of the day and open up at night if it is cooler outside. Use fans below about thirty-five degrees, where moving air still helps evaporation; above that, fans blowing hot air over skin can make matters worse unless the skin is also wet. A cool shower, wet cloths on the neck and wrists, and a cool room to retreat to are more effective than most people expect.

Check on elderly neighbours and relatives, daily, in person if you can. That single habit — someone knocking on the door — prevents more heatwave deaths than any equipment.

guides.title: Getting Medical Care: What Doctors and Nurses Do, and When to See Them
guides.summary: How to actually use a health service: who does what — doctors, nurses, paramedics, pharmacists and allied professions — what a doctor's job really involves, when to seek help and how urgently, how a hospital emergency department or emergency room triages, getting the most from a short appointment, how diagnoses are made and what tests can and cannot tell you, prescriptions, referrals and second opinions, consent and the right to refuse, your records, how health systems are paid for, and how to raise a concern.
guides.safetyNote: This guide is about navigating care, not about diagnosing or treating anything. It contains no doses and no diagnostic advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by a qualified clinician. If someone is seriously unwell or injured, call your emergency number now rather than reading.

sections.heading: Who Does What: Doctors, Nurses, Paramedics, Pharmacists and the Rest
sections.body: Health services are staffed by a large number of distinct professions, and knowing roughly who does what saves time, money and frustration — a great deal of what people describe as being sent from pillar to post is really a first approach to the wrong profession. Doctors are trained in diagnosis and in deciding treatment. Within medicine the largest division is between generalists, who see undifferentiated problems in whole people, and specialists, who see a narrow range in great depth. A junior doctor in a hospital is qualified and still training; a consultant or attending has completed specialist training and carries final responsibility for the patients under their name. Nurses deliver and manage the great majority of actual care, and the profession is far more layered than outsiders assume. Registered nurses assess, monitor, administer treatment and escalate. Specialist nurses run whole services — diabetes, stoma care, chemotherapy, heart failure — and often know their field better than any generalist doctor. Advanced practitioners and nurse practitioners can, in many systems, assess, diagnose and prescribe independently within their scope. Being seen by a nurse instead of a doctor is frequently the better appointment, not the consolation one. Paramedics and ambulance clinicians assess and treat at the scene and decide who needs transporting. Their judgement about whether someone can safely stay at home is a clinical decision, not a brush-off. Pharmacists know more about medicines than almost anyone else in the building. They check prescriptions for interactions and errors, advise on over-the-counter treatment, and in many systems can treat minor conditions directly. A pharmacist is the most under-used free source of medicines expertise available to most people. Beyond these sit physiotherapists, occupational therapists, dietitians, speech and language therapists, radiographers, biomedical scientists, psychologists, midwives, dentists, optometrists and podiatrists — each with their own training, registration and scope. Many can be approached directly without a referral, and which ones varies by country. Two practical points follow. First, ask who you are being booked in with and why; the answer is usually sensible and occasionally reveals a mistake. Second, everyone listed here is registered with a professional body, and registration can be checked publicly — which is the simplest defence against someone practising outside their competence or without qualification at all. Titles do not travel. A physician associate, a nurse practitioner, a consultant and an attending mean different things in different countries, and a role that requires a referral in one system is walk-in in another. Dentists, optometrists and pharmacists are the professions most often reachable directly, and in many places an optometrist is the fastest route to having sudden visual symptoms examined.

sections.heading: What a Doctor Actually Does, and Why Uncertainty Is Normal
sections.body: The popular picture of medicine is pattern recognition: the patient describes symptoms, the doctor identifies the disease, treatment follows. Real practice is closer to reasoning under uncertainty, and understanding that changes what a reasonable consultation looks like. A clinician takes a history, examines, and forms a differential diagnosis — a ranked list of what could plausibly explain the picture. The list is ordered by two things at once: what is most likely, and what would be most dangerous to miss. Those are different questions, and a great deal of medical behaviour that looks excessive to patients is driven by the second. Chest pain that is almost certainly muscular still gets investigated for the heart, because being right ninety-nine times does not help the hundredth person. From there the clinician either treats, tests, or waits. Waiting is a legitimate and underrated option, usually called watchful waiting or safety-netting: many conditions declare themselves within days, treating everything immediately causes its own harm, and the correct instruction is to come back if specific things happen. If you are told to wait, the important part of the conversation is what exactly should bring you back — and it is worth asking if you are not told. Doctors also spend a surprising proportion of their time on things that are not diagnosis: managing long-term conditions, adjusting medication, coordinating other services, completing paperwork that unlocks benefits and adjustments, and having conversations about deterioration and death. The uncomfortable part, and the part worth internalising, is that medicine is probabilistic. A diagnosis is a best explanation, not a certainty; treatments have expected benefits and real risks; and a good outcome does not prove the decision was right, nor a bad one that it was wrong. A clinician who says they are not sure and explains what would change their mind is demonstrating competence, not failing at it. That is also why second opinions are normal rather than insulting, and why guidelines exist: they encode what large numbers of studied patients suggest is the best default, which an individual clinician then applies — or departs from with a reason — to the person in front of them. A common and underrated tool is the time-limited trial: try a treatment for a defined period, agree in advance what improvement would look like, and review. That converts an uncertain diagnosis into a test, and it is why being asked to come back in three weeks is often the plan rather than a delay in producing one. Agreeing the review date before you leave is what stops the trial running for a year.

sections.heading: Primary Care and the Generalist's Job
sections.body: Primary care is the first point of contact with a health service: a general practitioner or family doctor, a community clinic, or in some systems a nurse-led service. It handles the overwhelming majority of all healthcare and it is, contrary to its reputation, the hardest branch of medicine. The difficulty is undifferentiated presentation. A specialist sees patients already filtered — the cardiologist's clinic contains people someone else has decided probably have a heart problem. The generalist sees a person with tiredness, and must distinguish, in ten minutes, between overwork, depression, anaemia, thyroid disease, sleep apnoea, diabetes, coeliac disease and cancer, in a population where the great majority genuinely do have something minor. That is why a generalist works differently. They rely heavily on knowing the person over time — a change from someone's baseline is far more informative than any single reading. They use time itself as a diagnostic tool. They tolerate a degree of uncertainty deliberately, because investigating everything would harm more people than it helped through false positives, incidental findings and the anxiety both produce. Continuity matters more than most people realise. Seeing the same clinician repeatedly produces better outcomes, because they are comparing you against yourself rather than against a textbook. Where a system allows you to request a particular clinician, doing so for anything ongoing is worth the wait. Primary care is also the gateway to the rest of the system in most countries: referrals to specialists, access to imaging, prescriptions, and the paperwork behind sick leave, benefits and workplace adjustment all pass through it. That gatekeeping is unpopular and it exists for a reason — unfiltered access to specialists produces worse outcomes and higher costs, because most people presenting to the wrong specialist get investigated for the wrong thing. Practically: register with a practice before you need one, use the same one consistently, keep your contact details current, and find out how it actually works — many now triage by online form or telephone first, and knowing that in advance is the difference between being seen today and being told to try again tomorrow. Out-of-hours cover is provided differently everywhere — a rota, a separate service, a telephone line — and finding out how yours works before a Friday evening is worth ten minutes. If you cannot get an appointment at all, the routes that usually exist are a telephone triage slot, a pharmacist for anything minor, and asking to be added to a cancellation list. Say plainly if something is getting worse; that changes how a request is prioritised, and receptionists are usually trained to ask.

sections.heading: When to Seek Help, and How Urgently
sections.body: The commonest question people actually have is not what is wrong but whether this warrants bothering anyone. Most health systems provide graded routes, and matching the route to the problem is the single most useful skill a patient can have. Emergency services — the ambulance number — are for immediate threat to life: unconsciousness, not breathing or struggling to breathe, choking, severe bleeding that will not stop, signs of stroke, signs of a heart attack, a seizure that will not stop or in someone with no history of them, severe allergic reaction, serious injury, or a baby or child who is floppy, blue, or will not wake. This library holds separate guides on each of those; the point here is that these are the situations where you do not wait, do not drive yourself, and do not seek a second view first. Urgent care sits below that: problems that need attention within hours but are not immediately life-threatening. Suspected fractures, wounds that may need closing, a fever in a very young infant, severe pain, a rapidly worsening infection. Many systems provide a telephone or online triage service specifically for deciding this, and using it is not an imposition — it is what it is for. Routine care covers everything else: something that has persisted, something new that is not alarming, medication reviews, screening, monitoring of a long-term condition. Waiting a few days for the right appointment is usually better than an urgent slot with someone who does not know you. Pharmacies handle a large slice of minor illness directly and immediately, with no appointment. Certain things justify seeking help sooner regardless of how well you feel otherwise: unexplained weight loss, a lump that is new or changing, bleeding from anywhere it should not come from, a mole that changes, a cough lasting more than a few weeks, difficulty swallowing, or any symptom that is persistent, progressive and unexplained. These are the recognised patterns behind most delayed diagnoses, and none of them is a reason to panic — only a reason to be seen rather than to watch for another month. ⚠️ If you are genuinely unsure how urgent something is, that uncertainty is itself the reason to use a triage line. Deciding is their job, not yours. Advice given at one moment applies to that moment. If you were told to wait and things then change — new symptoms, faster deterioration, a fever that will not settle — that is a new situation and calling back is expected rather than a nuisance. Say what has changed since you last spoke.

sections.heading: Emergency Departments and the Emergency Room: Triage, Waiting, and What They Are For
sections.body: An emergency department exists to identify and stabilise people who are seriously ill or injured. It is not a walk-in clinic that happens to be open late, and almost every frustration people have with one comes from that mismatch. On arrival you are triaged — assessed briefly and assigned a priority. Triage is deliberately not first-come-first-served, and it is not a queue at all in the ordinary sense. Someone who arrives after you and is seen before you has been judged more likely to deteriorate. That is the system working correctly, and it is worth knowing in advance because the experience of watching it happen without understanding it is corrosive. Waits are therefore long for anything not urgent, and the wait is not a punishment. It is also not a reason to leave: people who leave before being seen include a meaningful number who turn out to have needed to stay, and if you do decide to go, telling someone matters so that your notes reflect it. What happens next is assessment, initial investigation, and a disposition decision: treat and discharge, admit, or refer to a specialty team. The department's job ends at stabilisation and direction, so being discharged with an outpatient appointment is a normal outcome rather than a brush-off. Equally, being kept for observation is not necessarily alarming — some conditions can only be distinguished by watching how they behave over hours. Bring what makes assessment faster: a list of your medicines and doses, your allergies, any relevant past conditions, and the name of your usual clinician or practice. If the patient is a child or someone who cannot speak for themselves, bring whoever knows their history. Photographs of medicine packets on a phone are an adequate substitute for a list. Two things worth saying plainly. First, if you are waiting and you get worse, tell the desk — the triage assessment was a snapshot and can be revised. Second, alternative routes exist for a reason: urgent care centres, minor injuries units, out-of-hours primary care, telephone triage and pharmacies between them handle a large fraction of what arrives in emergency departments, usually faster and with someone better matched to the problem. Call an ambulance rather than driving when the problem could deteriorate on the way: chest pain, breathing difficulty, stroke signs, seizures, or serious injury. Treatment frequently starts in the vehicle, and arriving by ambulance means arriving with an assessment already made. For a child, bring the parent-held record if your country issues one, and be ready to say weight, since almost every paediatric dose is calculated from it.

sections.heading: Getting the Most Out of a Short Appointment
sections.body: A typical consultation is ten to fifteen minutes and is the scarcest resource in the whole system. Preparation roughly doubles what comes out of it, and the preparation is not complicated. Before you go, write down three things: what has been happening and since when, what you are most worried about, and what you want out of the appointment. The middle one matters more than people expect. Clinicians are trained to ask about ideas, concerns and expectations, and a patient who volunteers "I am worried this is cancer" gets that addressed directly rather than being reassured about something else entirely. Describe the problem chronologically and concretely. When did it start, what makes it better or worse, has it changed, what have you already tried. Vague duration is the commonest missing piece — "a while" is not usable and "since about the middle of March" is. If several things are wrong, say so at the start and say which matters most, rather than raising the important one as you stand up. Bring the list of your current medicines, including anything bought over the counter and any supplements, since both interact with prescriptions. Bring readings if you have been asked to take any, in whatever form you recorded them. Ask, before you leave: what do you think this is, what happens next, what should make me come back sooner, and how will I get results. Those four questions close most of the gaps that lead to people returning confused a fortnight later. If a word is used you do not know, ask what it means — nobody minds, and misunderstanding a term is far more expensive than asking. Take someone with you for anything significant. A second person hears what you miss, remembers what you forget, and can prompt the question you meant to ask. Writing notes during the appointment is normal and welcomed, and in many places you may record it if you say that you are doing so. If you feel you were not listened to, say so at the time — "I do not think I have explained this well" is a sentence that resets a consultation without accusing anyone. If it still does not work, asking to see someone else is a normal request rather than a complaint. If you are not confident in the language being used, ask for an interpreter rather than bringing a relative to translate. Health services are generally obliged to provide one, family members soften bad news without meaning to, and a child should never be asked to interpret for a parent. The same applies to an advocate if you find appointments difficult to manage alone.

sections.heading: How a Diagnosis Is Made, and What Tests Can and Cannot Tell You
sections.body: Most diagnoses come from the history — what the patient says — with examination and tests confirming or excluding rather than revealing. That order surprises people, who often expect a scan to be the decisive step, and it explains why clinicians ask so many apparently irrelevant questions. Tests are chosen to answer a specific question, and this is the crux of what patients most often misunderstand about them. No test simply reports whether you are ill. Each has a sensitivity — how often it is positive when the condition is present — and a specificity — how often it is negative when it is absent. Both are less than perfect, which means false positives and false negatives are not failures but expected outcomes at a known rate. The consequence is that what a result means depends on how likely the condition was beforehand. The same positive result in someone with classic symptoms and in someone tested at random carries very different weight: in a low-risk person, most positives are false. This is why clinicians resist testing for things there is no reason to suspect, and why enthusiastic broad screening can generate more harm than benefit through investigation of findings that would never have mattered. Incidental findings are the related problem. Scan enough of anybody and something turns up — a cyst, a nodule, a shadow — most of which are harmless and none of which can be ignored once seen. Every test therefore has a cost beyond its price, and a clinician declining one may be protecting you rather than rationing. Reference ranges are also less absolute than they look. They are usually set so that the middle ninety-five per cent of a healthy population falls inside, which means one healthy person in twenty sits outside by definition. A result slightly outside the range, on its own, in someone well, is frequently nothing at all — and a trend over time is far more informative than any single figure. Practically: ask what question a test is meant to answer, when and how you will get the result, and what will happen either way. And follow up if a result does not arrive. Systems lose results, and no news is not reliably good news. Screening and diagnostic testing are different activities and are easy to confuse. Screening looks for disease in people with no symptoms, is offered to whole populations by age or risk, and is designed around the balance of benefit and harm across everyone invited. A diagnostic test asks a question about you specifically. Declining a screening invitation and declining an investigation of a symptom are therefore very different decisions.

sections.heading: Prescriptions, Pharmacists and Taking Medicines Properly
sections.body: A prescription is an instruction with more parts than most people read: the drug, the dose, how often, by what route, for how long, and any conditions. Errors happen at every step of that chain, and a patient who understands the parts is the last and often most effective check. When a medicine is prescribed, four questions are worth asking. What is it for, in plain terms. How and when to take it, including whether food matters. What side effects are common, and which ones mean stop and seek advice. And how long to take it — whether this is a course to be finished, a trial to be reviewed, or something ongoing. Pharmacists check every prescription against your other medicines for interactions and against the dose for errors, and they are the right person to ask about anything practical: whether a tablet can be split, what to do about a missed dose, whether an over-the-counter remedy is safe alongside your prescriptions. This advice is free and immediate and is enormously underused. Some general points hold widely. Antibiotic courses should be taken as prescribed rather than stopped when you feel better. Medicines for blood pressure, cholesterol and similar conditions usually treat something that has no symptoms, which makes them easy to stop taking and important not to. Anything that suppresses a symptom without addressing a cause is worth reviewing rather than continuing indefinitely. And stopping some medicines abruptly is itself dangerous, so a decision to come off something is a conversation, not a unilateral act. Keep one current list of everything you take, including over-the-counter medicines, supplements and herbal remedies, and bring it to every appointment. Interactions with supplements are real and are missed constantly because people do not think of them as medicines. Repeat prescriptions accumulate. It is worth a periodic review — many services offer one formally — to ask of each item whether it is still needed, still working and still safe alongside the rest. Older patients in particular can end up on long lists where several items are treating side effects of others, and reducing that safely is a recognised piece of clinical work rather than a favour. ⚠️ Never take a medicine prescribed for someone else, and never adjust a dose yourself on the basis of how you feel without asking. Generic and branded medicines contain the same active ingredient to the same standard, and the generic is usually far cheaper; the exceptions, where switching genuinely matters, are few and your prescriber will know them. If a medicine looks different from last time, that is normally a change of manufacturer rather than an error, and the pharmacist can confirm it in seconds.

sections.heading: Referrals, Specialists, Waiting Lists and Second Opinions
sections.body: A referral is a request from one clinician to another, usually from a generalist to a specialist, and how it works determines a great deal of what patients experience as delay. Referrals are typically graded. Urgent or fast-track pathways exist for suspected serious disease and carry target times measured in days or a small number of weeks. Routine referrals join a waiting list whose length depends on the specialty and the system. Some referrals are for advice rather than an appointment, where a specialist answers a question by letter and the generalist continues to manage the problem — which is faster and just as good for many questions. Understanding what a referral is for helps. A specialist opinion is not the same as ongoing specialist care; many patients are seen once, given a plan, and returned to primary care to run it. That discharge is not abandonment, and the plan is the valuable part. Waiting lists are the standard failure point. Things worth doing: confirm the referral was actually sent, ask roughly how long the wait is, ask what to do if things get worse while waiting, and ask whether you can be added to a short-notice cancellation list. If you move or change contact details, tell them — a large proportion of lost appointments are lost this way. Second opinions are a normal part of medicine, particularly before major surgery, for a serious diagnosis, or where a proposed treatment carries substantial risk. Asking for one is not an accusation and most clinicians arrange them without difficulty; a clinician who reacts badly to the request has told you something useful. Bring the existing records and test results, so the second opinion is genuinely a second reading rather than a repeat of everything. Where systems mix public and private provision, the practical differences are usually speed and choice of clinician rather than the quality of the medicine, and the same consultants frequently work in both. The important questions are whether follow-up and any complications are covered, and whether records will flow back to your usual clinician — a private episode that leaves no trace in your main record is a genuine safety problem later. Prepare for a specialist appointment as you would for any other, with one addition: bring the history of what has already been tried and what happened, since the specialist may be seeing you cold. If a referral is refused, ask why in writing — the reason is often a missing test or a criterion not yet met, both of which are fixable, rather than a judgement that nothing is wrong.

sections.heading: Consent, Capacity and the Right to Refuse
sections.body: No one may examine, test or treat an adult without consent, except in narrow, defined circumstances. This is a legal rule in essentially every jurisdiction with a functioning health system, and it is also the foundation of the relationship. Consent must be informed, which means more than signing. You are entitled to know what is proposed, why, what it involves, what the material risks and benefits are, what the alternatives are — including doing nothing — and what is likely to happen without it. Modern standards ask what a reasonable person in your position would want to know, not what a clinician thinks you need to know, which is a real shift from older practice. Consent must also be voluntary, and it can be withdrawn at any point, including partway through a procedure where that is safely possible. A signature is evidence of a conversation rather than a contract you are bound by. An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, for any reason or none, even where refusal will cause serious harm or death. That right is not conditional on the clinician agreeing the decision is sensible. Capacity is decision-specific and is presumed unless there is reason to doubt it: the question is whether the person can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough to decide, weigh it, and communicate a choice. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity, and that principle is stated explicitly in most capacity legislation. Where someone lacks capacity, decisions are made in their best interests, taking account of their known wishes, values and beliefs, and consulting those close to them. Many systems allow people to plan ahead — an advance decision refusing specified treatment, or the appointment of someone with legal authority to decide on their behalf. Both are worth putting in place while well, and both are useless if nobody knows they exist. Children are handled differently by jurisdiction, generally with parental consent until an age or a demonstrated maturity at which the young person decides for themselves. The narrow exceptions are emergencies where the patient cannot consent and treatment cannot wait, and certain public-health and mental-health powers defined by statute. These are limited on purpose, and being told that one applies is something you are entitled to have explained. You are entitled to a chaperone for any intimate examination, whoever is conducting it, and asking for one is routine rather than an accusation. You may also ask for a clinician of a particular sex where that matters to you; it cannot always be arranged immediately, but the request is a normal one and should be recorded.

sections.heading: Your Records, Results and How to See Them
sections.body: Your medical record belongs to the health service that holds it, but the information in it is yours, and you have a right of access in essentially every jurisdiction with data-protection law. The record contains consultation notes, test results, letters between clinicians, prescriptions, imaging reports and often the images themselves. Increasingly it is available online without a request, and where it is, enabling that access is worth doing before you need it — reading the letter a specialist wrote about you frequently answers questions you left the appointment still holding. Where online access is not available, a written request obliges the holder to provide a copy within a statutory period, usually free of charge, with narrow grounds for withholding — chiefly serious harm to the patient or information about a third party. Records contain errors, and they propagate. A wrong allergy, a condition someone recorded and later disproved, an incorrect medicine, a duplicated entry — each of these will be read as fact by every clinician who sees the record afterwards. You are entitled to have factual inaccuracies corrected. You cannot delete a clinical opinion you disagree with, but you can have your disagreement recorded alongside it, which is often the more useful outcome. The single most valuable thing you can hold is a current one-page summary: your diagnoses, your medicines and doses, your allergies and what happens with each, your significant past procedures, and your emergency contacts. Kept on paper in a wallet and as a photograph on a phone, it converts the worst moment to explain your history into a moment where you do not have to. Results deserve their own habit. Ask when and how you will be told, and if the date passes, chase. Systems lose results, letters go to old addresses, and abnormal findings occasionally sit unread. No news is not reliably good news, and asking is neither rude nor paranoid. Confidentiality is the default and is strong, with defined exceptions: your consent, a court order, a legal duty to report certain infections, and a serious risk to the patient or to others. If you want information shared with a family member, say so explicitly and have it recorded — clinicians are often unable to discuss anything otherwise, however obviously well-intentioned the caller. If someone helps manage your care, most systems allow proxy access so that a named relative or carer can see records and book appointments on your behalf. It has to be set up in advance and with your consent, which is precisely why it is worth doing while everything is calm rather than during the week you need it.

sections.heading: How Health Systems Are Paid For, and Why That Changes What You Get
sections.body: Every country funds healthcare somehow, and the method shapes what a patient experiences far more than the medicine does. Broadly there are four models, and most real systems mix them. Tax-funded services provide care free or nearly free at the point of use, funded from general taxation, with access governed by clinical need and managed through waiting lists and gatekeeping. Social insurance systems require contributions to a fund or funds that pay providers, usually with broad coverage, more choice, and some co-payment. Private insurance systems make coverage a product, producing rapid access for the insured and gaps for everyone else. Out-of-pocket payment, still dominant in much of the world, means treatment is bought when needed, which is the arrangement most likely to bankrupt a family. The trade-offs are consistent. Where care is free at the point of use, the rationing shows up as waiting and as gatekeeping. Where it is bought, the rationing shows up as cost and as coverage exclusions, and access is faster for those who can pay. Neither eliminates rationing, because no system has infinite capacity; they differ in whether the limit appears as time or as money and in who bears it. Practical consequences worth knowing wherever you are. Find out what you are actually entitled to and what is excluded, because both surprise people at the worst moment. Understand referral rules — insurance often requires a referral and refuses claims without one. Check whether a provider is inside your scheme before treatment rather than after; surprise billing from an out-of-network clinician working inside an in-network hospital is a well-documented trap. Ask for costs in advance where you are paying, and ask what happens if a complication needs more treatment. Travel deserves specific mention. Emergency treatment abroad may or may not be covered by your domestic arrangements, reciprocal agreements between countries vary and change, and travel insurance frequently excludes pre-existing conditions unless declared. Repatriation is the expensive part and is what insurance is actually for. None of this is medicine, and all of it determines whether medicine reaches you — which is why it belongs beside the clinical guides rather than in a separate world. Charges frequently come with exemptions that go unclaimed — by age, income, pregnancy, or a listed long-term condition — and prepayment arrangements often cost less than a few individual charges. Ask; the categories are rarely advertised. Where you are choosing insurance, the questions that matter are the annual limit, what counts as pre-existing, whether chronic conditions are covered at all, and whether the policy pays for the complication as well as the procedure.

sections.heading: When Something Goes Wrong: Raising Concerns and Complaints
sections.body: Things go wrong in healthcare — errors, poor communication, delays, and outcomes that were nobody's fault. There is a graded set of routes for raising them, and using the right one at the right time makes a resolution far more likely. Start where it happened, and start early. Most problems are resolved by raising them with the person or team involved, or with whoever is in charge that day, while the situation is live and can still be changed. A large fraction of formal complaints describe something that could have been fixed in the moment had anyone been told. If that does not work, most organisations have a patient liaison or advocacy service whose whole job is to sort problems out informally, and a formal complaints procedure with a stated time limit for raising a complaint and for responding. Put it in writing, be specific about dates, people and events, state what outcome you are looking for, and keep a copy. The commonest requested outcomes are an explanation, an apology, and a change so it does not happen to someone else — and services respond better to those than to unfocused anger, which is not a moral point but a practical one. If the response is inadequate, an independent body normally sits above the organisation: a health ombudsman, a regulator, or a statutory review process. These bodies usually require you to have gone through the local procedure first, which is why skipping stages costs time rather than saving it. Concerns about an individual clinician's fitness to practise go to their professional regulator, which is a separate route from a complaint about care and has a different purpose — it protects the public rather than compensating you. Legal claims are a distinct thing again, requiring proof that care fell below a reasonable standard and that this caused harm. They are slow, adversarial and subject to strict time limits, and they are not the route to an explanation or an apology, which is what most people say they wanted. ⚠️ Raising a concern must not affect your care, and in most systems that protection is explicit. If you believe it has, that is itself a serious matter to escalate. And where you think someone is at immediate risk of harm, say so at once to whoever is senior and present rather than starting a process — urgency and procedure are different problems. Keep your own notes as you go: dates, names, what was said, what you were told would happen. Nobody does this while things are going well, and everybody wishes they had once a process starts.
